comment: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notice titled "Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information" and published in the Federal Register of April 4, 2019. The notice proposes changes to the Safeguards Rule that implements the Gramm-Bliley-Leach Act (the Act), The FTC majority stated in the notice (84 Fed. Reg. at 13170, col. 3) in reference to proposed 16 CFR 314.6: "This proposed section is intended to reduce the burden on smaller financial institutions." The two-member minority stated in dissent (84 Fed. Reg. 13177, col. 2): "The expansion of the Rule could create traps for the unwary, especially small and innovative businesses. Further, large incumbents can often absorb regulatory compliance costs more effectively than new entrants or smaller players, potentially decreasing competition." Thus, all FTC members agreed on the importance of not imposing undue burdens on small businesses. In this context, the proposed 16 CFR 314.6 intended to protect small businesses from undue burdens under the Safeguards Rule, I believe that the proposal in fact doesnt achieve the objective. As the proposed 16 CFR 314.6 exempts a financial institution that maintains "customer information concerning fewer than five thousand consumers" from some obligations to document its risk assessment, documenting the risk response plan, regularly update their assessment of risks, and exemption from having its CISO chief information security officer report yearly to the governing body. The proposal assumes that the only burden on a small business is because of the written reports and several assessments, but in fact, the rule imposes many burdens that do not take into account the size of small businesses. Also, the rule considered the number of consumers that the institution has to hold their information is dependent upon the size of the business and in fact, it does not. Accordingly, it is recommended to relate the number of employees/officers working in each institution with the administrative burdens imposed by the new rule.

This is highway robbery! Transporting sick patients to JCMC that need attention RIGHT NOW is unacceptable. I live in Hawkins County, way out in the county, and it is very concerning for me that if my family needed emergency services that we would have to travel to JC for care. The golden hour is gone by the time EMS gets to my residence and then back out to the main roads. And heaven forbid there be a slow down on I-26 because that could cost a life! And in this scenario it could be the life of one of my children. And I'm not ok with this!!!! To whoever reads these comments and makes decisions for this COPA, please take all of these things into consideration. There are so many stories out there that are concerning. How would you feel if it was your family fighting for their life in a Ballad facility right now? It's a scary thought!

comment: I despise Loot boxes, and to an extent other Microtransactions. I'm a strong supporter of getting what I pay for and knowing what that is, and all the loot boxes do is charge little money a pop for a chance to get what you want, just like slots and lottery tickets. It's the mentality of "just one more pack" to try to get what you want, until you have bought enough loot boxes to the point to where you bought the game twice. Before I had the passion about this, I would spend 25 dollars each Overwatch event to get at least some of the event skins because it's a chore to unlock normally. This is another concern. The game companies make Loot Boxes more enticing by slowing down rewards, thus the "You can unlock it in gsme" manipulation. If you don't buy, you either have a slow grind or one of those meters where you have to wait a certain time period. I don't particularly like that this is in every mobile game even if they are free, and I like it even less if it is in full price or payed games. Pay to win is the worst of it. When the best stuff is hidden in these loot boxes for an extremely low drop rate, it makes the game unfair to those who don't shovel money into the game, and it manipulates all players into purchasing this advantage. I think that these companies should be forced to offer their rewards through earning and not through luck, the earning should be reasonable, and if Microtransactions don't escape us, you should buy what you want and not submit to RNG. I don't know if it is on the plate, but DLC is another concern of mine, but this is a mixed bag. Some DLC is good, in the sense that the game becomes successful enough to offer unintended DLC, such as the original Battlefront 2 with it's original intentions to offer two playable heroes as DLC, Kit Fisto and Ventress, along with new maps. I don't care for DLC when it either takes content out of the previous game in the franchise and puts a price tag on it, or when the DLC is planned at day one, such as this new Mortal Kombat game with Shao Khan as pre order, and I think I saw that Shang Tsung is confirmed DLC before the game came out. I dought this is relevant to the discussion, but I wanted to address it later for future note. If you read this, thank you and I hope it helps.

Ignorant or complicit about these considerations, Consumer protection agencies remain silent allowing consumers to be duped in a complex and rigged game that has few rules and minor repercussions for bad actors. Undefined, undisclosed rules regarding which history reports or parts of them will be saved or omitted should not be left up to the reporting agencies alone.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry in Carthage, MS. For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will affect my small town practice in a very negative way. It will also cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: -Merit Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Special Considerations for Small Practices: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) developed the framework for MIPS acknowledging the regulatory burden that health care providers already are facing. Considering that reality, CMS reduced the number of clinicians that are required to participate. CMS supported this effort out of the agencys desire to give physicians more time with their patients, not computers. Additionally, CMS is mindful of the unique challenges that face smaller physician practices and added new bonus points for clinicians caring for patients in those settings. -Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients. -Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA): Currently, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is considering eliminating or modifying the requirement for covered health care providers to make a good faith effort to obtain individuals written acknowledgment of receipt of providers Notice of Privacy Practices. The stated aim of this potential change is to reduce burden and free up resources for covered entities to devote to coordinated care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, FEW complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. Philip Marler, O.D.

comment: As a practicing ophthalmologist in the state of Ohio, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. The prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses. We are already going to great lengths to comply with the existing Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that I believe puts our patients at risk. While we appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule. Instead, focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration in this matter.

comment: I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. It is my opinion that this will be harmful to the doctor-patient relationship, and create unnecessary burdens in the practice of eye and vision care, therefore I urge you to NOT sign-on to a letter proposed by Attorneys General Miller, Peterson, Stein, and Reyes. I agree that it is important that consumers be given a genuine opportunity to exercise choice in the contact lens market. However, before one considers offering support for far reaching government regulations to be imposed on small businesses, its important to know the true state of the contact lens market as the market has changed tremendously since the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act was passed. o Lens prices are competitive: The AOA conducted a price comparison analysis in which they compared online retailer cost vs the average in-office cost to determine the dollar price difference and percent change in price for 81 different contact lenses. Of the 81 lenses studied, 28 were more expensive online, while 53 were more expensive in the doctors office. Across all lenses included in the AOAs price comparison analysis, there was an average price difference of just $0.32 o Patients Have More Retailer Options than Ever: The fastest growing distribution channel for contact lens sales in the USA was the online / Internet channel. In 2017, online retailers generated $786 million in salesgrowing by 4.9% during the 12 month ending period Dec17 and growing by 11.1% over the 24 monthending period Dec17. o There is Widespread Agreement that the Current Rule is Working: The CEO of 1-800-CONTACTS itself acknowledged that the current rule is working in a March 2018 FTC workshop noting, The FCLCA and CLR have succeeded in encouraging greater competition and choice in the contact lens marketplace. Consumers today have more choice and more convenience. The competitive benefits have gone beyond price. I think that the FTC can consider this a successful rule. Doctors of optometry are concerned with the FTCs claims regarding non-compliance of prescription release requirements. Despite disagreeing with the accusation regarding compliance, the profession has offered an alternative to the signed acknowledgement proposal put forward by the Commission. The proposal supported by optometry would require all contact lens prescribers to post signage in their offices notifying patients of their right to their contact lens prescription. This is a less burdensome and less intrusive approach than the proposal put forward by the FTC. This approach would also do more to broadly educate consumers. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. In all, through letters, direct exchanges during committee hearings and committee report language, more than 100 Members of Congress Republicans and Democrats -- have spoken out against the FTCs misguided approach to updating the contact lens rule and called on the agency to prioritize a crackdown on illegal device sales, including those being reported on by the national media -- https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/21/business/media/hubble-contact-lens.html. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. Mobile games are psychologically designed to prey on the few addicts who spend thousands of dollars on in game purchases, which include loot boxes. comment: The Federal Trade Commission has a duty to protect users of consumer products including contact lenses. The debate for freer disclosure of prescriber results of ocular exams which help consumer buy the product at a competitive price has been going on for several decades. It is always prudent that the disclosure statement is given to consumers through a duty of the prescriber to work in good faith and with complete candor. Some but not the majority of providers fail in this effort. It is a problematic situation since the FTC does not punish violators to a major extent rather it can issue cease and desist orders and argue investigative cases in federal and administrative courts. The proposal to allow several new areas of disclosure and transmission of information will lead to a quicker response to consumer requests, help relieve a paperwork burden through electronic transmission, allows for more sellers to participate due to availability of prescription criteria, and creates uniformity throughout the network. If there are bad actors working in this system, possibly the Commission could further educate consumers on how to file a complaint in writing, phone, e-mail, electronic means or through other prescribed avenues. Those that skirt the regulations will eventually be revealed through the complaint process and dealt with administratively. This proposal is it becomes effective would be consistent with the public interest and with the policies previously released by the agency. There is no doubt that the modified Contact Lens Rule should be embraced by prescribers, sellers and consumers as an improvement to consumer products trade rules.

comment: COPA legislation is simply a mechanism for large hospitals to engage in monopolistic activities free from FTC oversight in clear violation of consumer protection laws. Hospitals wishing to illegally merge often employ lobbyists that work to convince part-time state legislators of the merits of such legislation. These efforts are well funded and can rarely be opposed by the smaller businesses they will ultimately harm or consumers that will be negatively impacted as a result of the monopolies that COPA allows. Most state legislators have very little understanding of the nuances of healthcare insurance and reimbursement and can be easily cajoled into supporting COPA legislation when it is presented under the banner of well-known supposedly not-for-profit hospitals and seemingly admirable goals such as eliminating waste, clinical integration or saving a struggling hospital. Economic studies regarding the impact of hospital consolidations are unequivocal in their condemnation of the negative impact these mergers have on pricing, quality, new competition and consumer choice. COPA legislation is extremely difficult to enforce post-merger even if states have the resources to do so, which they do not. The impact that mergers have on the marketplace often takes years to be fully realized. By the time their impact is apparent to consumers and enforcement agencies, there is very little that enforcement can do to truly "put the cat back in the bag". Certain aspects of the ACA have made hospital consolidation more likely and consumer protection more difficult. The FTC should clearly define it's position with respect to certain provisions of the ACA that tend to inspire hospital mergers. The FTC should aggressively seek to limit the state's ability to circumvent consumer protection laws through strong federal enforcement. The FTC should study and publish definitive empirical market data regarding not just COPA... but also hospital consolidations more broadly. The FTC should proactively and vigorously oppose COPA legislation at the state level. The FTC should address the growing issue of hospital prices and their impact on mergers with independent physicians, competition and consumer pricing. The FTC should study the impact hospital mergers have on "quality" through a framework of measurable standard outcomes.

comment: Lee County is currently without a hospital. Ballad Health has told our county that they intend to re-open our hospital, initially as an Urgent Care Facility, hopefully in October 2019 with aspirations of opening an emergency department by late 2020. An urgent care center is a convenient option when someone's regular physician is on vacation or unable to offer a timely appointment. Or, when illness strikes outside of regular office hours. The difference between urgent care and emergency rooms is the severity of the health problem. If the condition is life-threatening, go to an emergency room. If the condition is a minor illness or injury, go to an urgent care. When questions are raised about the type of care and the concerns the citizens have regarding the current situation with Ballad facilities we have been not been given answers but have been told by Alan Levine, CEO of Ballad Health, to show some gratitude for the $20 million Ballad plans to invest in our County. Due to the fact that those who are over-seeing the COPA merger have stated that no grade can be given for the COPA and stating that it would take 3-5 years to know if it was working then the responsible action from the FTC is to extend the time for merging the remaining assets until it can be determined if this merger is actually a public advantage or a disadvantage which so many of the stories shared by those who have had experience with Ballad have clearly shown. My first experience with Ballad came when my daughter was advised by her OB/GYN at the Ballad Facility at Lonesome Pine Hospital in Big Stone Gap Virginia that they didnt know how long the OB department would be open at Lonesome Pine and then advised that the ultrasound equipment they had could not get a good reading of her babys heart or head and that she should transfer to an OB at another hospital or they would be forced to place her as high risk and transfer her themselves. She chose a physician in Kingsport for delivery at Holston Valley, partly because of the excellent Level I NICU facility available at Holston Valley should anything happen during delivery. She went into premature labor on April 9, 2019. She went into labor in Lee County and we left at 7:30 am to get her to the hospital and due to school and commuter traffic we didnt arrive until almost 10:00 am, at which time she was dilated to 4 cm and progressing rapidly. She required an emergency c-section to deliver her child as the umbilical cord was wrapped around his neck twice. Her son was born at 35 weeks and weighed 5lbs 3oz at birth. He was immediately taken to the NICU where he spent 9 days and received excellent care. A friend of mine told me that she had a premature delivery in March 2019 and was told that she would have to deliver at Bristol Regional or Johnson City Memorial because the NICU at Holston Valley was closed. Funny, at the time my grandson was in the NICU at Holston Valley all the beds were occupied and included a set of twins and a set of quads. The NICU at Holston Valley was renovated to a state of the art facility in 2016 and it has been in constant use providing excellent care since then. The NICU at Holston Valley should not be down-graded. This is the closest facility for the people that Ballad serves in southwest Virginia and it is already over an hour away, to have to add another 30 to 45 minutes to that distance is dangerous to mothers and babies. Our next experience with Ballad Health was on May 28, 2019. The following is a break down of events as they occurred at Holston Valley. On that date my daughter called her OB/GYN with complaints of nausea and severe pain in right lower abdomen and concern about incision. At 2:30 pm - Nurse at OB/GYN office advised that from description of symptoms that it could be appendix and it could be about to burst. Advised not to eat or drink anything as surgery could be needed. This experience took over 6 hours and is detailed in my attachment.

Data already shows this is not in the best interest of the public. Much of this information has been delivered to Washington through representatives opposing this COPA. comment: I am Wayne Baxter and am a Registered Nurse and a Paramedic. I am a pediatric and adult Emergency Room Nurse, a pediatric transport nurse, and was the EMS Director in Loudon County, Tennessee. I am here to oppose the downgrading of Holston Valley Medical Center to a level 3 trauma center. In section 4.03(c)(ii)COPA, it states that the Department of Health pre-approved consolidation of Level 1 Trauma Centers, and while this was pre-approved, but preapproval does not mean downgrading, nor does it specify what is consolidated. Ballads plan in the COPA is vague but, now that we have found out what the actual plan is, the effects are publicly disadvantageous and dangerous to peoples lives. The State of Tennessee statistics on Trauma patients shows the absolute need to keep the Level 1 trauma services at Holston Valley Medical Center. The data I received from the Tennessee Injury Surveillance and Hospital Discharge Data System does not include citizens of Kentucky or Virginia. In 2016, Holston Valley received 1049 Level 1 and 2 trauma patients; Bristol received 393 Level 2 trauma patients. This total combined of ONLY Tennessee residents is 1,442. 61% of these patients came from Sullivan County. 43% of all TENNESSEE Trauma patients go to Holston Valley; this does not include the Virginia and Kentucky Trauma patients. Johnson City Medical Center received 1859 trauma patients. Of this, only 154 patients came from Sullivan County. (8%) This is only slightly above the 29 patients UT received in Knoxville from the Northeast Region. One large disaster at the major industries in Kingsport would quickly change these ratios. Senior citizens should be fighting to keep Holston Valley as a level 1 trauma center. 43% of all trauma patients were over 65 years of age. This compares to only 6% of trauma patients being 0-17 years of age. 32% of elderly trauma patients came from directly from Sullivan County leaving the other 68% originating in seven counties. My final comment is from my experience. I worked EMS since 1983 in various roles. I have visited both Holston Valley and Johnson City Medical Center, and from observing the infrastructure at both hospitals, I cannot fathom why Ballad believes it is better to keep Johnson City as a Level 1 and downgrade Holston Valley to level 3. The helipad at Johnson City is inadequate for a trauma center, and I believe the military aeromedical services would have a hard time landing on it. Holston Valley was purpose built to be a modern emergency department, and will not require any expenditure to rebuild. I want to thank you for recognizing that this venue is centrally located in Ballads Tennessee service area. Transportation issues are a large concern as well. Holston Valley is 6.2 mile to the I-81 corridor, nearest to the Hwy 11 corridor, and much of the I-26 corridor. If anyone experienced the delays getting to Johnson City during the interstate repaving, they are fully aware that alternate routes to Johnson City Medical Center are inadequate. Holston Valley has multiple direct routes to the Emergency Department. Census records demonstrateHolston Valley is centrally located to a great majority of the Ballad Service area, where Johnson City will drop a majority of the service area out of the golden hour. Area EMS services are going to be negatively affected by Ballads plan. Transport times are going to increase, unnecessary use of aeromedical services are going to increase, and there will be no extra help to ride in with the EMS crew because it will remove other emergency providers from their county for too long. This does not include Ballads bizarre plan of transporting NICU babies all over creation and back. I believe that the State of Tennessee believed that Ballad would use common sense when they agreed to consolidate trauma centers and use Holston Valley as the primary center with Johnson City and Bristol as backup as Level 2 and 3 respectively. Do not allow a vague sentence in a poorly worded COPA agreement destroy the chance anyone has of surviving a major trauma. The nurses are demoralized and concerned about their jobs. Ballad health has cut their pay, they have no recourse, are scared for their jobs, and if they could leave the area they could. Ballad has been financially damaging to much of the staff, shift differential pay decreased from $3.45 an hour to 12% of base rate. Nurse pay would have needed to reach $28.75 to meet this. The Ballad Health plan for the Holston Valley Trauma Center is bad for the patients, bad for the region, and bad for Tennessee, Virginia and Kentucky. Thank you. Wayne Baxter, BSN, RN/Paramedic Sweetwater, TN

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry in solo private practice in Honolulu, Hawaii. For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. Patients don't realize that soft or hard contacts can actually be harmful for their eyes and vision if they don't take the time to carefully try them out and then check if the vision and fit are acceptable. There is also a lot of NON-COMPLIANCE on the part of patients wearing their contacts until 'they don't feel comfortable.' It may be too late, they may already have a corneal ulcer or scarring if they are not careful. I wish the Federal government would not be continually more regulatory and make our paperwork requirements even worse. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: -Merit Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Special Considerations for Small Practices: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) developed the framework for MIPS acknowledging the regulatory burden that health care providers already are facing. Considering that reality, CMS reduced the number of clinicians that are required to participate. CMS supported this effort out of the agencys desire to give physicians more time with their patients, not computers. Additionally, CMS is mindful of the unique challenges that face smaller physician practices and added new bonus points for clinicians caring for patients in those settings. -Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients. -Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA): Currently, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is considering eliminating or modifying the requirement for covered health care providers to make a good faith effort to obtain individuals written acknowledgment of receipt of providers Notice of Privacy Practices. The stated aim of this potential change is to reduce burden and free up resources for covered entities to devote to coordinated care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. Eugene Young, O.D.

Loot boxes themselves has also brought the gaming industry which is supposed to bring entertainment to the people to its lowest point yet, as the game designers and publishers often set their games in a way that promotes loot boxes in their games in such a way that tries to maximize the chances of any player buying the said loot boxes, often at cost of the game itself, as they realize that there are more than enough people who are willing to waste enormous amount of money, often going into thousands, either because they are abusing their already existing gambling tendencies, or because the player is still an underage player who is attracted to the loot boxes far easily than an adult. There are far too many real problems that I could realistically voice in this comment, but I do believe that the customers and honest game developers who are interested in creating products for more than just abuse of gambling tendencies, young age of their customers or abuse of psychological factors in an individual which slowly over time make them more accustomed to the idea of loot boxes and in the end it will make the said customer crave the thrill of opening a loot boxes with a potential reward that he wishes to receive. It is a truly disgusting practice, not just because it abuses human nature to acquire something they want, but also because it decays the whole point of video games. In a video game that has been made with loot boxes in mind will always suffer in some way, as the designers or publisher made the game in such a way to make the players more willing to buy the loot boxes, which they wouldn't need in the first place if the loot boxes weren't implemented into the final product. This can be done through many means, be it through making it far harder for their customers to progress through the video game or by straight out offering ways to "cheat" the game which can be interesting for those with lacking knowledge about how things were in the past. I honestly wish, that the workshop will either lead to proper regulation of ALL loot boxes, on ALL platforms, be it a mobile game, console game, virtual reality game or a video game on desktop, and across ALL types of games and genres, be it a single-player video games, through MMOs and so on. Best regard and do the right thing!

comment: When a consumer purchases an item from a manufacturer, that item is no longer under the control of the manufacturer whatsoever. Private property rights are a cornerstone of our economy and laws, and the right to repair our own possessions is part of the definition of owning those possessions. As the purchases available from manufacturers are more complex today than in the past, the issue arises that the original manufacturer might be the only entity capable of performing necessary repairs on their products. While this may be true, manufacturers should not intentionally use their dominance in the market to prevent other entities from offering repairs to consumers under the guise of product quality while in reality the companies are concerned about their bottom lines. Allowing companies to control how their products are repaired would create opportunities for those companies to engage in anti-competitive practices by preventing third party repair services from offering an alternative to the demands of the manufacturer. Such practices are anti-consumer and damaging to the open market. In addition, by allowing companies to control both quality assurance on their products as well as their repairs, a conflict of interest is created where a company has an incentive to sell low quality, easy to damage products because such products would bring in revenue from repairs consumers cannot get anywhere else. Products purchased by a consumer belong to them and the right to repair those products as the owner sees fit is a cornerstone of private property. Any other approach to private property sets a dangerous precedent for the open market and our values as a nation.

comment: I recently attended the FTC workshop entitled A Health Check on COPAs held in Washington D.C. on June 18, 2019. My take aways from this workshop are as follows: There is no clear and convincing evidence that COPAs have succeeded in improving quality of care, access to services, or lowering patient costs That the creation of a health care monopoly, more often than not, is detrimental to the public it is supposed to serve That even where studies have been attempted to definitively define advantages vs. disadvantages, the data needed to make such determinations is often incomplete, unavailable, or deficient That once a COPA is granted it must forever require oversight to ensure that monopolistic practices do not disadvantage the public In the absence of oversight an unregulated monopoly results COPAs are risky adventures and should only be granted after extensive factual investigation has been conducted With regard to the Ballad Health COPA, panelist and Deputy Attorney General for the State of Tennessee, Janet Kleinfelter, stated unequivocally that after 16 months of operation the State was unable to determine if the COPA was working properly. She further stated that it may take 3, 4, or 5 years of operation before the state could adequately determine if the COPA was placing citizens at a disadvantage with regard to quality of care, access to care, and cost of services. In my judgment, this amounts to an admission that the State has created a health care monopoly that is out of control. The State has not done due diligence in having in place necessary controls and indices to effectively oversee the monopoly they have created. In other words, the State has failed to protect the public from what has become a coercive monopoly by Ballad Health. In my opinion, this amounts to regulatory negligence and warrants federal intervention by the FTC or DOJ to determine if federal antitrust laws have been violated.

comment: When the FTC initially proposed to mandate contact prescribers to obtain signed acknowledgement from consumers that they had received a contact prescription and had been notified they are free to purchase said contract from the seller of their choice, they did so to try and protect the consumer. The proposed modification still tries to accomplish this task, while providing multiple options to prescribers at the same time. This proposed rule allows prescribers the ability to mold the rule to best fit their practice, but still give the consumers the protection and the knowledge they need. Any objections based on added costs and time consumption in this part of the proposed rule are misguided, as added extra piece of paperwork and acknowledgement does not added significant costs or time with patients as noted in the general comments, especially for those keeping online records. The general purpose of the FTC is to protect consumers from unfair business practices by companies, and this proposed rule is guiding that protection. Based on evidence presented in the rule proposal, some consumers are not being presented with the option to retrieve their contacts from the seller of their choice or not being presented their prescriptions at all, which is a significant problem. If after 10+ years of regulation prescribers are still not fulfilling their duties at a 90% rate, there is a problem that needs to be fixed with regulation.

comment: To the Commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission: I write to urge the Commission, in the strongest possible terms, to pursue rulemaking and enforcement action that would make personalized pricing — the practice of charging different consumers different prices for identical goods or services based on data collected about them individually — unlawful in the United States. This practice is not a neutral pricing innovation. It is a systematic exploitation of the information asymmetry between firms and consumers, and it should be treated as an unfair and deceptive practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act. 1. Personalized pricing inverts the basic premise of a competitive market Markets are supposed to work because consumers can compare prices and firms compete for their business on a level playing field. Personalized pricing destroys that premise. When a firm knows a consumer's income bracket, browsing history, device type, location, purchase urgency, or even how long they hesitated before clicking "buy," it can calculate the maximum that specific individual will pay — and charge exactly that. This is not price discovery. It is the elimination of the consumer's ability to shop, compare, or negotiate in any meaningful sense, because the "market price" no longer exists as a stable, comparable reference point. Every consumer effectively faces a market of one, priced against them by an entity with vastly superior information. 2. It is built on nonconsensual surveillance Personalized pricing depends on extensive behavioral profiling: tracking cookies, device fingerprinting, purchase history, geolocation, and inferred demographic and psychographic data, frequently obtained and combined without consumers' meaningful knowledge or consent. Consumers do not expect — and did not agree — to have their willingness to pay algorithmically estimated and monetized. The Commission has long treated covert data practices that harm consumers as a core area of concern; personalized pricing should be recognized as one of the clearest cases where covert data collection translates directly into concrete financial injury. 3. It disproportionately harms the consumers least able to detect or resist it Evidence gathered by researchers and journalists has repeatedly shown that algorithmic pricing systems can charge more to consumers in lower-income ZIP codes, to consumers using older or lower-cost devices, to consumers with less time to shop around, and to consumers in areas with fewer retail alternatives. Far from personalization delivering better deals to price-sensitive shoppers, the incentive structure runs the other way: the algorithm's entire purpose is to find the highest price each individual will tolerate. This is regressive by design and falls hardest on people with the least market power. 4. Existing legal frameworks are inadequate to the scale of the practice The Robinson-Patman Act addresses price discrimination between business purchasers, not consumer-facing algorithmic pricing. State-level unfair-practices statutes are inconsistent and rarely equipped to address opaque, real-time algorithmic pricing at scale. Only the FTC, exercising its Section 5 authority over unfair and deceptive acts and practices, has both the jurisdiction and the technical capacity to address this as a nationwide practice. The Commission's own 2024 study on surveillance pricing confirmed that firms are actively developing and deploying these tools; the time for a study-only posture has passed. 5. Recommended Commission action I urge the Commission to: Issue a rule under Section 5 categorically prohibiting the use of individually-targeted, non-transparent price variation based on personal data unrelated to the actual cost of providing the good or service. Require disclosure at minimum, as an interim step, mandating that any price shown to a consumer that differs from a general list price due to personalized factors be conspicuously labeled as such, with an explanation of what data was used. Ban the use of protected or proxy-protected characteristics (race, income proxies, disability status, age, ZIP code as a proxy for demographic composition) in any pricing algorithm, full stop. Compel algorithmic transparency and audit rights, requiring firms deploying dynamic or personalized pricing systems to make them available for independent, ongoing regulatory audit. Impose meaningful penalties, including disgorgement of profits attributable to personalized pricing, sufficient to remove the financial incentive for noncompliance. Personalized pricing is not a minor pricing technique — it is a fundamental threat to the basic bargain of a fair marketplace: that price is public, comparable, and not secretly calibrated to extract the maximum a given individual can be made to pay. comment: Consumers own their products and should have the right to repair them as they wish. Claiming that a person leases something they have bought, an argument that major industry partners have done before, is akin to claiming that you lease the jeans you are wearing so you arent able to hem them, even though they are much too long. It makes absolutely no sense, no matter how you think about it. When you purchase a good, that good is yours to do with as you please. It does not continue to be the property of a company, under lease, and thus only able to be repaired by the company. When you purchase a car, you are able to repair that car. If a tire goes bald, or flat, then you are able to replace it. Tires are available to choose from, and you are able to replace it yourself, or take it to a repair shop to replace it for you. This is because parts are available, and manuals are available to show how. There is healthy competition in the tire industry so that parts arent priced so that its cheaper to buy a new car. This same logic out to apply to electronics. It should not be cheaper to replace a device than it is to repair it, as it currently is. Doing so merely encourages waste and discourages small business growth. Having the ability to repair your own goods creates technical skillsets that are transferrable to many job fields. If you are able to repair a cell phones hardware, than you learn a little bit of electrical engineering. If you are able to repair the software, then you are able to learn a little bit of software engineering. This would only make us a more powerful nation with a broader, better, skillset for our citizens. Electronic waste is the fastest growing waste stream in the US. This is a problem because of the difficulty disposing of electronic goods. Electronic goods leech toxic waste and require specially lined landfills. The ability to repair these goods is significantly more friendly to the environment and safer for our people and the world. In conclusion, as consumers we should have the right to repair our own goods, including our electronics. We own them, we should be able to repair them. The ability to repair gives consumers an expanded skillset that would lead to a more robust job market. For the safety of our environment we need to reduce our electronic waste, which the ability to repair our electronics would provide.

comment: COPPA Rule Review, 16 CFR part 312, Project No. P195404 I believe it is necessary to consider a further revision to the definition of Personal information (Question 13). First, the definition of Personal Information in 2013 revised COPPA Rule does not take a unified identifier of the devices into consideration. Sequences of data collected, such as the MAC addresses or IP addresses can tell the comparable physical presence of the user. When combined with other information collected from the user, it can generate a unified profile of the child or children using the device, which should also be regarded as personal information. Second, the behavioural data of the child using the device surfing should also be considered, which can be very identical and personal. Third, biometric data including facial and voice recognition should also be included as personal information. Forth, in an environment of peer-to-peer communication based online service, an identifier that can trace back to a certain child user either with certain behaviour or able to accept incoming information should be considered as personal information. For the Question 24, I dont think the Commission should consider a formal exception to verifiable parental consent when an operator collects an audio file with a child's voice without prior parental consent even if the audio file is collected solely as a replacement for written words, such as to perform a search or the audio file is held for a brief time and used only for that purpose. Voiceprint recognition has already been adopted by several call centres including those of financial institutions as a technology to identify the clients. Being a biometric identifier, there is a potential risk that processing such data might be misused. Even the storage of data can be attacked or hacked.

comment: August 1, 2019 submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov Federal Trade Commission Office of the Secretary 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW Suite CC-5610 (Annex B) Washington, DC 20580 Re: Safeguard Rule, 16 CFR part 314, Project No. P145407 Dear Sir/Madam: I am writing to comment on the above-captioned proposed amendment to the Safeguard Rule, 16 CFR part 314. The New York Insurance Association (NYIA) is the state trade association that has represented the property and casualty insurance industry in New York for more than 135 years. Our membership includes numerous insurance carriers in varying size. As you are aware, the New York Department of Financial Services (DFS) issued its Cybersecurity Regulation for Financial Services Companies (Regulation 500, 23 NYCRR 500, et seq.) in 2016. The final implementation date for this regulation, however, did not go into effect until March 1, 2019. While these proposed amendments to the Safeguard rule are based in part upon DFS Regulation 500, it is NYIAs view that it is premature for the Commission to adopt such rules at the federal level before sufficient data on the experience of both regulated entities and consumers with this regulation is available for public review. DFS, for example, could issue periodic changes to Regulation 500 as it gathers additional information about the efficacy of its regulation leading to inconsistencies between the Commissions rules and the cybersecurity laws and regulations in New York, the nations leading financial center. Furthermore, NYIA has concerns about the proposals provision that would seem to substitute the Commissions judgment over a companys governance decisions as overreaching. A company board has every reason to safeguard its personal identifying information (PII), as well as its reputation and future growth prospects which would be jeopardized by poor stewardship of PII. An additional concern is the proposals provision to include encryption for all consumer data, except where a chief security information officer (CISO) has approved of effective alternative compensating controls. This runs the risk that companies might feel compelled to encrypt all consumer data regardless of whether the CISOs compensating controls would be second guessed in the event a company were to lose unencrypted customer information. Another concern with the proposal is the mandate of multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing a companys internal networks that contain customer information. The proposal, were it enacted, should clarify that multi-factor authentication should only apply to access from outside the internal network. As always, please feel free to contact me if you have any questions or wish to discuss this matter further. Thank you for your consideration of our comments. Sincerely, Ellen D. Melchionni, CAE President

comment: July 29, 2019 Federal Trade Commission Office of the Secretary 600 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW Room CC-5610 (Annex B) Washington, DC 20580 Contact Lens Rule Review, 16 CFR part 315, Project No. R511995 Dear FTC Commissioners and Staff, Below please find a statement from the National Hispanic Medical Association and the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) in response to the Federal Trade Commissions (FTC) request for comments on its Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on the Contact Lens Rule (16 CFR Part 315, Project No. R511995). We want to thank the FTC staff for all the time and attention they have put in over the past years to craft a final Contact Lens Rule that will help millions of Americans, especially Hispanics and other underserved populations, understand their rights as contact lens consumers, to have access to their own contact lens prescriptions and be afforded more choice, more competition and more access in the marketplace. LULAC & NHMA STRONGLY SUPPORT THE FTCS PROPOSED CONTACT RULE As we have stated throughout this process and in our comments around the original NPRM and the Workshop, the Federal Trade Commissions proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule are an important victory for Hispanic working families who rely on the convenience, choice and savings that comes from being able to take your prescription for contact lenses and shop where you want, when you want. Every day, more and more Hispanics enter the market for contact lenses. We are the fastest growing demographic but our families simply do not know their rights as consumers, especially our right to a copy of prescription and this is critical because you cant buy contact lenses without a prescription. The system here in the US for buying contact lenses is stacked against consumers because the people who issue you your prescription are also allowed to sell you contact lenses at the very same time. Consumers who dont know their rights are getting trapped in the exam chair so to speak, unaware that they can buy lenses elsewhere for lower prices. Consumers can buy contact lenses online, at the drugstore or when they are doing their weekly shopping at Costco, comparing prices and getting the best deal for their families. We are not opposed to Hispanic consumers buying their contact lenses from their eye doctors but they should have a choice and a copy of their own prescription. RESPONDING TO THE QUESTIONS IN THE 5-28 SNPRM ON THE CONTACT LENS RULE PRESCRIPTION RELEASE ACKNOWLEDGMENT IS ESSENTIAL TO ENSURE THAT HISPANIC CONSUMERS KNOW THEIR RIGHT TO THEIR CONTACT LENS PRESCRIPTION When the proposed new Contact Lens Rule was first introduced, LULAC and NHMA applauded the addition of a requirement for optometrists to obtain a signed acknowledgement after providing a prescription to a consumer, and to keep that acknowledgement on file for three years. A signed acknowledgment gives the FTC a means to track those who are failing to follow the prescription release requirement under FCLCA and to take action on behalf of consumers' rights when a case warrants. We understand that the optometrists and their allies have since raised questions about the burdens that they claim could result from adding a signed acknowledgment form to the exam and contact lens fitting process. We do not share their concerns. Our community continually has been victimized and denied their prescriptions by prescribers and doctors at a higher rate than most other Americans. We strongly believe that more must be done to ensure patients are informed of their rights and given copies of their prescription, as many copies as they need and ask for. This focus on burdens that providers might face is upsetting when one remembers just how many patients are being robbed of their right to lower prices and more convenient shopping and being denied a copy of something that they worked hard to pay for, namely their own prescription. USING TECHNOLOGY TO ENSURE HISPANIC CONTACT LENS CONSUMERS KNOW THEIR RIGHTS AND CAN ACCESS THEIR PRESCRIPTION IS A GOOD IDEA AS LONG AS IT IS DESIGNED FAIRLY AND IS EASY TO USE The question of prescribers and sellers creating portals for customers in order to share prescription information is a little more of a complex question and may in fact create a greater burden initially on doctors and their patients. There is no doubt that more and more families and medical practices are storing critical health and wellness information in secure clouds and portals. In conclusion, the most important point we can stress to the FTC is the critical and time sensitive need to finalize and start enforcing the Contact Lens Rule as soon as possible. We urge you to swiftly issue the final Contact Lens Rule. Sincerely, Dr Elena Rios, President & CEO of the National Hispanic Medical Association Sindy Benavides, Chief Executive Officer of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) FULL COMMENTS ATTACHED

As we have stated throughout this process and in our comments around the original NPRM and the Workshop, the Federal Trade Commissions proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule are an important victory for Hispanic working families who rely on the convenience, choice and savings that comes from being able to take your prescription for contact lenses and shop where you want, when you want. RESPONDING TO THE QUESTIONS IN THE 5-28 SNPRM ON THE CONTACT LENS RULE

PRESCRIPTION RELEASE ACKNOWLEDGMENT IS ESSENTIAL TO ENSURE THAT HISPANIC CONSUMERS KNOW THEIR RIGHT TO THEIR CONTACT LENS PRESCRIPTION

comment: Microtransactions and lootboxes have a lot of thought and numbers behind how they work. They work in subtle, yet solid, methods of strong-arming players through carefully planned roadblocks developed into games to create a feeling of wasting time or limiting access to highly desired content in the game. Whats worse, is the "reward" is often "randomized". Creating a situation where a player could buy a box or pack hundreds of times without getting any of the items that are actually desired. Paying real money (or in game money that can be purchased with real money) for a "chance" to win/get a few rare select items is the essence of gambling. The ESRB states that ANY gambling in a game will be rated A for adult only. Lootboxes are not 'legally' defined as gambling, so we have games rated E for everyone or T for teen that has disguised gambling. I would argue that the fact that game content (skins, power ups, items) are locked within this 'roll the 1 in 10,000' odds is worse than gambling with money, because kids are playing these games and will have an emotional attachment to the games they are playing. This attachment is likely stronger than their attachment to money. This is a recipe for disaster.. unless you are the company making thousands off children throwing away their allowance (and sometimes their parents bank accounts) chasing a game reward they perceive they need. If a game has randomized, in game purchases, it needs to be rated for adults only. Period. The government had to step in against tobacco/smoking targeting children. Why? Because targeting them was profitable for the companies. Why would they ever stop making more money on their own? They won't. These types of in game purchases can be just as addictive as any other drug. The companies profit from this. I urge my government to make laws regarding this in-game transactions, particularly the random 'loot box' style purchases. They are far too close to gambling for our children to be exposed to. comment: I am a resident in the Ballad healthcare system. My daughter has needed many pediatric specialists and we have incurred multiple road blocks due the merger and the limited competition in the medical field. Here are the facts we have lived. We have 1 Pediatric Trauma Surgeon. When we needed this doctor in the Niswongers ER she was unavailable due to her high work load. We have 2 Pediatric Gastroenterologist. When we needed this doctor we had to use the FNP due to the high demand on these doctors. The FNP ended up giving us bad medical advice which resulted in us needing to be hospitalized at Niswongers for 5 days. We have been hospitalized twice at Niswongers. Both hospitalizations have been horrific in care. We had problems getting specialty formula, broken chairs in rooms for the parents to sleep on, overcrowding of the pediatric wing, hard time getting nurses to help, missing specialists and techs to run tests for my daughter, and much more. Niswongers in my opinion should not be called a childrens hospital, it is a hospital with a childrens wing missing lots of specialties and technicians needed for sufficient pediatric care. When my daughter needed a pediatric neurologist there are NONE in our area. We have to drive to Knoxville (almost 2 hours away each direction) to receive care. We have 1 geneticist. This doctor is also in high demand and has been an issue to get adequate care. When this office messed up our tests for the 4th time, it was recommended that we find a new one as they are to busy to give adequate care. We now have to drive to Knoxville for this doctor as well. Getting therapy services have also been an issue. We ended up driving to Knoxville for this as well. We were in the intensive program and required me to move to Knoxville with my daughter for over 3 weeks. My daughter still needed so much care that we drove weekly to Knoxville for over 6 months before I was able to find anything adequate in our area. We now drive to Elizabethton (40 min each way) which is closer but still a burden. After being hospitalized at Niswongers and having such horrible experiences, we ended up going to Nashville (4 hours away) for our last hospitalization. Our area lacks the resources to provide care in pediatric cases. To summarize we already have to drive to Knoxville for our Neurologist as a we do not have one in this area, drive to Knoxville for tests as Niswongers have messed my daughters care up several times, drive to Knoxville for therapies in the past, drive to Knoxville to find a new geneticist doctor as ours can not provide adequate care, and we will drive to Knoxville or beyond for any hospitalization if possible as our area is missing resources to provide sufficient pediatric care. Ballad has also become almost harassing in their billing system. The problem that I have with the billing system is every doctor, hospital bill, specialty item is all billed separately. While $50 a month, the demanded minimum payment of each bill does not sound like a lot, it quickly becomes $300 or more for us depending on what doctors we have seen. During the merging of hospital systems and accounts our bills are continuously incorrect and require hours, sometimes days, of phone calls using our time and energy to fix THEIR mistakes. Since our area has a medical monopoly due to this COPA it is highly unlikely that we will ever have any competition and this will become the new normal of care. I have NOT seen ANY benefit with this COPA in our daughters medical care. I beg and urge you to delay the merging of MSHA and Wellmont assets, look closer at this COPA, and the closing of services in Kingsport.

comment: I am a small business owner and IT professional who is also passionate about automotive repair and modifications. I am also an open-source developer and free software enthusiast (to quote Richard Stallman, free meaning free speech rather than free-beer). This comment was typed on an open-source operating system from an open-source browser. I recognize the significance of having control over your property and your devices and I am not in favor of allowing companies to "license" every aspect of a product so as to leave a consumer powerless. I am also against allowing companies keeping repair and diagnostic information proprietary for the purpose of increasing their revenue via the creation of "certified" repair locations. I am ESPECIALLY against allowing companies designing products which require specific manufacturer only tools, such as in the farming or automotive or software engineering industries, for the purpose of preventing the end-user from servicing a device or piece of equipment which typically would be considered serviceable in the past. If something truly weren't "safe" or "worthy" or "capable" of being repaired; that's what warning labels and documentation is for. Creating a device for a specific purpose, marketing that device and selling it to a consumer just so the device can become self-defeating once the owner/end-user tinkers with it is, among other things, immoral and dishonest. For large, too-big-too-fail companies with near monopolies in their markets it is unacceptable to allow them to continue to dissuade small repair shops and competitors from introducing options into an otherwise stagnant industry. For these behemoth conglomerates; preventing Farmer John from tending his crops with a tractor held together by a rubber-band and a 2-by-4 is just another revenue stream, but that's what built America and I'll be damned if I'm gonna stand by and watch Deere and Amazon and GM and Apple and Microsoft put me and Farmer John out of business so they can increase their market cap 0.002% this year. Where is the humanity in these companies?

When creating laws for stopping this tactic, you must fully stop the purchase of randomized goods entirely. Seen in other countries they created laws to stop them by showing the next loot boxes goods, but that only pushed the gambling back one set of boxes. Another failed attempt was forcing purchase items as not randomized. Companies like Blizzard decided a tactic to sell "coins" but reward players with a loot boxes on top of that purchase. Simply put, loot boxes have shifted the developers of games into exploitation mechanics to maximize their profits. The laws to stop this MUST not allow or reward any random items at all. You must avoid having loot boxes in any purchasable form, whether that is with in game coins earned by playing, coins purchased, or given as a bonus to any purchases made. The only feasible tactic to keep loot boxes would be directly tied into playing only. There must be rules to avoid circumventing the desired goal of this law, and you must be ready to pursue those who attempt doing so.

comment: Loot boxes are nothing but a draining experience on both game play and finances and have no purpose in video games other then to get more money out of players. Here's my personal experience of what loot boxes can do to a person. Back in 2012 I came across a Team Fortess 2 community who was running their own servers, on one of the servers they were running a mod called Verses Saxton Hale, VSH. VSH is a juggernaut mod where one player is a powerful boss trying to kill all the other players on the enemy team. The player who was the boss got to choose from a list of bosses they wanted to pick, but here is where loot boxes come in, you see the list of bosses only allowed you three choices all the rest were locked in crates that the server owner had designed and implemented, and just like Valves crates you had to unlock them with keys you could buy on the community website. When you unlocked these crates you would get passes for other bosses to use and a rare chance to permanently unlock them, this system over the course of 3 years had me spend nearly $4000 on keys to unlock these bosses before the community shutdown. So from a first hand experience I can say these loot crates, in any game they appear in, are nothing more then an addictive unneeded form of gambling that exploits people to nickle and dime them for as much money as they can and should not be allowed at all in video games.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a practicing doctor of optometry and the Government Relations Chair for Arizona Optometric Association. I was directly involved with the 2014 -2016 1-800 Contacts supported bills that were introduced in Arizona that would have taken contact lenses out of the realm of medical device and made them purely a commodity with no health protections or oversight. I have directly experienced the misleading statements and outright lies told by this company to the public and legislators solely for profit and with no regards to their eye health. Anyone you speak with will say that their eyesight is the most important sense to them and they would rather lose a limb or hearing rather than lose their sight. Our citizens deserve to have laws and rules in place to help them protect their eyesight. I have directly witnessed 1-800 disregarding the current FTC regulations and have shipped lenses off of expired prescriptions to children underage a week before faxing my office for a verification. I myself have ordered lenses and received them for over a year (three times) for lenses that I have never been prescribed and were not even the powers of my submitted (by my eye doctor) Rx. I got lenses shipped to me in 2015 that were off an expired Rx from 2007. I have the boxes and the confirmations of shipment and their website showing a 2007 Rx only. Because my doctor responded to the verification request, they counted that as an approval and will ship for 2 years from receipt of an invalid Rx. These are blatant disregard for the 2003 rules that the rest of us abide by. I see these proposed changes, which add additional burden on our offices, as a reward for bad behavior for a company that doesn't even follow the current set of Rules. I am always surprised when 1-800 Contacts says that people don't realize that they can purchase lenses somewhere other than their doctors office. Really?! Their name...1-800-contacts...was their phone number in the 1990's before the internet that people called to order their contact lenses. EVERYONE knows that they can purchase lenses anywhere they want. Poor argument. How about we make sure that patients are getting the proper lenses and have regular evaluation of their ocular health no matter where they purchase their lenses. Please show some common sense thinking and see through the misleading statements. LEAVE THE RULE AS IT HAS BEEN since 2003. Annette Hanian, O.D.

comment: Honorable April J. Tabor Acting Secretary Federal Trade Commission Office of the Secretary Constitution Center 400 7th Street SW 5th Floor Suite 5610 (Annex B) Washington, D.C. 20024 Re: Franchise Rule Regulatory Review 16 CFR Part 436 Matter No. R511003 Dear Acting Secretary Tabor: I write to submit these comments in response to the Federal Trade Commission's ("FTC") request for public comment on its Trade Regulation Rule entitled "Disclosure Requirements and Prohibitions Concerning Franchising" (the "Rule"), published in the Federal Register on March 13, 2019 (84 Fed. Reg. 9051). Under the franchise business model, every franchise brand involves both a franchisor and a network of franchisees. Franchisees are individual business owners who have secured a license from the franchisor, or parent brand, to own and operate a business using that brands trade name. Such arrangements typically require the franchisor to provide support for the franchisees, including standards regarding quality and uniformity, as well as brand-related investments such as national advertising, but the business owner is responsible for his or her own business, particularly hiring, firing, scheduling, and maintenance. The franchise business model allows many small business owners to be in business for themselves, but not by themselves. This system is based on the principle that every franchisee, owns and operates his or her own business and are responsible for their own decisions. Franchisees also retain their own business-related profits. Nationwide, franchising accounts for more than 733,000 franchise establishments in over 300 different business format categories, which support nearly 7.6 million jobs and $674.3 billion of economic output for the U.S. economy. Additionally, around 30% of franchise businesses are minority-owned, compared to less than 20% of non-franchised businesses. Over the years, the franchise community has collaborated with public officials to shape the laws and policies that govern franchising, and have consistently supported regulatory policies designed to ensure that prospective franchisees receive relevant and material information about their proposed franchise purchases sufficiently in advance of such purchases to enable them to make informed and unpressured purchase decisions. Specifically, franchisors and franchisees alike continue to support a proper balance between the legitimate disclosure needs of prospective franchisees and compliance burdens and costsborne by both franchisors and franchiseesthat such disclosure inevitably entails. Just as many in the franchise community supported the FTCs early initiatives in the disclosure area in 1978 and the Rules modification in 2007, I strongly endorse continuation of the Rule in substantially its current format. The current Rule provides an adequate, minimum threshold for disclosing relevant and valuable information to prospective franchisees in considering the cost and nature of the proposed investment in advance of their franchise acquisition decisions, minimizing the potential for franchisors to misrepresent the health of their systems at the expense of franchisees. Much more, the Rule establishes a predictable, transparent, and understandable process that both franchisors and franchisees have become familiar, which prospective franchisees have come to expect, and with which franchisors have become increasingly compliant. The absence of such information in the franchisees decision-making process would only lead to unacceptable levels of uninformed business decisions, distrust, investment losses, litigation, and additional government regulation, all of which would tarnish the reputation and integrity, and threaten the ever-growing economy- and life-enhancing benefits, of the franchise model itself. As now written, the Rule should be treated as inviolate and essential to the continued growth and success of the franchise model. I hope that the foregoing comments are helpful and express my appreciation for the FTCs role in preserving a trade regulation rule that contributes to the well-being of an essential and vibrant segment of the United States economy. Respectfully submitted, Shelly Sun, CEO and Founder of BrightStar Care

comment: Dynamic pricing and personalized pricing are plain and simple discrimination, and should be banned. Beyond that, the collection of such personalized data by retailers and employers constitutes an unwanted invasion of privacy, particularly because many consumers have no idea how their data is being collected or by whom, and have little recourse to opt-out or request its removal. Such practices turn even non commercial personal activities such as internet browsing, and consequently the individuals behind them, into commodities that are sold to retailers in a transaction where the party sold has no leverage to negotiate the terms of their own sale. Therefore, even if it is beyond the scope of the FTC's current power, they should take steps to prohibit such discriminatory pricing practices to the extent possible until congress creates appropriate legislation fully banning it.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in Staten Island, NY. For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. In addition, I have witnessed at least one hundred cases of contact lens sellers filling expired prescriptions, asking for verification of prescriptions for patients we have never seen, asking for verification of prescriptions via robo-calls where we cannot understand the name of the patient, etc. Dozens of patients have told me that their contact lens seller never asks them for a prescription. These market sellers of contact lenses need to be brought to task over these violations. Thank you for your attention, Frank Pirozzolo, O.D.
