comment: As a physician with 19 years of experience caring for patients in the Northeast Tennessee / Southwest Virginia region, I supported the merger when it was proposed, and I remain supportive today. The merger of Mountain States Health Alliance and Wellmont Health System to become Ballad Health has created new opportunities for healthcare providers to not just treat the sick, but to reach upstream of acute encounters to address the root causes of the health issues that disproportionately affect our region, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity and cardiovascular disease. Prior to the merger, both health systems had the desire to address these issues but neither had the resources. Now, instead of putting our limited resources into unnecessary duplication, were able to shift our focus toward population health improvement. This means building a structure and a long-term plan for addressing the specific health problems that plague our region. By reinvesting the efficiencies obtained through integrating the two health systems, Ballad Health has committed to invest more than $300 million over 10 years in improving the health of our region, including $28 million specifically toward rural health services. Weve already partnered to launch an Accountable Care Community to address regional health needs with participation from more than 220 regional organizations. Ballad Health has also partnered with East Tennessee State University to help create the Center for Rural Health Research to identify new mechanisms to improve health in rural and nonurban communities. These are major steps forward that will truly make a difference in the lives of people in our region for generations to come. As an emergency physician, Ive seen the problems first hand. Now Im excited to be part of a comprehensive solution that has the potential to transform the health of our region. None of this would be possible without the creation of Ballad Health. Clay W. Runnels, MD

I respectfully urge the agency to require transparency in algorithmic pricing practices and to investigate whether current personalized pricing practices violate existing consumer protection standards. Respectfully submitted.

comment: As a cardiologist and a lifelong resident of Northeast Tennessee, I am closely familiar with the health issues that are particular to our region. We suffer from disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, and tobacco use. Every day, I care for people who represent one or more or frequently all of these health risks. It is clear to me, and to many of my colleagues, that a greater effort is needed to intervene upstream of these issues and work to address health determinants before they result in significant comorbidities and early mortality. I strongly supported the Ballad Health merger in the beginning, and now that I have worked with the new health system for 18 months, I am even more convinced that this model of region-wide collaboration is the best way for us to address both the challenges that are unique to our region (such as health disparities) and those that all physicians and health systems in the United States share (such as payment reform). As separate health systems, Wellmont and Mountain States were not able to achieve the scale necessary to make the maximum impact on population health, nor were we able to fully align our efforts to participate in value based contracts in a way that would make the greatest impact. Since the merger, Ballad Health has formed a department of population health and an Accountable Care Community with more than 120 participating organizations, all focused on addressing the upstream causes of heart disease and other health problems. Ballad Health is working toward closer integration with the physician practices supported by the health system in rural parts of our region, creating access to specialty services like cardiology in places that previously had no such resource. Through collaboration within Ballad Health, my practice has also been able to participate in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, creating the opportunity to reduce the overall cost of care by participating in value based contracts on a scale not possible before. I remain a strong supporter of Ballad Health and the innovative approach to population health improvement, cost reduction and quality improvement that the system represents.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, We are a husband and wife optometry team practicing in Thornton, Colorado. We started our practice in 2010 and see patients of all ages in a primary eye care setting. Our practice sees a large number of contact lens wearers, many of whom wear specialty, and medically-necessary contact lenses. We practice optometry to the highest standards, and in accordance with the American Optometric Associations standards of Professional Conduct, our primary ethical responsibility is to place our patients interests above our own. Recent news in our profession has brought several concerns to our attention that we would like to share with you. Through the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act (FCLCA), Congress charged the FTC with enforcing contact lens prescription release. Despite eye doctors dutifully complying with their requirements under the law, the FTC has issued a proposed change to the Contact Lens Rule which would mandate that eye doctors meet new Confirmation of Prescription Release requirements, by retaining either a patient-signed document or, with patient consent, evidence that the prescription was delivered and made available electronically. Doctors would then be required to maintain compliance evidence for each contact lens patient for a period of three years and be able to produce this evidence in the event of a federal investigation. The FTC proposal is being advanced despite FTCs own data showing that over a recent five-year period the Commission received a total of 309 consumer complaints out of roughly 200 million contact lens prescriptions issuedwith half of those complaints being unrelated to any violation of the Rule. The FTC estimates that the new mandate will cost the industry more than $13 million annually. Eye doctors have offered a proposed alternative backed by the National Consumers League (which is already law in California) to instead require the posting of signage informing patients of their rights under the law. We firmly believe that the patient-doctor relationship should be less about bureaucracy, and more about addressing patient issues, instituting preventative eye health measures, and patient education than adding to an unneeded paperwork burden. Patients are aware that they can purchase their contact lenses anywhere they like with the contact lens prescription we provide to them, and filling out more forms over the matter doesnt benefit the patient. The additional time required for this unneeded paperwork would disrupt the patient-doctor relationship by communicating to the patients that they should be wary of their physician, and assume that their doctor is a violator of Federal law. Time that would otherwise be spent on patient care would be spent satisfying the misdirected aims of this requirement. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. Brian Abert, O.D.

comment: As many have stated, the current design of loot boxes has all the hallmarks of gambling, be it lottery tickets, slot machines, etc. The same thrills, risks, and potential for addictive behavior. There is no need for me to reiterate that here. I'm proposing an amicable solution and debunking a comparison. Some equate loot boxes to currently existing in products not seen as gambling such as packs of baseball cards, another product that is aimed at a market including children. Baseball cards have a strong secondary market allowing the consumer to find individual items and pay what is deemed market price for those specific items. Also, the secondary market allows the consumer to sell or trade their unwanted cards at what is deemed market price for those items. The majority of current game Loot boxes do not allow for a secondary market of their items, and virtually none of them allow for real money sales of their digital items. Not that I am advocating for that, just pointing out the large distinction between the current loot box economy and baseball cards and the like is the lack of a secondary market giving value to the items purchased. The creation of a secondary market for these digital items creates more issues than it solves, and that shouldn't be the path forward. From a consumer protection standpoint, we should want to make all the risks clear and visible from the start as well as making the undesired items purchased from loot boxes not worthless without creating a real money secondary market. To that end, here is my set of recommendations: All Loot Boxes should have the odds of receiving an item of certain rarities very clearly marked before and after purchase. i.e., this Loot Box has a 1:4 chance of getting a rare item, a 1:9 chance of getting an elite item, and a 1:100 chance of getting a legendary item. Also, no item within a specific rarity should be any more or less likely to be obtained than any other item of that rarity. i.e., a specific legendary item should not be any harder to get from a Loot Box than any other legendary item. Every game that has Loot Boxes will be required to allow the exchange of any item found in the Loot Boxes by trading in no more than 5 items of the same rarity of the desired item received from those Loot Boxes. i.e., a game has Loot Boxes and the elite rarity is a 1:9 drop from the Loot Box, Player A has obtained 5 elite rarity items from Loot Boxes, Player A must be able to trade those 5 elite rarity items from Loot Boxes to receive any 1 specific elite rarity item possible from that Loot Box that they want in exchange. The game will have the option of lowering that number if so desired, but they cannot require more than 5 items of that rarity to be traded in exchange for another specific item of that rarity. Lastly, to ensure there is a way around the gambling aspect of Loot Boxes every item available in a Loot Box that is purchased with cash must also be purchasable by cash and also display the estimated cost to acquire the item by buying Loot Boxes and trading in game at the in game ratio (no higher than 5 to 1) for that item. i.e., using the 1:100 chance of getting a legendary item and the game has chosen to stick to the 5 items required to trade in and that the Loot Boxes cost $1 each, the Estimated Price to Acquire a specific legendary item would be $500 (1:100 so on average 100 $1 Loot Boxes needed to get 1 legendary item, then you would need 5 legendary items to trade in for this specific one.) and that $500 Estimate to Acquire via Loot Boxes would be required to be shown on the item page to purchase the item. The price the game decides to charge in cash for the item without purchasing the Loot Boxes will also be displayed on this page and that price is to be determined by the game company. Also, game companies will not be required to exchange any number of lesser rarity items to equal a higher rarity item. They may do so if desired, but that will not be required. i.e., even though the pack says 1:100 legendary it does not mean the game has to let you trade 100 common items for a legendary. This reduces risks for consumers and puts both a clear price of plainly purchasing the item and the estimated price it would cost if you tried your luck with the Loot Boxes in front of the consumer from the start and explains the risks to the consumer then. It also provides the consumers with value for their unwanted items. From the game company standpoint, this is a much better solution than creating a real money secondary market and all the issues that will cause. This also allows game companies to continue with this practice in a way that is not as harmful to the consumer. It would still need to be regulated to avoid minors from being able to engage in the Loot Boxes with real money, but allowing them to purchase the item for cash if allowed by state and federal laws and agreed upon from their parents or guardians per the game's EULA. Thanks for your time.

comment: The city of Kingsport has a rich tradition of valor and patriotism. During WW2, Kingsport developed the only explosive that could finally stop Germany's submarines. In addition, the USS Kingsport Victory served as a cargo ship supplying troops on the Pacific Front and saw action during the Battle of Iwo Jima. That same fierce determination to go above and beyond in the service of others extends to our doctors and nurses, who have been proudly serving not just their communities, but the communities of southwest Virginia, southeast Kentucky, and northwest North Carolina. Since 1935, Kingsport's flagship hospital, Holston Valley Community Medical Center, has been a proud bastion of hope for not just our community, but our entire region. We are a proud city that embodies the volunteer spirit of our state and the pioneer spirit of our country's founding fathers. But now that capacity to serve others is threatened by monopolistic practices that are creating a culture of fear in our hospitals and communities. Because of the joint TN-VA COPA and the subsequent Ballad Merger, amazing doctors and nurses are leaving in droves, as they are unable to speak out against the changes incurred by Ballad under threat of termination. The Federal Trade Commission itself said that the merger would "likely lead to higher prices, lower quality, and reduced availability of care." And we are already seeing the ramifications of all of that. Countless patient horror-stories of inadequate care, excessive wait times, ridiculous billing expenses, disturbing uncleanliness, potential HIPPA violations, and life-threatening situations abound. Despite the fact that data from a Ballad-commissioned study by the firm Bishop & Associates of CA showed that leaving Johnson City as the only Level 1 Trauma Center in this region would exclude 84,147 people from the "Golden Hour" of trauma, Ballad is trudging ahead with their plans to downgrade Holston Valley. In comparison, 17,750 would be excluded if Holston Valley was selected as the Level 1. In addition, Kingsport is home to the headquarters of the Eastman Chemical Company (which has exploded twice, most recently in 2017), the Domtar Paper Mill, and the BAE Army Ammunition Plant (which exploded in January of this year). While America has seen its fair share of monopolies, I can think of none more egregious than a monopoly that results in a profit-focused approach to healthcare. There are also numerous conflicts of interest at play here. An Eastman executive is also on the Ballad Board of Directors and the ETSU Board of Trustees. Several individuals on the Ballad Board of Directors are also on the ETSU Board of Trustees, and they have been named in a recent federal antitrust lawsuit from a lawfirm out of Greenville, TN. In addition, I have attached the minutes of an ETSU Board of Trustees meeting from April 27 2018, wherein several members of their Board are noted on page 24-25 discussing how crucial it is that ETSU lands the $175 million that Ballad Health has set aside for research. My name is Joe Carr, and this year at the age of 23, I became the youngest person in the history of Kingsport to run for Mayor. My hometown has never asked for help before, but we are now. There has been a 24/7 protest outside of Holston Valley Medical Center for 91 straight days now in opposition to Ballad's plans to downgrade our Trauma Center and move our NICU to Johnson City. Over 26,000 people from this region have signed a petiton against Ballad's changes and mismanagement. Please, do the right thing and halt this merger before it can cause anymore harm.

comment: While I could speak to several very bad personal experiences with the former Mountain States Health Alliance (now Ballad Health), I will make my comments more to the issue of choice and the healthcare monopoly we now have in our region. Prior to the merger of Mountain States Health Alliance (MSHA) and Wellmont Health System, I was able to choose where I would go if I required hospitalization or outpatient services. This was vitally important to me over the last 10 years since I was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2010.At that time, I chose an oncologist with the Kingsport Hematology-Oncology group with the knowledge that I would use Holston Valley Hospital for any in-patient care. I must mention that I live in Carter County, Tennessee, which is approximately 25 miles from Kingsport, TN. Thankfully, my care during my battle with cancer was excellent and I am a healthy 70 year old survivor. During the 1 1/2 years of treatment in 2010 and 2011, I was hospitalized 6 times and had many visits to the emergency room. The difference in quality of care at Holston Valley Medical Center and my previous experiences, both personal and with family and friends, at the Johnson City Medical Center were at opposite ends of the spectrum. Following completion of treatments for breast cancer, which included 38 radiation treatments at HVMC's Christine LaGuardia Radiation Center, I have had several instances to use Wellmont services and have continued to see my oncologist at Kingsport Hem-Onc. In the months since the merger, I have seen very unfortunate and even frightening changes in healthcare in our region. My oncologist's medical group was recently FORCED to move to a hospital owned facility which has increased costs to patients due to the addition of "facility fees and charges". Drugs previously available for treatment of certain blood issues are no longer used, incurring additional visits to the new office, additional costs and poorer outcomes. While I am currently in good health for a 70 yr old woman, I am very aware that I am at high risk for health problems and all those possible health issues of aging. My husband and I have talked at length about what we would do if either of us required hospitalization. I am aware of serious issues and incidents that have happened at Holston Valley Medical Center since the merger including serious staffing problems and the loss of many doctors. Following a devastating medical error after major surgery in 1999, I made the decision never again to be a patient at the Johnson City Medical Center. Until the merger, I was at ease with the fact that I had a CHOICE to use HVMC if I needed hospital care of any kind. I no longer have that choice. In addition, the FTC must be well aware of the entanglement of local politicians and the leadership at Ballad Health. If you aren't, you can contact State of Tennessee Senator Rusty Crowe who was a leader in getting the COPA legislation put in place. Senator Crowe's email address is Rusty.Crowe@BalladHealth.com. His company is under contract to provide wound care and other services to Ballad Health (and for a considerable period of time previously to MSHA.) In addition, his wife is contracted to Ballad as a psychologist. These are only two of the serious conflicts of interest that now exist between legislators in our state and this health care system. I, like many others in our part of northeast Tennessee and southwest Virginia, could go on at even further length about the critical issues that have arisen from the merger of our TWO health systems into Ballad Health. But the basic issue is that we now have a monopoly in our region. The COPA process is not adequate to protect our communities from the frightening outcomes we are seeing. The Federal Trade Commission has the power to protect consumers (even though I find it hard to call a premature infant who is in the NICU a "consumer") from the effects of this merger. I plead with those who will hear and review the testimony and comments of those of us who live in fear of our hospitals now. Please do what is right.

comment: In Regards to the COPA held by Ballad Health , creating a medical Monopoly in Northeast TN and SW VA ,. It is my opinion that the merged Healthcare system does not pose an Advantage , but rather a substantial Disadvantage in the healthcare and well being of those it serves. In a time of changing and growing healthcare in our country, this Monopoly has proven to limit the quality and quantity of medical professionals of which it serves. The anti-trust laws passed by legislatures that protect Ballad from any federal government intervention allows the health system to manipulate the narrative as how and what information the public receives. For example , in May 2019 , I accompianed my family member to the Emergency Room at Holston Valley in Kingsport TN. During this visit, I observed many patients being held in the waiting room. In fact, the waiting room were at capacity. As we were in the waiting room upward of 8 hrs. I witnessed many people being asked insurance information , verification of SS #s, reason for their visit etc. My relative , as were others would be taken back and having tests and bloodwork done then returned to the lobby. The staff told us it was because the ER was full. The lobby was full, the treatment areas were not. There was not enough staff to treat the people. My relative was given a urine specimen cup and told to go into the public restroom and place the specimen on the check In desk out front. The outcome of the visit was her being told to schedule a follow up diagnostic test with her PCP. She was given a RX for her nausea, which she was unable to take due to contraindication. No one mentioned this to her when she inquired about taking the medication. Sadly, I have heard similar stories from at least a dozen of my friends and family. In July, 2019 , another immediate family member was transported by ambulance to Indian Path Medical Center from SW VA this is about a 60 mile trip. She was admitted and stayed 24 hrs. Upon discharge, she had a episode of dangerously high BP and heart rate, and difficulty breathing.(which is the reason for her visit to ER ) . She was told to go outside and re admit to ER . She left this Ballad Health Hospital and went 40 more miles to Johnson City Medical Centers ER where she was admitted and spent a week there for the same problem. I live within 15 minutes of 3 Ballad Hospitals. I had to drive in terrible weather, to a city I know little about, at night , alone in order to be with her, this being a hardship and disadvantage . The quality is declining , and we are left with no choice in an emergency but to pray for timely and quality care. Our COPA is unique, and in spite of having State oversight, the State officials have remained quiet and tell those who inquire that there is nothing they can do. So if the State oversight can't help,and the ftc can't help, who prevents the public from the effects of a declining health system? Who protects the medical staff from overwork, underpay and "burn out"? It is my opinion that this type of Monopoly should never be in existence when it comes to public health.

comment: Since the merger which has created Ballad here in Greeneville, I personally have seen a major decline in our local health care services. I was being treated by the Cardiology Team at Takoma Hospital, and for several years had received excellent care. It was easy to communicate with the staff, my appointment waiting times where minimal, and if I had to call with a question or concern the phone call was either answered then, or if I had to leave a message I received a return call promptly. Then one day I needed to refill a prescription , and my Pharmacist stated he needed to contact my Cardiologist. 2 days later they still had not received a return call. I called the Cardiology Dept, left messages, and no reply to my calls either. So I went to Takoma, and there , taped to the Doctors door, was a note saying the Cardiology Dept had been moved to Laughlin Hospital. No call, no email, no mailed letter, nothing. So I finally drove to Laughlin, found my Cardiologists new office, and inquired about why suddenly it was so hard to contact them. They stated that they never received the messages from either myself or the Pharmacy. And to this day it is hard to contact them other then going to the office in person. Any testing which was required was scheduled, a date set, and the tests performed without any problem. Not so since Ballad took over. Now the tests are requested, weeks later the date set, now being performed at Laughlin, and I checked in 1/2 hour prior, as I have always done.Then I waited, and waited, and waited. 3 hours before I was seen for the test ( a sonogram). Emergency room waiting time use to be minimal. Now it's hours, only to be told we must travel to Johnson City because they are understaffed. Nurses are leaving, Doctors are leaving. In fact, My Cardiologist is leaving. Many local doctors have spoken out against Ballad and their practices. And now we find out that the people charged to oversee this have not filed a report, or done what was promised when Ballad filed their petition for the merger. I urge you , as those who have been entrusted to watch over our health care, to take a long , deep, hard look at Ballad and this COPA, and then tell me why we all here in East Tennessee smell the smoke, and are waiting for the fire.

comment: As an ophthalmologist, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. While I would welcome changes to the Contact Lens Rule that prioritize patient safety, the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses that are already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that we believe puts our patients at risk. While we appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

comment: Dear Office of the State Attorney General, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. I agree that it is important that consumers be given a genuine opportunity to exercise choice in the contact lens market. However, before one considers offering support for far reaching government regulations to be imposed on small businesses, its important to know the true state of the contact lens market as the market has changed tremendously since the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act was passed. o Lens prices are competitive: The AOA conducted a price comparison analysis in which they compared online retailer cost vs the average in-office cost to determine the dollar price difference and percent change in price for 81 different contact lenses. Of the 81 lenses studied, 28 were more expensive online, while 53 were more expensive in the doctors office. Across all lenses included in the AOAs price comparison analysis, there was an average price difference of just $0.32 o Patients Have More Retailer Options than Ever: The fastest growing distribution channel for contact lens sales in the USA was the online / Internet channel. Consumers today have more choice and more convenience. The competitive benefits have gone beyond price. I think that the FTC can consider this a successful rule. Doctors of optometry are concerned with the FTCs claims regarding non-compliance of prescription release requirements. Despite disagreeing with the accusation regarding compliance, the profession has offered an alternative to the signed acknowledgement proposal put forward by the Commission. The proposal supported by optometry would require all contact lens prescribers to post signage in their offices notifying patients of their right to their contact lens prescription. This is a less burdensome and less intrusive approach than the proposal put forward by the FTC. This approach would also do more to broadly educate consumers. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under FTCs threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions at both the state and federal levels.

Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses that are already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that we believe puts our patients at risk. While we appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices.I have had detailed discussions with our office manager about the work implications of your requirement for patient acknowledgement and filing for three years. FTC believes this adds only one minute extra work perpatient. We strongly disagree: we believe that this requirement will take an extra ten minutes per patients and subsequently will add an extra 850 man hours burden to our ophthalmology practice. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

The European Union has very strict rules concerning children, perhaps we can learn about what is working for them in this area because it's does not working for us in the United States. We cannot expect corporations to monitor themselves considering so much money can be made by selling children's data. Thank you.

comment: The excuse that this lets budget travelers “pay only for what they use” doesn’t hold up when basic things like a carry-on or a assigned seat have quietly become “extras.” Airlines aren’t offering optional luxuries — they’re carving mandatory costs out of the base fare and calling it choice. Meanwhile the psychological trick is well known in the industry: once someone’s 10 minutes into a booking flow, they rarely walk away over a $40 surprise fee, even if they would’ve picked a different airline had they seen the real price upfront. This isn’t free-market pricing flexibility. It’s a deliberate strategy to win the click with a fake low number and extract the real price after the customer is already committed. Full transparency — one price, all fees included, before checkout — is the bare minimum standard other industries are held to. Airlines fighting that tooth and nail tells you exactly whose interest they’re protecting.

comment: Dear Office of the State Attorney General, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. It has come to my attention that a call to your colleagues was distributed last week that requested support for a letter regarding the FTCs contact lens proposal. It is my opinion that this effort will be harmful to the doctor-patient relationship, and create unnecessary burdens in the practice of eye and vision care, therefore I urge you to NOT sign-on to a letter proposed byAttorneys General Miller, Peterson, Stein, and Reyes.Before one considers offering support for far reaching government regulations to be imposed on small businesses, its important to know the true state of the contact lens market as the market has changed tremendously since the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act was passed. Lens prices are competitive: The AOA conducted a price comparison analysis in which they compared online retailer cost vs the average in-office cost to determine the dollar price difference and percent change in price for 81 different contact lenses. Of the 81 lenses studied, 28 were more expensive online, while 53 were more expensive in the doctors office. Across all lenses included in the AOAs price comparison analysis, there was an average price difference of just $0.32 Patients Have More Retailer Options than Ever: The fastest growing distribution channel for contact lens sales in the USA was the online / Internet channel. In 2017, online retailers generated $786 million in salesgrowing by 4.9% during the 12 month ending period Dec17 and growing by 11.1% over the 24 monthending period Dec17. There is Widespread Agreement that the Current Rule is Working:The CEO of 1-800-CONTACTS itself acknowledged that the current rule is working in a March 2018 FTC workshop noting, The FCLCA and CLR have succeeded in encouraging greater competition and choice in the contact lens marketplace. Consumers today have more choice and more convenience. The competitive benefits have gone beyond price. I think that the FTC can consider this a successful rule. Doctors of optometry are concerned with the FTCs claims regarding non-compliance of prescription release requirements. Despite disagreeing with the accusation regarding compliance, the profession has offered an alternative to the signed acknowledgement proposal put forward by the Commission. The proposal supported by optometry would require all contact lens prescribers to post signage in their offices notifying patients of their right to their contact lens prescription. This is a less burdensome and less intrusive approach than the proposal put forward by the FTC. This approach would also do more to broadly educate consumers. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. In all, through letters, direct exchanges during committee hearings and committee report language, more than 100 Members of Congress Republicans and Democrats -- have spoken out against the FTCs misguided approach to updating the contact lens rule and called on the agency to prioritize a crackdown on illegal device sales, including those being reported on by the national media --https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/21/business/media/hubble-contact-lens.html.And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under FTCs threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions at both the state and federal levels. Sincerely, Priya Patel, O.D.

comment: To: FTC/Made in USA Workshop / Attn: Julia Ensor Solomon Re: Made in USA Claims, Project No. P074204 : Response to the request for public comment on guidelines for Made in USA: I respectfully request that the unqualified claim for Made in USA as applied to the $50 Billion plus (per year) watch industry be made equal or similar to worldwide standards used by segment leaders including Swiss, Japanese, and Chinese/Hong Kong manufacturers. Swiss Made = 60% Swiss sourced component VALUE and final assembly in Switzerland for a finished watch. Domestic value factor is reduced to 50% for watch movements to be considered a Swiss watch movement. http://www.fhs.swiss/eng/strengthening.html Made in Japan = Last major transformation of components to take place in Japan. No stipulated values. Industry estimates show nearly 50% of Japanese watches use majority Chinese components and partial assembly. Made in China/Hong Kong = No specific component values applied. Companies must be based in country. As our own American wristwatch industry begins a cycle of rebirth and reinvigoration, the US government is restricting the ability of domestic brands to compete with a crippling all or virtually all standard for an unqualified claim of Made in the USA. All or virtually all may be attainable for less complex products such as pillows or molded rubber floor mats, but with a complex product such as a wristwatch that can have 150 or more individual components; the existing standard is beyond crippling. It virtually eliminates the possibility to earn the esteemed status and benefits commensurate with an unqualified Made in USA status. Twenty two years ago a 75% value standard (plus final transformation) was proposed but never written into the FTC guidelines. https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/press-releases/1997/05/ftc-proposes-new-standard-made-usa-claims-seeks-public-comment Even this standard is substantially higher than any competitive member of the watch manufacturing countries, yet was never enacted. If we cannot play on a level playing field with the Swiss, Japanese, and Chinese, at least we should activate this reasonable guideline. I write this as both a 30 year veteran reporter on the watch industry and also as a recent entrant into the watch making arena here in the USA. With a growing list of over 200 American based watch brands I encourage a plan of action that will release the brakes on an industry that can train and employ thousands of Americans in the future. Thank you in advance for your kind attention. Gary G. Girdvainis Editor-in-Chief iW Magazine, AboutTime Magazine / Isochron Media LLC

comment: If a game allows items obtained from loot boxes to be traded to other players in any way, then those loot boxes should fall under the standard regulations applied to other forms of gambling, as players are paying actual money for loot boxes, and have the potential to make actual money back from them (whether sale of items is facilitated by the game publishers or must be done external to any systems set up by the publishers). This includes insuring that no minors can possibly purchase loot boxes. If a game does not allow items obtained from loot boxes to be traded to other players, then they should still be regulated in some ways, but not necessarily in exactly the same way as other forms of gambling. At a minimum it should be required that the odds of obtaining any specific item from a loot box should be clearly stated and/or a system should be set up to allow players to allow players to purchase any specific item after a certain number of loot boxes have been opened (for example: a system whereby items obtained can be traded in for an in-game currency that can be used to buy any loot box items for set prices, with a minimum guaranteed amount of the in-game currency that can be obtained from each loot box). The key is that players need to be able to make an informed decision when there's a specific item from a loot box that they hope to get. A player should be able to look at a specific item and say "based on those odds I'm likely to have to spend X amount to get that item" or "based on the amount of in-game currency I can get from each loot box I'll be able to buy that item after buying no more than X loot boxes", and it should be easy for players to come to such conclusions. Anything less than that is simply unethical, as it relies on player ignorance and predatory psychology to obfuscate the actual amount that players are likely to have to spend while encouraging players to sink more and more money into gambling (the psychological effect of the sunk cost fallacy is a major factor) in the hopes that this time they'll be lucky. Some protections for minors are likely appropriate for these types of loot boxes as well, and experts on child psychology and the psychology of gambling addicts should be consulted to determine how extensive these protections should be.

At a minimum it should be required that the odds of obtaining any specific item from a loot box should be clearly stated and/or a system should be set up to allow players to allow players to purchase any specific item after a certain number of loot boxes have been opened (for example: a system whereby items obtained can be traded in for an in-game currency that can be used to buy any loot box items for set prices, with a minimum guaranteed amount of the in-game currency that can be obtained from each loot box). The key is that players need to be able to make an informed decision when there's a specific item from a loot box that they hope to get. A player should be able to look at a specific item and say "based on those odds I'm likely to have to spend X amount to get that item" or "based on the amount of in-game currency I can get from each loot box I'll be able to buy that item after buying no more than X loot boxes", and it should be easy for players to come to such conclusions. Anything less than that is simply unethical, as it relies on player ignorance and predatory psychology to obfuscate the actual amount that players are likely to have to spend while encouraging players to sink more and more money into gambling (the psychological effect of the sunk cost fallacy is a major factor) in the hopes that this time they'll be lucky. Some protections for minors are likely appropriate for these types of loot boxes as well, and experts on child psychology and the psychology of gambling addicts should be consulted to determine how extensive these protections should be.

comment: Re: FTC-2026-1057 — Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing I strongly oppose personalized pricing based on consumer data and support the FTC’s efforts to investigate and restrict this practice. Consumers reasonably expect that a listed price is determined by the product, service, and ordinary market conditions—not by a hidden calculation of how much a particular person might be willing or forced to pay. Using browsing history, location, purchase history, household composition, medical circumstances, financial information, or other personal data to charge different consumers different prices is fundamentally deceptive when it occurs without their knowledge. Personalized pricing also undermines meaningful comparison shopping. A competitive market depends on consumers being able to compare the same offers. If each consumer sees a different price based on information collected about that person, there is no longer a reliable market price to compare. Consumers cannot make informed choices when they do not know whether the displayed price reflects the value of the product or an algorithm’s estimate of their vulnerability, urgency, or ability to pay. I am particularly concerned about pricing based on sensitive circumstances. A person should never pay more because data suggest that the person is experiencing a medical emergency, traveling for a funeral, caring for children, recently experienced a crime, lacks transportation, or has few practical alternatives. Disclosing that such exploitation is occurring would not necessarily make it fair. Certain uses of personal data should be considered unfair even when disclosed because the consumer may have no reasonable way to avoid the harm. Personalized pricing also creates serious privacy and discrimination concerns. Algorithms may use seemingly neutral information as a proxy for income, disability, race, age, family status, religion, health, or geographic location. Consumers may never know what information was used, whether it was accurate, or how to correct it. Businesses should not be permitted to avoid responsibility by outsourcing these decisions to data brokers, software vendors, or pricing algorithms. As a small-business owner and healthcare professional, I recognize that not every price difference is improper. Prices may legitimately vary because of differences in products, services, costs, insurance contracts, publicly disclosed discounts, geographic markets, or changing supply and demand. Those ordinary and explainable differences are distinct from secretly charging an individual more because data suggest that the person will tolerate a higher price. I urge the FTC to finalize and strengthen its proposed policy by: 1. Requiring clear, prominent disclosure whenever personal data influence a consumer’s price. 2. Requiring disclosure of the specific basis and categories of data used—not vague phrases such as “special price” or “personalized offer.” 3. Giving consumers access to a non-personalized price and a meaningful opportunity to opt out. 4. Holding businesses responsible for pricing decisions made by their vendors and automated systems. 5. Treating the use of health information, emergencies, personal hardship, or other vulnerabilities to increase prices as presumptively unfair. 6. Requiring a practical process for consumers to identify and correct inaccurate information. 7. Preserving the FTC’s ability to find that certain personalized-pricing practices are unfair even when technically disclosed. A person’s private information should not become a tool for extracting the highest price that person can be pressured into paying. Americans deserve transparent prices, genuine competition, and confidence that personal data will not be used against them. I encourage the Commission to adopt the strongest protections available under its existing authority and to recommend additional congressional action if further authority is needed.

I am writing to urge the Federal Trade Commission to streamline the process for contact lens prescriptions as well as create regulations that make it so that contact lens bought online have to go through the same prescription process as regular contact lens purchases. Kyle Gould

comment: I really don't understand the purpose of the proposal to require a signature from patients certifying that their prescriber gave them a copy of their contact lens prescription, except to waste my time and frustrate my patients. I have been a practicing optometrist for 19 years. When I prescribe contact lenses, we give the patient a copy of their prescription, and we ask them if they want to buy their lenses. Most do; they appreciate that the sale of contact lenses is part of my business and they are happy to support me. They also have more assurance that they will receive what they were prescribed, rather than some knockoff from Korea. But some patients choose to buy their lenses elsewhere, and that is totally cool. We don't treat them any differently if they want to shop around - that's the beauty of a free economy. I have to keep my prices competitive with the likes of Walmart of Costco. The idea of me having to have a patient sign a form certifying that I actually gave them a copy of their contact lens prescription - because "Big Brother" is watching - is insulting to myself as a person, and to my profession. It's (potentially) just the latest overreach of a government that should have better things to worry about. First it was HIPAA, then Meaningful Use/MIPS, now this. At my small office we spend sooo much time, thought, and effort just to satisfy the growing burdens of governmental regulations that have done nothing to improve patient care or outcomes. Healthcare is becoming too complicated - please stop the insanity and reject this ridiculous proposal.

comment: The Certificate of Public Advantage written by the Tennessee state legislature that resulted in a monopoly is detrimental to the quality of our healthcare. Competition keeps prices down, gives the healthcare system motivation to provide the most quality care. Sadly we now have one healthcare system with no competition and no federal oversight. It is up to the state to oversee the monopolized healthcare system. Poor decisions are being made by Ballad Health. Downgrading the level one trauma center at Holston Valley Medical Center, leaving only the level one trauma center located at Johnson City Medical Center to care for the region. Just one level one Trauma Center for 23 counties in a rural area. Transporting a trauma patient to the hospital quickly and can be a life or death situation. Cost of transport puts a financial burden on the patients, possibly costing tens of thousands of dollars to airlift them. Holston Valley Medical Center is centrally located and within 60 mins travel time for nearly half of those 23 counties. It is not of public advantage moving the level one trauma center from Holston Valley Medical Center to Johnson City Medical Center leaving only one trauma center for the region. Ballad plans to move the level three NICU to Johnson City,TN. The level three NICU at Holston Valley was renovated in 2016 spending 2.5 million dollars of funds raised in large and small public donations. It is a highly rated facility, family centered. Premature newborns, NAS newborns and newborns in need of intensive care are treated in one of best NICU's in the country. It is definitely not of public advantage to move this NICU. Doctors are resigning, nurses are also finding work outside the Ballad System. Poor working conditions and low pay are driving our good doctors and nurses away! Because of under staffing the emergency room at Holston Valley Medical Center and Johnson City Medical Center many times are full and overflowing. Patients waiting many hours for care. So many things are going wrong in this situation. This medical monopoly is not of public advantage. Who is overseeing the quality of healthcare and our ability to access it? Who is monitoring the cost we are charged for our healthcare? What is the state of Tennessee doing?

comment: Issues 1 & 2: Yes, the Rule definitely helps the potential franchisee to get information about the franchise. One of the most valuable information is the contact for the existing franchisee in the system. It provides unbiased information that potential franchisee to access to. Issues 3 a,b,c: Modifications should be made Suggestion One: Maintain a list of franchisees who left the franchise system in the last 10 years, with the following information: - Franchisee First Name, and Last Initial - Franchisee City and State - Franchisee e-mail contact (at the time of separating from the system) - Reason of leaving: terminated, transferred, non-renewal, purchased agreement but not open - The year that franchisee joined the system - The year that left the system - Any litigation or arbitration history with the franchisee - Non-disclosure statement signed or not The franchisor is not responsible for maintaining the contact info to be current. But the franchisor must maintain this info in FDD until it passes 10 years mark. Therefore, it will not incur extra cost for the franchisor to maintain such a list in the FDD. If there is any problem with the franchisor, those franchisees who left the system are more willing to share any bad experience. Even if those franchisees cannot share their experience, a long list of high turnover franchisees would indicate the franchisor problem of maintaining long term valuable franchisee. Also, an indication of the franchisor concentrate on profit from the initial franchise fee, rather than provide adequate supports to maintain long term franchise relationship. Suggestion Two: Agree with both Lagarias, Napell & Dillon, LLP, and Witmer, Karp, Warner & Ryan LLP. "The Franchise Rule Should Prohibit Disclaimers of Additional Representations and of Reliance By Prospective Franchisees. This practice stands the Franchise Rule on its head and must end." I agree that the FTC should prohibit disclaimers in disclosure documents. Franchisor shall be responsible and liable for all information provided on the FDD, especially financial performance, cost and fees for buying and operating a franchise. No additional cost impact for the franchisor for removing disclaimers from FDD. Suggestion Three: On item 19, prohibits franchisor to post store profits for just a group of selective stores. Posting profit for selective stores will definitely provide a skewed and deceptive picture. Instead, the franchisor should post stores average revenue (individually, in a group by geographic, or in total). Since most Franchisor has all the stores revenue (royalty usually calculated from % of revenue), Franchisor will be forced to report ALL stores, instead of pick and choose which stores to report. If a particular store revenue is not obtainable, it should be noted. And a count of how many stores do not report revenue should be provided. Minimal cost impact for the franchisor since franchisor should have this information in their system already. Suggestion Four: On item 3, Litigation. Record of any litigation and arbitration related to the franchise should maintain for 3 years in the FDD in order for the potential franchisee to have easy access to this information. Minimal cost impact for the franchisor to maintain the last 3 years record. Suggestion Five: A histogram of the years of experience of franchisee in the system should be provided in the FDD. The vertical axis shows the years of experience in the franchise system, from year 1 to year 10+. The horizontal axis shows the number of franchisee. Franchisee who left the system should also be counted in this statistic until it passes 10 years of history. Therefore, if there are a lot of short-timers in the system, it is easy to show in this histogram. The initial cost impact for franchisor this modification may be a concern. But once it is implemented, the continuation of maintaining such a record is minimal. Issue 12: Instead of franchisee address and phone number listed on the FDD, personal e-mail contact would be more appropriate to list. Franchisee most likely does not want to expose personal information on the list. E-mail contact provides enough privacy protection for a franchisee.

comment: FTC PUBLIC COMMENTS: Question #1 What are the effects of COPAs in terms of price, cost, and quality of healthcare services, access to healthcare; innovation of healthcare delivery models, or other dimensions of healthcare competition? How are these effects measured? PRICE: While Ballad Health has been restricted from overall price increases above the standard annual percentage increase patients previously experienced, they have been innovative in other ways to increase prices/costs to patients. Among these are: Facility Fees, Minimal Payment Arrangement Amounts, Selective Medication Offerings, Medically Unnecessary Transports, etc. Facility Fee: This fee was not supposed to be charge to active cancer patients at all or current patients for 6 months when Ballad moved to the new location on Indian Path campus March 4th. However, both are receiving these charges. Note If an active cancer patient stops the current regimen and starts a new one, they are considered a new patient and charged this fee. Sleep Center Facility Fees Ballad moved the Sleep Center onto the Holston Valley Medical Center Campus inside Wilcox Hall and now charges a $70 facility to those patients as well. All of these fees are new and this is just an example of how prices have increased to patients with the addition of these fees. 2. Payment Arrangement Minimums Patients are now being told that Ballad Health cannot accept a payment arrangement of less than $50 per month PER Account. 3. Selective Medication Availability Specific example of this would be with the new Cancer/Infusion Therapy Center. Previously, patients were given the medication prescribed by their physician regardless of its costs and if the patient was inpatient or outpatient. Ballad Health has changed this practice. Heres an example: Teresa Allgood was prescribed and had been receiving Infed injections from 2014 through summer 2018 at the Allendale facility for an average cost of $3500-4100 per injection. In the summer of 2018, she was told her Infed was no longer available to her. At that time, Ballad Health made the choice to only offer Infed to those who were inpatient because there is a set bundled rate at which they are compensated at itis more financially beneficial for them to include a low-cost drug in this bundle. Outpatient status were now required to receive Feraheme injections as a replacement. This medication required two injections instead of one administered one week apart. Her bill for Feraheme was $13,449. After the move from Allendale to the Indian Path Campus March 4th, she was told Feraheme would no longer be available to her and that she must now use Injectafer. She has yet to be able to get a bill for this injection administered in March 2019. However, the bill I have seen for this injection is $51K from a similar patient. Additional Note: She has experienced a significant reaction to this unnecessary change in her medications and her condition has been worse in the few months than in years. 4. Medically Unnecessary Transports Due to severe staffing losses and shortages, patients are being transported to sister facilities often after being to the original facility. Because these are not medically necessary transports, insurance will not cover the bill, and it is passed on to the patient at a cost of $500-1500 on average. 5. Increased patient and family costs when high risk facility on diversion necessitating transport to facility at least 2 hours or more away. Also cost increase for patients on the opposite end of the service area needing high level care; face higher ambulance fees. comment: Hello, my name is Sofiya Karinova I manage a Credit Reporting Organization (CRO) in the state of CA. We find it very difficult to work with CRAs. Most consumer don't know their options and right to demand accuracy of their credit report. As a CRO we spend a lot of time educating, analyzing credit, and auditing each negative account for errors and violations. Credit Repair Agencies should have a department that would accept inquiries and demands from properly licensed CRO such as us. In most cases we do not submit our dispute for the client until we have enough facts and supporting documentation to support our claim, and even then it takes numerous attempts to get the information correction or removed. Even when we have a deletion letter from the creditor/collector CRA response comes back stating "account was validated and will stay on report.." when creditor clearly stated they are NOT reporting to the CRAs and our dispute should be with them. It becomes a never ending and very stressful process that they put us running in circles. CRAs should be and must be willing to work with CROs, at the end of the day we are not working against them but actually doing their job by thoroughly auditing each file, and providing them all they need that supports our claim and more than enough to make the correction/deletion on the file As a CRO we should be able to obtain by purchase or free subscription full credit report for our clients. Instead CRAs refuse to even accept our calls... Annual credit reports are in three different formats, with no scores and are very confusing for an average consumer to read. Consumer report sites like from each bureau do provide combined tri-merged credit report but for a fee, why can't annual credit report be in the same format and have a side by side comparison report? I can't help but to think this is done on purpose, to further confuse and mislead consumers Dismissed BKs should not be reporting on credit. Although it is their policy to keep reporting bankruptcies which are filed or adjudicated for 10 years, the Fair Credit Reporting Act mentions nothing in Section 1681c relating to bankruptcy about dismissals or filings. The law states from date of adjudication or date of order for relief. Any case, civil or otherwise, that has been dismissed no longer exists in the eyes of the law and a case filed may never have actually been adjudicated. Therefore, they have no right to maintain information which the government has deemed nonexistent. However, almost all dismissed BKs are reported and our attempts to correct/remove them in accordance with rules and regulations goes ignored with CRAs immediately treading our dispute as frivolous without even reviewing court docs we send in to support our claim. It is only fair that in accordance with Section 1681(a)(5) of the FCRA to delete this information from our consumers credit report EFX is now automating their phone access, and NOW requesting phone # for the client for "identity verification" and we are witnessing calls and texts from Equifax to our consumers with advertisement and/or "alert" messages. This is nothing short of threat tactic, to scare the client to purchase their monitoring service. Purchasing credit monitoring service should be from choice not from fear, this is unfair to average consumer. CRAs should not be outsourcing phone centers to different countries... when consumer calls in to question information on their report, they are forced to speak with agents in Philippines-EFX, India for TU, and EXP. Consumer is then forced to release all of their personal information i.e. ss #, date of birth, account numbers and etc to someone with minimum training and below than average English...How can they say they use lates technology to protect consumers identity, when someone in those countries can just walk out with all that info, and what is the guarantee that they are not collection our citizens personal identification that can later be compromised by another country. With as much revenue as CRAs make they should be able to have local offices and call centers in USA, it would only be fair for our consumers to have easy and safe access to THIER OWN records. We would have love to attend this workshop in December but due to prior engagements can't. Would it be possible for us to join the workshop electronically ?

comment: I am about to tell you something that you likely have NOT yet heard: I am a Board Certified Ophthalmologist, a Fellow of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, a Fellow of the New York Academy of Medicine and a Fellow of the American College of Surgeons. I FIT AND DISPENSE only specialty contact lenses. I do not delegate the fitting process (which is a truly on-going process) to anyone. The vast majority of my contact lens patients have tried contact lenses elsewhere and have not been successful at being fitted with lenses, which achieve best-corrected visual acuities, satisfactory comfort and ophthalmic SAFETY. I do NOT fit ANY disposable contact lenses. Contact lenses are PROSTHESES, which sit upon our most sensitive and vital sense organs. Unfortunately, contact have become treated as commodity items, fitted by non-physicians, and obtainable by phone, internet, pharmacies, or mail-order. This has occurred for many reasons: 1) The contact lens manufacturing industry has trivialized the PROSTHETIC nature of contact lenses. In its efforts to capture the profits from the contact lens solutions market, they prefer patients to pay their contact lens dollars for disposable mass-produced plastic, rather than for fluids. This is solely an economic issue. 2) In the interest of giving patients "what they want", rather than what is safe, eyecare providers (many are non-M.D.'s, i.e., optometrists and dispensing opticians) have jumped on the bandwagon. This also in solely an economic issue. 3) The Government, in its quest to assist consumers in saving money, has ignored SAFETY concerns, in efforts to enable patients to obtain contact lenses from non-professional sources, to the point that after the fitting process, the clinician no longer has the ability to monitor, or to modify the contact lenses. This is also solely an economic issue. NOT ONE of these reasons is based on patient HEALTH, or SAFETY. Once the patient has the ability to obtain contact lenses from a multitude of sources, they often make uninformed choices in the interest of cost. In my practice, ALMOST ALL infectious keratitis cases (corneal ulcers, infected corneal abrasions) are caused by DISPOSABLE contact lenses (not obtained from me) and foolish wear choices (i.e. continuing to wear a commoditized contact lens on an inflamed eye), which are COMPLETELY AVOIDABLE. When, several years ago, New York State enacted a mandate to provide consumers with their contact lens "prescriptions", my fellow ophthalmologists and I were inundated with unreasonable requests from patients for contact lens prescriptions, for which they were NEVER FITTED! I spent weeks negotiating with the NYS Attorney General to develop a form to comply with NYS law, yet not to leave me with unlimited liability, should the patient get him/herself into trouble, in the act of using their data in unwise, or dangerous ways. I argued successfully that a "prescription" (from the Latin order, "MAKETH THOU") is literally an ORDER FROM the clinician for a pharmacist, or device dispenser to make, or to give something to the patient. The NYS law forcing clinicians to provide contact lens DATA, is truly NOT A PRESCRIPTION, since the request almost never comes from the clinician, but from the PATIENT, under GOVERNMENT mandate. The NYS Attorney General agreed, and permitted me to use the language "contact lens DATA", and further permitted me to include the statement, "these DATA do not constitute a PRESCRIPTION", since the request for same originated with the patient, and NOT the clinician. He agreed that should the patient incur injury, for having used these data improperly, that this statement would shield me from liability, for being forced to do something that I consider CLINICALLY UNWISE. In addition he permitted me to release the requested contact lens data (like any other part of the medical record) with only a written, signed request. There was NO mandate for requiring the patient to acknowledge RECEIPT IN WRITING, other than keeping a copy of the data form in the patients chart. It is hard enough to get patients to sign the myriad of already government-mandated forms. In addition, my experience has demonstrated that most patients, who request contact lens data, do not want to travel to the office for the data and only want the data mailed to them. Once requested, I have found that these patient RARELY EVER return to my office, initially saying that they just want the data "for travel purposes", resulting in un-ending, un-supervised contact lens dispensing and use, from then on. I truly hope that the FTC will put patient SAFETY ahead of FINANCIAL considerations. The FTC's mandating that patients have the right to inflict injury upon themselves, without the medical knowledge to make such a decision, is immoral. Do NOT enact such an FTC mandate! The eyes of America are precious to both patients (who usually don't realize it until injured) and to clinicians, who care for them.

comment: Speaking strictly in regards to the U.S. watch industry, the Made in the USA designation has such restrictive and arduous rules for sourcing and manufacturing that it is absurd for almost any American watch brand attempting to obtain it. Most Americans are unaware that for 150 years America boasted a thriving and successful watch industry that employed thousands. We pioneered precision mass production, making reliable and accurate watches. However, by the 1960s American companies had gone out of business or had been bought out by foreign companies. The American watch industry has joined a long list of manufacturing sectors that have disappeared from the scene and with it millions of high paying, secure industrial jobs that had been built by the American middle class. The story of the long-lost American watch business is really the story of American manufacturing, with jobs and production gone overseas to save costs. While theres an increased demand from the consumer for American watches, the FTC restrictions place American watch brands at a distinct disadvantage with respect to our Swiss counterparts. The importance of American watches and the revival of the American watch industry cannot be overstated. Thanks to a renewed interest in American-made goods, a few smaller startup American watch brands are attempting to bring U.S. production back. While Switzerland and Asia are capable of churning out mechanical movements at scale and at low price points, America has not had the same kind of manufacturing support since the decline of the industry nearly 60 years ago, and revitalizing the industry has become the objective of quite a few companies in the past 5 years. More people are taking a moment to flip over an item or fish for a label and ask, is it Made in the USA? The biggest hurdle to the American watch industry may be that a new mind-set is needed we put men on the moon and three rovers on Mars, yet we cant see that we are competing in a global watch market worth $43 billion dollars which is Switzerland's 2nd largest sector, is 22% of their GDP and employs over 57,000 people? This is the most industrious nation in the world and the cynics are saying we can't do what the Swiss and Chinese are doing? The British and the Germans are doing it so surely we can do it. American companies are however at a disadvantage due to the stringent FTC requirements. If the clothier Patagonia can't achieve the label (https://www.patagonia.com/blog/2012/04/patagonia-clothing-made-where-how-why/) then what hope does a fledgling US watch company have?

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. I have filed numerous complaints with the FTC regarding the unscrupulous practice of on-line retailers such as Hubble Contact Lenses *dba Vision Path, Inc). Hubble actively exploits the passive verification system allowed by the FCLCA to send prescription required medical devices to people who have never been fit nor even examined for their brand of contact lenses, in clear violation of the law. Recently, they sent 6 passive "verification" requests to me for people whom I have never even met, let alone never examined, The FCLCA does NOT allow them to passively create a prescription, only to passively verify one that already exists. The FTC's continued efforts to punish Drs with ridiculous extra paperwork when you turn a blind eye to the farce that on-line retailers have made out of a prescription required medical device is appalling. If you were actually concerned about patient access to their actual prescription, you will stop this nonsense that you openly allow to continue on a daily basis. Additionally, why do you not apply such a ridiculous paperwork equirement to pharmacies? Why does a pharmacist not have to inform patients and make them sign a piece of paper stating that they are free to take a prescription anywhere, and that there are places that may offer lower prices? comment: Despite public outcry and many consumer complaints, it is not at all obvious that loot boxes should be considered a form of gambling or that they represent a cause of serious harm. The main problem seems to revolve around a confusion among the gaming public between genuinely harmful products and products that are simply unappealing to consumers. Many gamers dislike loot box mechanics because they feel they disrupt the gameplay experience, especially by providing ways to unfairly unbalance competitive play by providing rewards that incentivise "pay-to-win" tactics. This frustration is understandable, but it is not equivalent to making the case for regulating game developers and their revenue models. Much of the outcry over loot boxes consists of the same kind of moral panic that appears around practically every innovation in art or media, including radio, television, comic books, trading cards, board games, and virtually every original genre of music in the last century. And like those older innovations, loot boxes (and microtransactions in general) must be understood in their appropriate economic context. The economics of the game industry are changing rapidly and revenue models must evolve if the industry hopes to survive. Loot boxes are a case study of this kind of experimentation, and one that is still being played out. Crucially, we do not know whether consumers will ultimately decide for or against loot boxes. Likewise, the existing academic literature on loot boxes and addictive behaviours, though well-intentioned, suffers from a wide range of problems relating to issues like choice of research methods and models, sampling, self-selection bias, and data interpretation. As a result, it does not provide a rationale for regulating loot boxes or for restricting their marketing or sale. Furthermore, game developers and publishers, as well as industry trade associations and other stakeholders have demonstrated that they are taking the controversy seriously by modifying loot boxes to reduce or remove risk elements and by making draw rates transparent and/or more favourable to players. In several cases loot boxes have been removed completely from games. Parental warnings have also been updated and new educational initiatives have been launched by trade associations like the ESRB. Together, these examples show that self-regulation--which is really just a way of talking about how businesses try to satisfy customers by constantly updating their products--is active in the industry. A study of these self-regulatory efforts is available in a peer-reviewed paper titled, "The Macro Problem of Microtransactions: The Self-Regulatory Challenges of Video Game Loot Boxes" (see the attached file, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bushor.2019.03.001). A brief summary is also provided in the second attached file, which was submitted to the UK Parliamentary inquiry on Immersive and Addictive Technologies.

comment: I'm glad to see this rule being reviewed. Having two children, it is extremely worrisome to see schools using technology in a way that children's personal information of all types can, and are collected on a regular basis. My kids MUST use google classroom in school, and turn in assignments via google. This information which is the result of teacher assignments, asking for kids to write about opinion pieces, demonstrating decision making, among other assignments can be used to develop an entire personality profile on a single child. I have witnessed online apps where the app simply asks the child's age, with no additional proof requirement, then proceeds to asks series of questions, again, all of which are developed to produce a data profile of the children playing. I believe our government, which guarantees certain rights under the 4th and 9th Amendment, has an obligation to protect our children, above all else, from unknowingly giving up their rights of all forms of privacy online, to include, IP Address & other computer identifiers. I would like to see where all biometric identifiable information becomes the property of the person to whom it belongs, and is not allowed to be used in any form as data mining information. Within the past two years or more I am witnessing more and more of our personal identifiable information being collected without proper permission. I enter the doctor's office with my children and the front desk persons are asking my children to have their palm read for the biometric identifier without even asking parental permission. They act as if it is a requirement. We enter another office and they tell us they need a facial picture to be scanned into their software for identification. My son recently called our bank about his debit card and was asked to perform a voice identifier so his voice could be used for his identification. Our family has the been the victim of identity theft on three occasions. Although we did not end up with a breach of our credit or monetary loss, it shows the risk involved with allowing our children to have their identifiable information on the web in ANY way. Some of this information (biometrics) cannot be "re-made". Once it has been breached and misused, there is no making a "new" hand, eye, face, etc. Please raise the age limit for the collection of any private data, please make ALL private data the property of the person whom entered the information, and please make a very stiff penalty if it is ever found misused. We seem to be going down a slippery slope of losing all right to privacy.
