comment: As a practicing ophthalmologist, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. While I would welcome changes to the Contact Lens Rule that prioritize patient safety, the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses that are already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that we believe puts our patients at risk. While we appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices. Because of the administrative burdens of dealing with contact lens prescriptions I have severely reduced my prescribing of contact lenses. The economic burdens of administrative compliance with this new regulations would except in rare cases encourage me not to fit or prescribe contact lenses. This is just another example of an uncompensated economic and regulatory burden imposed on Ophthalmologists. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

comment: As of writing this, I am close to obtaining an Associate's Degree as a Paralegal. Yet despite adulthood, I am a gamer; I play video games for fun and have since my days as a child. I have seen the video game industry grow and change in a vast amount of ways. Today, the pressing issue with the industry is the matter of Microtransactions, game content that a player would purchase with real money in a video game that they may have already spent money to purchase, but rather specifically on Loot Boxes. For those who are not aware, Loot Boxes are a form of video game Microtransaction, which players open to reveal a random selection of in-game items. Make no mistake with this; Loot Boxes are a form of gambling, and so are in dire need for regulation, if not being banned from video games. Why are Loot Boxes gambling? Presently, gambling is defined to have three components: Consideration, risk (or chance), and a prize. Loot Boxes, as they stand, have all three of these components. First, Loot Boxes are typically obtained through the purchase of real-world money, which is the Consideration. Second, the risk or the chance. This is perhaps the most ambiguous, since Risk is often interpreted to the likelihood of loss. I would argue that the focus should be more on the fact that the outcome itself is uncertain. The player has absolutely no input on the outcome, or in this case, the player has no control over what prizes are in a Loot Box. Another way to see Risk in Loot Boxes is the possibility of the player not receiving their desired loot; often times, the desired loot are the most rarest, which leads to Prize. Third, Prizes are obviously present in Loot Boxes. They come in the form of in-game items that players then may use, which these uses ranging from gaining a competitive advantage or simply for cosmetic purposes. These are the items that players seek, and often times these Loot Boxes are the only means for players to obtain them. These Prizes often have real-world value; an example of this is in the online tactical game Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, where players may open up crates for weapon "skins" which players may sell on the online Steam marketplace. Even if players cannot trade these in-game items, these in-game items still retain real-world value, through the fact that it has costed money to purchase the Loot Box they came in. With all this in consideration, it is safe to say that Loot Boxes are a form of gambling, simply in a different form targeting a different demographic. Then, there are the feelings elicited. comment: Subject: Complaint Regarding Airline Fee Practices and Declining Passenger Comfort/Value To the U.S. Department of Transportation, Office of Aviation Consumer Protection: I am writing to file a formal complaint regarding the current practices of U.S. airlines related to pricing transparency, escalating ancillary fees, and the corresponding decline in passenger comfort and service quality. Fee Concerns: Airlines routinely advertise low base fares that do not reflect the actual cost of travel. By the time mandatory or near-mandatory fees are added — for carry-on bags, seat selection, and other items that were once included in the ticket price — the final cost is often significantly higher than the advertised fare. This practice misleads consumers and makes genuine price comparison across airlines difficult or impossible at the point of search. Value and Comfort Concerns: At the same time these fees have increased, seat pitch and width have shrunk, legroom has decreased, and basic amenities once included in the fare (snacks, checked bags, seat assignments) have been stripped out and resold as add-ons. Passengers are effectively paying more for less — higher total costs paired with a materially reduced level of comfort and service compared to prior years. Requested Action: I urge the Department to: 1. Enforce and strengthen upfront, all-in fee disclosure requirements at the point of search, before a consumer begins the booking process 2. Investigate whether current fee structures constitute deceptive pricing practices 3. Consider minimum standards for seat pitch/width or other passenger comfort protections, given that shrinking space has coincided with rising total travel costs As a paying consumer, I should be able to see the true, total cost of my ticket before I commit to a purchase, and I should not be expected to accept declining physical comfort as the tradeoff for fees that continue to rise. Thank you for your attention to this matter

comment: My name is Forrest and I'm 22 years old. I'm currently enrolled in college studying computer science and am supporting myself through YouTube. Over the past few years I have created my own business through content creation on the YouTube platform. My generation and the ones coming after me find our entertainment in YouTube and other online video sharing sites. Please consider changing COPPA laws to suit the needs of today and allow YouTube to continue being the #1 entertainment platform in the world. Thank you for your time.

comment: The discussion seems to be centered around the cost of loot boxes in general. So far as I can understand, people have not necessarily had an issue with microtransactions. It has been with loot boxes. Loot boxes are predatory in that they prevent a player from purchasing the specific item they want. They are introduced into a game to balloon costs and promote gambling. There is a chance that the cost can be lower than what you would have otherwise paid if you had been given the opportunity to purchase the item directly (gambling). Keep in mind also that nobody's arguing against the free loot boxes that are handed out for free. It's specifically the loot boxes that are being sold that are the issue. I'll give a great example. Vindictus comes out with a new character. In their shop they happen to have a bunch of outfits. However, all of the good outfits are locked behind loot boxes. That is to say, you can't purchase them directly. If you want them, you must continue to buy loot boxes until you get them. Rather than spending $30 on that outfit, Vindictus squeezes out $300-$700 depending on how lucky you are. Tera has two qualities of outfits. They have the crappy quality that you can buy directly. They also have the legendary glowing quality that is locked behind a loot box. Get ready to spend a solid $300-$500 if you want the glowing one. My personal problem with loot boxes is that games that employ them due so specifically to squeeze money out of its consumers. It's not about gambling. It's not about surprise mechanics. There are plenty of other gamers I see that go through the same thing for these outfits. Keep in mind that right now I'm just talking about outfits. I'm just talking about looking great in a game. When a game starts introducing stats to give players an unfair advantage, that's when stuff really starts getting crazy. Now you have to go through this loot box paywall to even be competitive. One can argue to simply not purchase those items. I'd argue to not even play the game at that point as you aren't going to be competitive without spending that $300-$500 or more every other month. These loot boxes have proliferated to such a degree that choosing not to play will quite literally leave you with nothing to play. I enjoy the MMORPG genre. My choices, if I want to avoid loot boxes, are more or less games from 20 years ago. That's how staggering this issue is. It isn't going to go away because not everyone is willing to give up all online games of particular genres to avoid loot boxes. We've got a counter wave of games coming in with the mantras of "No P2W" and "No Loot Boxes," but they are going to be very few and they are years and years away. This is more than being about protecting children. This is about protecting the consumer from predatory practices designed to squeeze them for all they're worth.

comment: The problem I have with loot boxes and in-game purchases of coins/gems is this: Often as a gamer you have 100's if not 1000's of hours invested in the game. Then you buy a loot box or coins in-game. And it doesn't work. You try to work it out using these arcane in-game ticket systems but that fails, too. You've paid for this often using a credit card so you have recourse to complain about a purchase "not as described" or you simply never received it. But here's the problem. They've totally got you and they know it. If you file a credit card charge complaint, they simply permanently ban you from the game. So as you have so much time and money invested already, you don't dare complain too much. You have very few rights as a gamer. And some gaming companies are very unscrupulous, taking your money, making you think it's a great deal, and it's not, or you fail to get it, and then you have almost no recourse unless you want to lose everything you've put into the game. Games can ban you for any reason and often there is no right of appeal. I have known people that had over ten years and thousands of hours in game, as well as thousands of dollars invested, only to lose everything due to some misunderstanding with customer service. And they have no recourse. They are just banned. They can't even email the game managers as you have to be in-game to do that. Trying to call them via phone or other contact methods are often impossible. In several cases I have personal information about, this game was that person's entire life. All their friends were in the game. Everyday they would be there, joyfully chatting with all their friends. And then some little thing happens, and the game executes it's terms of service and bans the person, and they commit suicide. This is an unseen and seldom discussed epidemic among gamers that have isolated themselves for years doing almost nothing in their life but playing a game, often they are disabled people who live alone, and when they complain about the loot box and get banned, they kill themselves. It's not a rare occurrence, although it doesn't happen often. They become addicted to the game and when that's suddenly turned off it's too much for them to bear. Playing Ultima Online for over 10 years when it first came out I knew one person who committed suicide after being banned. In playing Eve Online for over 10 years I knew several people who committed suicide, and there were rumors of others that I couldn't verify. At least two of these people were banned when they complained to customer service about issues with in-game purchases.

comment: September 14, 2019 Federal Trade Commission 600 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW Washington, DC 20580 Safelite is not only the nations largest purchaser of Original Equipment Equivalent (OEE) replacement vehicle glass, we are also the nations largest purchaser (outside of vehicle manufacturers themselves) of Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) logoed/branded vehicle glass which we typically purchase directly from the vehicle manufacturers. So, we dont see ourselves as a competitor but a partner of the vehicle manufacturers. However, this partnership is becoming increasingly strained because of how vehicle manufacturers are positioning OEM vehicle glass parts and service with the advent of new Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) features such as Lane Departure Warning, Lane Keeping Assist, etc. When a vehicle with ADAS enabled by a front facing camera system has a windshield replaced, vehicle manufacturers require that a recalibration of the ADAS system be performed and it is that specific situation where vehicle manufacturers are Nixing the Fix. Over the past eighteen months, using state of the art equipment manufactured by Bosch, Safelite has successfully performed 400,000 front camera ADAS recalibrations on vehicles representing twenty eight vehicle makes from Audi to Volvo. These recalibrations have been successfully performed on OEM and OEE windshields. We are confident this volume of experience qualifies us as not only vehicle glass repair and replacement specialists, but also ADAS recalibration specialists. In fact, as part of a multi-national company our dedicated technical innovation team exists for the sole purpose of developing the best technologies to serve our customers. Our commitment to ADAS recalibration across all vehicle makes, models and years is unmatched in the VGRR industry, investing millions of dollars in ADAS recalibration technology in the past five years. It is disturbing then to have our customers, who for whatever reason, make contact with a new vehicle dealer and when inquiring about ADAS recalibration, they are told in the best case your vehicle MUST have an OEM windshield or worst case you must use OEM branded glass and the car needs to be (re) calibrated at a dealer for the system to work to the most incriminatory using non-OEM glass will void your warranty. These difficult situations are a regular occurrence for Safelite to have to manage with individual vehicle owners, as well as our fleet customers. Regardless of how bold and aggressive the tactics, all such statements are purposefully intended to sow fear and doubt in the mind of the customer with the hope that the customer will feel compelled to go to the dealership to purchase OEM glass and have the dealership perform the recalibration. In some situations, after Safelite installed an OEE windshield, having learned of the scare tactics of the dealer and/or the vehicle manufacturer, the customer demanded OEM glass be installed. So, we unnecessarily had to remove a perfectly good piece of OEE glass, wait for the delivery of OEM glass and then reinstallall at Safelites cost. Not fair to the customer, nor Safelite or any other service provider qualified to perform ADAS recalibration services. This unfortunate but recurring problem is increasing in frequency, as most new vehicles are equipped with ADAS. But dont take just our word for it. As seen in Exhibit C vehicle manufacturers are boldly publishing documents clearly stating that only an OEM part and dealer service will work in ADAS situations while casting any OEE products or non-dealership repair services as dangerous for the driver. Exhibit D goes even further with this vehicle manufacturer stating that only their dealers can perform the recalibration servicepatently untrue, misleading and deceptive to the reader. Upon hearing or reading such scaremongering it is no surprise that an individual vehicle owner will turn away from the aftermarket and head to the new vehicle dealer to ensure that their warranty and safety not be jeopardized. Over the past seventy-two years, Safelite, as the nations largest vehicle glass repair, replacement and now recalibration specialist, has worked tirelessly to build trust and confidence with individual vehicle owners and fleet customers alike. The attached examples and statements from vehicle manufacturers and their affiliated service departments which impugn our reputation, and create fear and doubt in our customers minds is a genuine concern and antithetical to the very pro-competitive and fair trade mission of the Federal Trade Commission. We appreciate that the FTC is seeking input on this vital area of commerce. We trust the FTC will continue to protect consumers and competition from false, deceptive and misleading statements of vehicle manufacturers regarding ADAS recalibration services. More details attached. Sincerely, Edward Sprigler Vice PresidentStrategic Initiatives Safelite AutoGlass

Safelite is not only the nations largest purchaser of Original Equipment Equivalent (OEE) replacement vehicle glass, we are also the nations largest purchaser (outside of vehicle manufacturers themselves) of Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) logoed/branded vehicle glass which we typically purchase directly from the vehicle manufacturers. So, we dont see ourselves as a competitor but a partner of the vehicle manufacturers. 

However, this partnership is becoming increasingly strained because of how vehicle manufacturers are positioning OEM vehicle glass parts and service with the advent of new Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) features such as Lane Departure Warning, Lane Keeping Assist, etc. When a vehicle with ADAS enabled by a front facing camera system has a windshield replaced, vehicle manufacturers require that a recalibration of the ADAS system be performed and it is that specific situation where vehicle manufacturers are Nixing the Fix.

Over the past eighteen months, using state of the art equipment manufactured by Bosch, Safelite has successfully performed 400,000 front camera ADAS recalibrations on vehicles representing twenty eight vehicle makes from Audi to Volvo. These recalibrations have been successfully performed on OEM and OEE windshields. We are confident this volume of experience qualifies us as not only vehicle glass repair and replacement specialists, but also ADAS recalibration specialists. In fact, as part of a multi-national company our dedicated technical innovation team exists for the sole purpose of developing the best technologies to serve our customers. Our commitment to ADAS recalibration across all vehicle makes, models and years is unmatched in the VGRR industry, investing millions of dollars in ADAS recalibration technology in the past five years. 

It is disturbing then to have our customers, who for whatever reason, make contact with a new vehicle dealer and when inquiring about ADAS recalibration, they are told in the best case your vehicle MUST have an OEM windshield or worst case you must use OEM branded glass and the car needs to be (re) calibrated at a dealer for the system to work to the most incriminatory using non-OEM glass will void your warranty. These difficult situations are a regular occurrence for Safelite to have to manage with individual vehicle owners, as well as our fleet customers. Regardless of how bold and aggressive the tactics, all such statements are purposefully intended to sow fear and doubt in the mind of the customer with the hope that the customer will feel compelled to go to the dealership to purchase OEM glass and have the dealership perform the recalibration. 

In some situations, after Safelite installed an OEE windshield, having learned of the scare tactics of the dealer and/or the vehicle manufacturer, the customer demanded OEM glass be installed. So, we unnecessarily had to remove a perfectly good piece of OEE glass, wait for the delivery of OEM glass and then reinstallall at Safelites cost. Not fair to the customer, nor Safelite or any other service provider qualified to perform ADAS recalibration services. This unfortunate but recurring problem is increasing in frequency, as most new vehicles are equipped with ADAS.

But dont take just our word for it. As seen in Exhibit C vehicle manufacturers are boldly publishing documents clearly stating that only an OEM part and dealer service will work in ADAS situations while casting any OEE products or non-dealership repair services as dangerous for the driver. Exhibit D goes even further with this vehicle manufacturer stating that only their dealers can perform the recalibration servicepatently untrue, misleading and deceptive to the reader. Upon hearing or reading such scaremongering it is no surprise that an individual vehicle owner will turn away from the aftermarket and head to the new vehicle dealer to ensure that their warranty and safety not be jeopardized. 

Over the past seventy-two years, Safelite, as the nations largest vehicle glass repair, replacement and now recalibration specialist, has worked tirelessly to build trust and confidence with individual vehicle owners and fleet customers alike. The attached examples and statements from vehicle manufacturers and their affiliated service departments which impugn our reputation, and create fear and doubt in our customers minds is a genuine concern and antithetical to the very pro-competitive and fair trade mission of the Federal Trade Commission. We appreciate that the FTC is seeking input on this vital area of commerce. We trust the FTC will continue to protect consumers and competition from false, deceptive and misleading statements of vehicle manufacturers regarding ADAS recalibration services.

comment: The concerns for Loot Boxes should be looking toward Gambling and the components that make up its psychological profile and effects to establish relevancy vs deviation between the two things, especially as it relates to children, adolescents, and development. I do believe there are psychological reasons why gambling is illegal for minors, not only because of their general lack of overall wealth and the increased likelihood for undue risks but because of the potential for addiction that it has? But other people would be better to highlight those facets and I hope the FTC looks into those issues seriously. Likewise, the difference between a digital-only, non-tradeable good should be considered versus the physical, resellable good of a physical good (i.e., a baseball card, a toy). Games Terms of Service explicitly disallow selling of in-game goods and services (leveling up your character for you, trading an in-game item for real world money/etc), and have and will continue to shut down people's accounts, and lock them out of service or ever participating in that game, when caught. However, in the same environment, it is not illegal to take your baseball card and sell it to another person, even if the creator company of that baseball card doesn't want you to. They have no recourse (legal or otherwise) to stop you from doing that, because it is "your" property. But in the digital space, the creator of the game has absolute say; if they say you can't trade this rare item you just found for someone else's real-world (or even in-game!) money, and ban you for it, you have no consumer protection, nor any legal opportunity to fight that undue punishment as a consumer. Likewise, when it comes to gambling, I suggest you look toward other countries: China now forces games with loot boxes (like Overwatch, a game by blizzard entertainment) to disclose percentage chances for items and objects of specific rarities (common is the most likely type of item you will get, followed by 'rare' quality, followed by mythic quality, with legendary quality being the most rare). Allowing (and keeping) the consumer aware of their chances to obtain items by quality allows them to decided with a more informed opinion on whether they do or don't want to spend money to try and acquire specific items from specific qualities, and should be a bare minimum for every single game.

comment: I comment regarding the downgrading of the Level 1 Trauma Center in Kingsport TN and Level 2 Trauma Center in Bristol TN/VA to Level 3 Trauma Centers due to the Ballad Merger. As a part of the emergency response community for 20+ years and a past chair of the Sullivan County Emergency Preparedness Council, I am well aware of the need for prompt and expert response in a mass injury incident. With today's terrorist concerns this is even more of an issue. Kingsport/Sullivan Co. have major industries and also several potentials for terrorist activity. I am not aware of any questions asked or reviewed before Ballad planned their downgrading. Reliable ground transportation to Johnson City in an emergency is limited. In our area air transport is not always possible - and ability to land multiple helicopters in Johnson City is far less than in Kingsport. The Level 1 Trauma Center in Kingsport was built to the Level 1 standards and stood ready due to years of community and staff support. The Center in Johnson City does not have that capability. In everyday -non major emergency or disaster status - State statistics showing the number of citizens of the Ballad Service area who are OUTSIDE the 1 hour (Golden Hour) for Johnson City is over 70,000 - the number of citizens OUTSIDE the 1 hour for Kingsport is less than 20,000. And we choose Johnson City for the only Level 1 center - why? Never to my knowledge have these issues been addressed by Ballad. The public advantage to the community at large is seriously at risk. While major emergencies do not happen everyday - when they do the community expects their government and health care facilities to have planned for them....that is certainly doubtful with the current plan.

comment: I would like to make a comment in emphatic opposition to the current FTC proposal on the contact lens rule. Firstly, additional regulation on doctors is not what is required here to ensure patient safety. We as doctors always have the patients' best interest in mind when recommending regulations changes for contact lenses. Adding requirements to doctors' schedules to ensure patient safety is putting pressure on the wrong party; it is illegal contact lens sellers who are the problem here, and they should be the ones who are regulated to ensure patient safety. Robocalls should be outlawed; I have had myriad instances of patients in my chair wearing contact lenses that have temporarily or, in some cases, permanently damaged that patient's eye health. The patients do not know any better because of false advertising on the part of these sellers. But the robocalls so often are impossible to verify, and if they are rejected the lenses get dispensed to the patient anyway. In many other cases, the robocalls come to my PERSONAL phone. I do not pick up for phone numbers I do not recognize on my personal phone for my own safety. In these instances, the seller is unequivocally getting their lenses with false verification strategies. There is NO adequate way in today's healthcare system to safely and accurately ensure that a patient's prescription is correctly verified with a robocall-based system. I have only been a licensed doctor for ONE year at the point that I am typing this, and I have already seen an astounding number of patients with permanently damaged vision and eye health due to the indiscretion of the current contact lens regulation policy. This responsibility and lack of oversight lies partially on the seller, but mostly on the FTC. I am sorely disappointed in the FTC's poor treatment of the American Contact lens consumer. The FTC is doing these patients a disservice by continuing to allow predatory companies to sell them unsafe products without their doctor's approval.

comment: Hi, I made a comment a few days ago on how this would affect my job as a YouTuber. But now I'm making another comment about how it will affect young viewers. There are a lot of content creators that make educational videos for children. A lot of them have announced that they will discontinue this, as COPPA will not allow them to make enough income to be able to afford to continue. The ones who really lose out are children. Teachers use these videos in schools. To lose these videos would be a shame. It also discriminates against low income children. There are a lot of families that live paycheck to paycheck who don't have cable or wifi. All they have is a smart phone with a free YouTube app. Taking away incomes from kid friendly content creators will cause them to stop making videos for children. The low income children who ONLY have YouTube to watch because it's free, will then have less to watch, including less educational videos. This would be terrible. COPPA needs to be updated badly. It would be a shame for so many to lose jobs and for so many kids to lose high quality content to watch. When there is less kids content, they are more likely to watch inappropriate content not made for kids, and would still get targeted ads. So in the case of YouTube, COPPA not only doesn't protect children at all, but makes things worse for them. Also, there are so many videos on YouTube starting from 2005, that it will be impossible to go through every single one and mark which are directed at kids. And then there is the huge gray area of content that both kids and adults enjoy that people will not know whether or not to flag them as for kids, and risk getting in trouble for choosing the wrong way. This law also discriminates against parents. As a content creator, I like to make videos of myself with my children. I would rather see the FTC actually protect children, like the kidfluencers who are on YouTube. I already save for my children in savings accounts, but it would make more sense to make sure children who are on channels that generate a lot of revenue have savings for their futures similar to how child actors do. Also COPPA will make videos of toys seem like they are all for children, and there are many adults who collect toys and create art dolls such as reborn dolls. This discriminates against adults who are interested in legos and reborns. I myself am a reborn doll collector, and subscribe to many channels about dolls. It would not be right for me not to get notified to watch these videos because the rule would treat me as if I were a child. I also have reborn doll videos that all ages watch. So in conclusion, there must be another way to protect children without obliterating the content and destroying jobs. Kids should have a right to good content and the creators who only tried to make family friendly content could keep their jobs.

comment: Im happy to see that this current review of the Childens Online Privacy Protection Rule is looking to address application to the educational technology sector and specifically asking the questions: Should operators be able to use the personal information collected from children to improve the product? Should operators be able to use the personal information collected from children to improve other educational or non-educational products? Should de-identification of the personal information be required for such uses? I do believe that there are types of personal information that would be useful to operators to improve their products, and that they should be allowed to do so, since improved educational products would be beneficial to future students. I also believe there should be a limit, both in what types of information can be used and what it can be used for. Considering that the children in question are not yet old enough to give their own consent for the collection and use of such information, and the potential for any electronically gathered information to persist in databases for long periods of time is very real, its vitally important that the information only be allowed to be collected and used for any purpose if it can be de-identified and is general in nature such that it could not be reasonably used to re-identify any specific individual or group of individuals.

comment: as the situation presently stands Consumers are frequently given either no choice or a monopoly choice in their internet service providers. this is caused by a number of factors such as local and state regulations and infrastructure limitations, vertical agreements and integration designed to limit competition, and horizontal agreements between existing providers meant to limit competition. this hurts consumers by keeping prices unnaturally high without providing any service benefit. even with near monopoly power over markets ISP's continue to take unfair advantage of consumers by 'throttling' connection speeds to well below advertised rates a practice which has already begun to have an impact on critical government services such as emergency response. this also adversely impacts business consumers in an age where such 'throttling' can impede workflow or hinder delivery of services. ISP's also collect and sell data based on consumers internet traffic without their knowledge or consent. this data is often poorly protected and puts millions of Americans at a high risk of suffering Identity theft when these databases are breached, which they are on a regular basis. this practice if left unregulated will have severe economic impacts as these breaches and the identity theft resulting from them renders credit reporting agency reports useless in determining the risk level of borrowers. In closing i would like to see the FTC enact the following changes to how ISP's are regulated: 1- ISP's may not collect consumer information and browsing history without that consumers informed consent 2- ISP's may not sell consumer data and browsing history without that consumers informed consent including exactly who that data is being sold to 3- ISP's must ensure that any data collected is stored in accordance with information security industry best recommendations. 4- ISP's must advertise the slowest speeds that a consumer can expect for any given service level. 'more than' rather than 'up to' 5- if the government cannot take action to encourage direct competition among ISP's then the ISP's must have their service quality and costs regulated in the same manner as other utilities.

comment: My name is Blake Hunter Yagman, I am the managing attorney and principal of YAGMAN PLLC - a plaintiffs litigation boutique which challenges corporate malfeasance in courtrooms across the country. My firm filed the first ever surveillance pricing case against JetBlue Airways, as well as the first ever surveillance wage fixing case against Uber. I was also responsible for helping to prepare the Senate Judiciary Committee for its investigatory hearing on dynamic and surveillance pricing. For years, companies have weaponized consumer data against their own consumers. This started with the differentiation of pricing in catalogues and persisted, becoming more advanced, into the digital age. The harms are two-fold: (1) different pricing and price discrimination for individuals seeking to purchase the same goods and services or looking to perform the same type of labor and (2) the privacy related harms associated with the mass surveillance and surreptitious data collection needed to power the surveillance pricing apparatus. It is imperative that we protect both consumer and labor rights, as well as privacy rights, which are fundamental legal cornerstones in an age where the use and sale of personal data is the secondary practice of every corporation. The Federal Trade Commission has an obligation to ensure that Section 5 of the FTC Act protects the rights of Americans vulnerable to data that they generally never know is being collected. Respectfully Submitted, Blake Hunter Yagman

comment: We appreciate the opportunity to comment in this important proposed rule related to security of personal information. Regarding the added guidance on specific aspects of information security programs, we disagree with the proposed change because we understand that it may be derive in a tick the box mentality, which could be ineffective to the rapid changing environment of information security. We believe a better approach would be to incorporate non-mandatory guidance or best practices as published informative documents, not part of rulemaking. Regarding the added provisions for accountability, we agree with the proposed changes as it may create a greater sense of accountability for leadership of the financial institutions without generating burdensome requirements. Regarding the exemptions for small businesses, we agree with the proposed changes to alleviate the administrative burden for small business without significantly affecting public interest. Regarding the expanded definition of financial institution, we disagree with the proposed change as it may have unintended future consequences in the constantly changing economic environment potentially affecting new businesses. We think it would be preferable to specifically include finders in the definition of financial institution. Regarding the proposal to include the definition of financial institution and related examples in the Rule itself, we agree with the proposed change because it would provide with greater clarity about the scope of the Rule without generating any negative impact.

comment: I would like to provide an institutional and personal perspective on the Ballad merger. As an unpaid citizen member of the board of one of the larger hospitals in the system, one that not only serves the immediate community but the larger region, I have seen where the merger has already begun to allow for greater resource reallocation (both in terms of quality personnel and essential supply chain) to enhance services and lower costs. That provides for greater quality of life for them and allows the system to continue to benefit from their services and allows their expertise to serve the region. Additionally, savings associated with the greater purchasing power of the system as a whole can and will be returned to those areas most in need of increased medical services. On a more personal level, I have had an immediate family member who was provided critical care by what was once a competitor hospital to the one on whose board I serve. comment: The FTC should absolutely regulate personalized pricing schemes. At the very least, sellers who use this pricing technique should be required to disclose at the point of sale the distributions of sale prices offered and accepted so that consumers can have the information necessary to make rational economic decisions. Capitalism works best when information flow is maximized. The problem with “covert” pricing schemes like this is that the consumer doesn’t know when they’re being fleeced or rewarded. Yes, it’s extra trouble to provide this information, but if a seller has the resources to use this pricing technique, they have the resources to keep track of offers and acceptances, and make those available to prospective buyers. This way, you preserve a sellers freedom to charge as they want, but you also allow consumers to make more optimal choices.

comment: I am a physician who came to the region roughly ten years ago, and am not employed by Ballad. My tenure in the region has afforded me the opportunity to witness the changes the merger has brought to our healthcare. Holston Valley, the flagship hospital of Wellmont was consistently losing money year after year. It was a victim of the redundant services Wellmont believed it needed to offer in order to compete with Mountain States. For example, two Level I trauma centers and two NICUs in a region of this size did not make economic sense nor did it improve care. Two hospitals within a few miles of each other, Indian Path (Mountain States) and Holston Valley (Wellmont), also duplicated services as the systems competed to attract patients. Competition is good! It lowers costs to consumers, and improves quality. Except in this sort of situation. Both systems were spending (wasting) resources to compete with the other, duplicating high revenue services, while neglecting other services needed in the community; mental health and addiction medicine. There simply wasnt enough money to compete and have resources left to fill those needs. Enter, the COPA. With the merging of the systems, under the close supervision of the TN and VA Departments of Health, the foolish waste of money spent duplicating services could be eliminated while improving the actual quality and available services to the community. No longer would there be a need to have two level one trauma centers, or two NICUs when one would concentrate the skilled personnel required to run such programs, effectively improving care and reducing costs. With the commitments made under the COPA, the resultant savings would not serve to pad the Health Systems bottom line, but instead be reinvested in the community, adding the much needed services mentioned above and ensuring solvency into the future, rather than risking an unserviceable debt burden that could threaten the existence of lower producing hospitals, like those in the rural parts of the region. Is it working? Since the merger the system has been able to consolidate services, improving efficiency and reducing costs, while improving quality in almost every metric. Still in its infancy, Ballad is already delivering on the promises it made to the community; with the improvement of quality mentioned above, recruitment of new physicians to the area, maintenance of rural hospitals, and development of mental health services. The region is finally on track to improve care at all its hospitals, and reduce wasteful spending at the same time. Despite the initial successes, the challenges put upon the new health system has resulted in anger by some who believe healthcare in the region is deteriorating. A nursing shortage affecting many cities (not just here) has negatively impacted the efficiency of our emergency departments and reduced our effective capacity. As a patient it would be easy, and understandable, to attribute this change to the merger, when in reality, the merger has made it possible to increase nursing salaries, and improve retention and recruiting efforts. Another change is that the citizens of Kingsport no longer have a Level I Trauma Center or NICU, and now must drive 20-30 minutes to Johnson City. As a result some of them believe Ballad and the COPA is failing them, and it is understandable that they feel this way; they are experiencing what they perceive is a decrease in available services. The reality paints a different picture, however. One important aspect of the change is that by consolidating care in one hospital, the quality can improve. Our region simply does not have the population to support the number of specialized physicians required to maintain two high-quality Level I centers and NICUs. This is evident in the squandered resources prior to the merger and missed quality measures prior to the consolidation. As a physician, husband, father, and occasional patient, I am confident in the decision made by our Department of Health to allow the merger between Wellmont and Mountain States. Reduced cost, improved quality and access and new services are already in progress. I believe, through adherence to the COPA, care will continue to improve, and citizens of our unique region will benefit for years to come. I also believe that those who are rightfully concerned will come to appreciate the advantages the merger brings to region; quality, access, and sustainability.

comment: This comment is regarding Safeguards Rule, 16 CFR part 314, Project No. P145407. We appreciate the opportunity to comment in this important proposed rule related to security of personal information. Regarding the added guidance on specific aspects of information security programs, we disagree with the proposed change because we understand that it may be derive in a tick the box mentality, which could be ineffective to the rapid changing environment of information security. We believe a better approach would be to incorporate non-mandatory guidance or best practices as published informative documents, not part of rulemaking. Regarding the added provisions for accountability, we agree with the proposed changes as it may create a greater sense of accountability for leadership of the financial institutions without generating burdensome requirements. Regarding the exemptions for small businesses, we agree with the proposed changes to alleviate the administrative burden for small business without significantly affecting public interest. Regarding the expanded definition of financial institution, we disagree with the proposed change as it may have unintended future consequences in the constantly changing economic environment potentially affecting new businesses. We think it would be preferable to specifically include finders in the definition of financial institution. Regarding the proposal to include the definition of financial institution and related examples in the Rule itself, we agree with the proposed change because it would provide with greater clarity about the scope of the Rule without generating any negative impact.

comment: The Federal Trade Commission and other regulatory bodies have not yet provided to the public a clear definition for reasonable cybersecurity management. In April 2018 Center for Internet Security (CIS) published their method for assessing cybersecurity risk to determine whether safeguards are reasonable and appropriate as regulators, litigators, and information security practitioners use the terms. CIS Risk Assessment Method (CIS RAM) describes a process for evaluating cybersecurity risk to determine whether an organizations controls environment: 1. Creates the foreseeability of harm that would be acceptable to the organization and to others. 2. Presents a reasonable burden on the organization. CIS RAM based on the Duty of Care Risk Analysis (DoCRA) Standard provides a model for analyzing risks that supports: 1. Long-established standards for regulatory oversight using cost-benefit analysis (viz. Executive Order 12866, 1993). 2. Common regulatory requirements for using risk analysis to establish reasonableness of security controls (e.g. HIPAA Security Rule, GLBA Safeguards Rule, 23 NYCRR Part 500, Massachusetts 201 CMR 17.00, etc.). 3. Multifactor balancing tests used by courts to determine the reasonableness or negligence of defendants. 4. Information security standards for assessing information security risk (NIST Special Publications 800-30, ISO 27005, RISK IT). Additionally, the model in CIS RAM supports FTCs consistent guidance to the public and to breached organizations for using risk management as a basis for comprehensive security and risk management programs (even despite the benefit of security certifications, e.g. Statement of the Federal Trade Commission. FTC v. LifeLock, December 17, 2015). Because CIS RAM and DoCRA are simply practical models for long-established standards and requirements, FTC and other regulators who refer to these methods will be consistent with well-established enforcement practices. 1. Oversight actions that evaluate whether an organization uses reasonable controls may include review of the organizations risk assessments. Because risk assessments are common requirements to determine the reasonableness of safeguards, these documents should be in-hand as a record of the organizations evaluation of reasonableness. Lack of risk assessments that demonstrate the balance of safeguards against the likelihood and impact of foreseeable threats could clearly constitute an organizations lack of managing reasonable and appropriate controls. 2. Consent orders and injunctive relief that require organizations to improve their security programs can be based on an evaluation of their controls environment, and a proposal for controls that evaluate as reasonable and appropriate as described in the CIS RAM and DoCRA documents. CIS (Center for Internet Security, Inc.) is a forward-thinking, non-profit entity that harnesses the power of a global IT community to safeguard private and public organizations against cyber threats. Our CIS Controls and CIS Benchmarks are the global standard and recognized best practices for securing IT systems and data against the most pervasive attacks. These proven guidelines are continuously refined and verified by a volunteer, global community of experienced IT professionals. CIS is home to the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MSISAC), the go-to resource for cyber threat prevention, protection, response, and recovery for U.S. State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial government entities. (www.cisecurity.org) HALOCK Security Labs Established in 1996, HALOCK Security Labs is an information security professional services firm based in Schaumburg, IL. For more than 20 years, HALOCK has provided Purpose Driven Security services to help organizations achieve their mission and objectives through sound security practices. HALOCK uses their deep background in the legal and regulatory landscape, security technologies and standards, business governance, and data analytics to provide evidence-based security analysis and guidance to their clients. (www.halock.com) For guidance in implementing the CIS RAM: (www.halock.com/cisram)

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. Rachelle Lin, O.D.

comment: National Floors Direct; File No. 182 3085 I was looking to upgrade my house and thought I would start with National Floors Direct. The salesperson arrived on time and was very nice. Before coming up with a price for us, we had a long conversation about the ceramic tile we already have. We asked if we would need to demo the floor and he assured me that I wouldnt need to do that. He explained that the floor gets installed right over the flooring I already had. He said that the floor goes underneath fridge and stove and up to the dishwasher. He also said that the floor would go up to the toilet. This was also hand written on my contract. He also said that I would be responsible for pulling out fridge and stove and unplugging and plugging back in after the job. The day before the installment I received a confirmation call about the floors being installed and they wanted to make sure my toilet was disconnected. I said no. I was told that I would be charged a restocking fee if i did not have the floors installed the next morning. I told them that this is not my fault and that I was not paying that fee. Finally, after my disapproval they agreed to "waive that fee" so finally we rescheduled for a different day when I could have someone come in to remove my toilet along with the fridge and stove. The day before the floor installment was supposed to take place, I had someone come in to remove and unhook fridge, stove and toilet. This person noticed that there was not enough room to install a floor underneath fridge because the fridge went rightup to the cabinets. He said the floor would need to be taken up underneath or we would have to cut our cabinets down or buy a new refrigerator. Thank you Madelyne Adlin

comment: My name is Kevin Kenney and I am an AG Engineer '86 (BS-UNL). I've worked at Southwest Research Institute - Locomotive Test Center San Antonio, TX performing patent research on fuel for internal combustion that lower emissions. I am holder of multiple patents for multi-fuel options for diesel engines. (Patent numbers:#9441560/September 13, 2016 & 8826888/September 9, 2014) My area of expertise is in diesel engine tuning for the purpose of lowering emissions - specifically substituting 'High Octane' clean alcohols (ethanol & methanol) and gaseous fuels (propane & natural gas) in place of diesel fuel. My customers are farmers. I know many of the local technicians working for both company dealerships (with repair software) and independent mechanics (without software). I have also been actively involved with the Nebraska Farm Bureau, testing of biofuels "Ethanol used in Diesel Engines" at University of Nebraska, Lincoln at the Tractor Testing Lab and multiple other activities biofueled/diesel projects. Government Affairs representatives from AEM/EDA filed comments taking the position that the only reason Farmers & Ranchers want Right to Repair legislation is to hack their emissions to avoid EPA Tier 4 emissions compliance. The implication is that farmers are trying to harm the environment which is both insulting and factually unsupported. My experience with farmers tells me that farmers would far prefer to use cleaner fuel than diesel and are frustrated by OEM created software limitations on engines that restrict the use of cleaner options. My patents would allow such options so I have paid very close attention to this issue. The US Copyright Office made software tuning legal in 2016 and expanded the opportunity in 2018 for farmers to hire experts, such as myself, to deliver fuel tuning options they prefer. While the USCO has made hacking technically legal, the practical ability to do so remains blocked in the same way as owner-directed repair. Manufacturers have not made any software, manuals schematics, diagnostics, parts or tools available to the owner, functionally blocking owner control of tunes as well as of repair. Independents techs need the same information made available to dealer techs to help farmers legally Modify or hack their tractors. Without capabilities to retune and re-tune existing firmware and software settings, these tractors will remain belching dirty diesel fuel for the rest of their lives. Tellingly, CASE IH and AGCO both design and make propane and natural gas tractors for, "FOREIGN SALES ONLY" leaving US farmers stuck with diesel. My clients are only able to use clean fuels as an alternative to diesel by hacking/modding. We need the repair software to re-set codes and program/re-program existing engine control units (ECUs) capable of operating with different specs but not yet accessible with manufacturer limitations. Yet farmers seeking to tune their engines do not have the same options as owners of over-the-road vehicles are doing under existing Right to Repair voluntary agreements where software is available. In response to the AEM/EDA survey posted as empirical data - I did my own survey calling my 'Hacker Buddies' (roughly a dozen techs, 'Hackers' & enthusiasts that specialize in engine ECU work). They laughed at the AEM/EDA survey's calculation of the percentage of modified (Hacked) tractors. Their experience is the percent of hacked tractors is extremely low - maybe 1-5% with 5% being extremely unlikely at the high end. Dealers undoubtedly see modified or hacked equipment in their service bays where they wouldnt likely be able to discern any of these purported emission 'Hacks' . When a tractor rolls in the shop it will appear normal unless the diesel particulate filter (DPF) was removed. Most common hacks don't leave a digital signature after the exhaust gas return (EGR) or diesel emission fluid (DEF) is adjusted nor do they leave an electronic signature on a horsepower tune. A dealer would have to put a tractor on a DYNO to prove such improvements which is both time consuming and costly. In the real world, I know of many "Tractor Hackers who work quietly for the dealership to help support their customers unofficially in ways that the dealership cannot. In my experience, nearly all Nebraska John Dealer dealerships have used outside 'Tractor Hackers' one way or the other based on my exposure to this scenario. Dealerships want to help their customers, and if they need to call in a 'Hacker Buddy' to fix and/or modify their 'Electronic Junk' they will. You'd be surprised as to how many service managers order these 'Hacks'.... Please let me know if you have any questions or if I can be of service. Yours Truly, Kevin Kenney R2R Advocate for Farmers & Ranchers AG Engineer '86 (BS-UNL) Raymond, Nebraska

comment: The proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule that require doctors to have each patient sign that they received a copy of their contact lens prescription is over-regulation. Doctors are already required to give a copy of the prescription to the patient. This is a poor use of time and money that could be better spent on patient care. Patients not receiving prescriptions is hardly the problem. There are so few complaints of that as compared to complaints about contact lens retailers filling expired prescriptions and substituting lenses, calling to verify in the evening or on the weekend, and verification calls that you can't even understand the patient's name. These are the problems that the FTC should be worried about. This causes patients to get old material or improper lenses which could lead to eye infection or injury that could lead to blindness. I have had patients who have come in the office who have not had an exam in years and have been receiving contacts without a current valid prescription. I have had patients who have bought contacts with no prescription verification who have had eye injury or infection because they had no education on how to clean or wear the lenses. Please reconsider this unnecessary over-regulation.

comment: As a former retailer of consumer electronics I believe in customers rights to obtain repair parts and to choose who performs repairs. Both from keeping prices competitive and reducing waste this is good policy. I have seen countless examples of devices and equipment worth hundreds of dollars scrapped due to hindered access to repairs (like requirement to ship it off and do without product for extended times) that could easily be repaired with a part that costs a few dollars at most. Consumers think little about these impediments (access to repairs and cost) when making a purchase, but feel stuck when faced with a need for repair. Without the access to parts and outside repairers the manufacturers are in effect leasing you the product until a fault occurs, at which time, by controlling repair access and price, they economically prematurely obsolete your device. Further, most retailers have phased out repairs. The major national chains (Best Buy, Staples, etc.) either replace within 14 to 30 days after purchase or tell their customers to ship to and deal with manufacturer. If parts and third party repairs were law the consumer would benefit from significantly more and local places to have them performed competitively priced and quicker. Good policy. Thank you

comment: The second set of proposed new Regulations to be added to the Contact Lens Rule differs in substance very little from the first set of proposed new regulations. In other words it is still very deeply flawed, unnecessary, and onerous to optometrists and ophthalmologists. The Spectacle Rule has been in effect since the 1970's, ie, for over 40 years, and during that time NO ONE has suggested that doctors be required to have patients sign a form that says they have a received a copy of their spectacle prescription and that they have right to fill that prescription somewhere else. The reason that no one has suggested this is because there is nothing in the spectacle industry equivalent to 1-800-Contacts and it's allies in the contact lens industry. comment: The Federal Trade Commission's (the FTC) enforcement action and proposed consent agreement with We Give Loans, Inc. (a.k.a. the Perpetrators), FTC File No.: 072-3205, is deplorable. What we have here is an advertiser of consumer loan products who willfully, knowingly and negligently failed in each and every way to disclose important loan terms in their consumer loan advertising as is required by the federal Truth-in-Lending Act (TILA) and Federal Reserve Board Regulation Z, the TILAs implementing federal regulations. However, in response to We Give Loans, Inc.'s innumerable violations of federal consumer protection advertising laws, the FTC proposes a consent order that merely requires these Perpetrators to comply in the future with all of the consumer lending advertising laws that they failed to comply with in the past. Why the hell is the FTC letting them off with less than a slap on the wrist. Obviously, all the Perp's will have to do is set up a new corporation that is entirely unrelated to We Give Loans, Inc. and run their business through it and entirely outside the watchful eyes of the FTC. They'll slow down the operations of We Give Loans, Inc. to the point that corporation is listed as active and in good standing by the Delaware Secretary of State. Eventually, after 5 years have passed, they'll just dissolve We Give Loans, Inc. and disburse any remaining assets to the principals. There will be no need to notify the FTC of the new corporation they've been running their business through because it's unrelated to the We Give Loans, Inc. I'll bet the We Give Loans, Inc. folks were about the happiest deceptive advertisers in the country once they read through your proposed consent order and found out they were going to be required to do what they should have been doing all along. Unfortunately, whenever enforcement actions are issued against violators of consumer protection laws that are barely even a slap on the wrist, the public begins to wonder why the government enforcement agency went so easy on the consumer protection violators. With human nature as it is, the public begins to wonder if the reason for violators got off so easy is because of certain incentives that may have been offered to, and accepted by, agency personnel. While it's distressing to even imagine this could happen, we know that it has been somewhat common in certain other enforcement agencies. We are prayerful that this is not what has happened in this case. Perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the FTC's enforcement of consumer advertising regulations against We Give Loans, Inc. is the absence of any civil money penalties. Why the hell the FTC doesn't hit the Perpetrators up for somewhere between $100,000 and $1,000,000 dollars for their deceptive consumer loan advertising is a question we must all ask over and over. By giving the Perp's a slap on the wrist instead of busting them on their ass for deceiving consumers, the FTC is inviting others to follow in the footsteps of We Give Loans, Inc. In fact, the risk of these deceptive advertisers being caught in the first place is very low, and if they are caught, chances are high that they'll just get a slap on the wrist and no civil money penalties. Add all this together and these consumer loan advertisers end up with a Risk Assessment that tells them they're nuts to even bother with adding required consumer disclosures to their advertising. Way to drop the ball FTC. Given the fact that the enforcement actions you issue are nothing more than a fractional fraction of all the consumer protection violations that go unchallenged, uninvestigated and unenforced day in and day out, the FTC should make the most of each opportunity it has to enforce the law to show all the baddies that the last thing they'll ever want is to get caught violating consumer protection laws. As it is now though, there's little if any fear that any consequences will be suffered by the baddies.

comment: Franchise Rule Regulatory Review, 16 CFR part 436, Matter No. R511003 Response to Question 1 "Is there a continuing need for the Rule? Why or why not?" I think there is a continue need of this rule. On one hand, the rule requires the franchisors to provide specific and detailed information about the franchise business for the prospective franchisees, which is helpful for the legality of the contract. Prospective franchisees might better know about the franchise business before entering into the contract and thus avoid a lot of loss that might be caused by the "fradulent franchise business" contract. In addition, if there is any dispute between the two parties, the detailed disclosure might be a powerful and informative lawful evidence in the potential lawsuit. On the other hand, the rule should be continued because franchisors can also benefit from this rule. Intangible assets such as brand name will be involved in the franchisor-franchisee relationships and sometimes the intangibles might be diminished if they are not fully stated and specified in the Franchise Disclosure Document . If these intangibles are clearly stated in the document, both parties can see their rights and obligations and deal with them properly. The last reason would be that fully disclosed info is good for being audit, and audited info is more reliable.

comment: The FTC and Congress must coordinate efforts to address data-driven discrimination. Right now we have weak, piecemeal regulations and weak enforcement. The U.S. must create and enforce regulations similar to the EU's GDPR. A targeted regime of surveillance, analytics, modelling, and selling undertaken by data brokers and other private companies (Google, Facebook, etc) exposes individuals to a plethora of consequences that were not imagined when most data segmentation relied on the use of records in the aggregate. The invasiveness and the exposure that individuals endure and the construction of a potentially false "data self" are clear indications that current Fair Information Practices need an ethical update to reflect the omniscience of Big Data discrimination. A democratic society REQUIRES that citizens be treated with dignity and that citizens have some power to combat the discrimination wrought by opaque data collection/use by data brokers and other companies.

comment: I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care at a charitable clinic in Texas. I agree that it is important that consumers be given a genuine opportunity to exercise choice in the contact lens market. However, before one considers offering support for far reaching government regulations to be imposed on small businesses, its important to know the true state of the contact lens market as the market has changed tremendously since the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act was passed. o Lens prices are competitive: The American Optometric Association (AOA) conducted a price comparison analysis in which they compared online retailer cost vs the average in-office cost to determine the dollar price difference and percent change in price for 81 different contact lenses. Of the 81 lenses studied, 28 were more expensive online, while 53 were more expensive in the doctors office. Across all lenses included in the AOAs price comparison analysis, there was an average price difference of just $0.32 o Patients Have More Retailer Options than Ever: The fastest growing distribution channel for contact lens sales in the USA was the online / Internet channel. In 2017, online retailers generated $786 million in salesgrowing by 4.9% during the 12 month ending period Dec17 and growing by 11.1% over the 24 monthending period Dec17. o There is Widespread Agreement that the Current Rule is Working: The CEO of 1-800-CONTACTS itself acknowledged that the current rule is working in your March 2018 workshop noting, The FCLCA and CLR have succeeded in encouraging greater competition and choice in the contact lens marketplace. Consumers today have more choice and more convenience. The competitive benefits have gone beyond price. I think that the FTC can consider this a successful rule. Doctors of optometry are concerned with your organization's claims regarding non-compliance of prescription release requirements. Despite disagreeing with the accusation regarding compliance, the profession has offered an alternative to the signed acknowledgement proposal. The proposal supported by optometry would require all contact lens prescribers to post signage in their offices notifying patients of their right to their contact lens prescription. This is a less burdensome and less intrusive approach than the current FTC proposal. This approach would also do more to broadly educate consumers. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under FTCs threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions at both the state and federal levels. Thank you, Jenny Terrell, OD, FAAO, DiplABO

The transport time for a patient in need of trauma or emergency services from southwest Virginia/Eastern Kentucky/ Kingsport is between 30 minutes to an hour if by ambulance thus patients are being forced to use helicopter service to get to Johnson City costing the patient more out-of-pocket expense because a majority of insurance companies dont cover this charge. You need to remember that there are a lot of people that doesnt have insurance and if they cant afford to pay for a helicopter to transport them for emergency services then their lives will be lost! Ballad Health is wanting to monopolize with its health care with money at the top of their list being the driving force for the merger for their investors. Educating patients to strive for better health is at the top of the list but saving lives is what Physicians and Nurses work toward. To do no harm is in our oath as a Nurse or a Physician, so I feel like the service at Holston Valley will do harm to the patient that if this COPA approves Ballad Healths plan of reducing services to this hospital. As a Healthcare Professional who has spent 34 years in healthcare taking care of patients, Im very disappointed in our government in allowing Ballad Health to try to become a monopoly looking at dollar signs instead of the Healthcare of Patients and saving lives!

comment: I am writing as the son of a disabled American who relies on online grocery and delivery services because they have voluntarily stopped driving. I want the Commission to understand how surveillance pricing affects people like my father, and why disclosure alone will not be enough to protect him and other like him. When a grocery chain or delivery service learns that my father does not drive, that information becomes a lever. They know he has fewer alternatives and less ability to shop around, walk out, or drive to a competitor for a better price. That is not a hypothetical risk. It is the direct, foreseeable consequence of combining personal data with pricing algorithms, and it falls hardest on people whose circumstances are already visible in their data: the elderly, the disabled, and anyone with a fixed income and limited mobility. He has no meaningful way to see what profile these companies have built on him, correct it, or remove himself from it. He did not consent to have his mobility limitations used as pricing input, yet there is no default protection preventing it. The same is true of his finances. Because there is no default “no data sharing” standard for financial data, his bank balance and spending patterns are likely already available to data brokers and, by extension, to the very companies pricing his groceries. I want to raise three specific concerns with the proposed policy statement: 1. Disclosure is not enough. Telling customers that a price was personalized does not restore their bargaining power. He still cannot drive, still cannot shop elsewhere, and still has no leverage. A company can fully “disclose” that it is charging him more because of his disability and still be acting unfairly. I ask the Commission to treat pricing based on disability status, age, or mobility limitations, whether used directly or through proxies like delivery frequency or address type, as inherently unfair under Section 5, not merely as something that becomes acceptable once disclosed. 2. Consumers need a real right to see and remove their data. Disclosure of pricing practices means little if customers cannot see the underlying data profile driving the price, correct it, or opt out of its use. I ask the Commission to pair any disclosure requirement with an enforceable right to access, correct, and delete the personal data used in pricing decisions, at no cost and through a genuinely accessible process. 3. Financial data needs default protection. Static savings and fixed incomes should not be treated as fair game for pricing algorithms simply because banks and financial services lack a default no sharing standard. I ask the Commission to consider whether the undisclosed use of financial account data for pricing purposes should be treated as a per se unfair practice, not something cured by fine print disclosure. I recognize the Commission has stated it lacks authority to ban personalized pricing outright. But within the disclosure framework you are proposing, I ask you to draw a clear line: disclosure may be sufficient for ordinary personalization, but it cannot be a safe harbor when the underlying data reflects a protected characteristic like disability or age. People in my father’s position are not simply seeing a different price. I am writing as the son of a disabled American who relies on online grocery and delivery services because they have voluntarily stopped driving. I want the Commission to understand how surveillance pricing affects people like my father, and why disclosure alone will not be enough to protect him and other like him.

When a grocery chain or delivery service learns that my father does not drive, that information becomes a lever. They know he has fewer alternatives and less ability to shop around, walk out, or drive to a competitor for a better price. That is not a hypothetical risk. It is the direct, foreseeable consequence of combining personal data with pricing algorithms, and it falls hardest on people whose circumstances are already visible in their data: the elderly, the disabled, and anyone with a fixed income and limited mobility.

He has no meaningful way to see what profile these companies have built on him, correct it, or remove himself from it. He did not consent to have his mobility limitations used as pricing input, yet there is no default protection preventing it. The same is true of his finances. Because there is no default “no data sharing” standard for financial data, his bank balance and spending patterns are likely already available to data brokers and, by extension, to the very companies pricing his groceries.

I want to raise three specific concerns with the proposed policy statement:

1. Disclosure is not enough. Telling customers that a price was personalized does not restore their bargaining power. He still cannot drive, still cannot shop elsewhere, and still has no leverage. A company can fully “disclose” that it is charging him more because of his disability and still be acting unfairly. I ask the Commission to treat pricing based on disability status, age, or mobility limitations, whether used directly or through proxies like delivery frequency or address type, as inherently unfair under Section 5, not merely as something that becomes acceptable once disclosed.

2. Consumers need a real right to see and remove their data. Disclosure of pricing practices means little if customers cannot see the underlying data profile driving the price, correct it, or opt out of its use. I ask the Commission to pair any disclosure requirement with an enforceable right to access, correct, and delete the personal data used in pricing decisions, at no cost and through a genuinely accessible process.

3. Financial data needs default protection. Static savings and fixed incomes should not be treated as fair game for pricing algorithms simply because banks and financial services lack a default no sharing standard. I ask the Commission to consider whether the undisclosed use of financial account data for pricing purposes should be treated as a per se unfair practice, not something cured by fine print disclosure.

I recognize the Commission has stated it lacks authority to ban personalized pricing outright. But within the disclosure framework you are proposing, I ask you to draw a clear line: disclosure may be sufficient for ordinary personalization, but it cannot be a safe harbor when the underlying data reflects a protected characteristic like disability or age. People in my father’s position are not simply seeing a different price. They are being charged more for the exact vulnerability that put them online in the first place, and a disclosure notice does not change that we have nowhere else to go.

I urge the Commission to strengthen this policy statement accordingly.

Respectfully submitted.
