comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. For more than two years, I have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from patient care and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again. I have always and will continue to fully comply with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. Nicholas Olberding, O.D.

comment: Under historical precedent and the "first sale" doctrine individuals and businesses have been able to repair anything they purchase especially after the item is no longer under any manufacturer's warranty. Manufacturers have increasingly begun to use misuse copyright, trademark, & patent methods to prevent consumers from repairing the items they have purchased. A common method is where a company calls the diagrams copyrighted and will prevent anyone who determined how to repair a product from freely publishing the repair instructions. Another anti-competitive method used is where a manufacturer of a product will use software encryption combined with misusing the DMCA to prevent repair. This is also used to prevent certain non-approved repair parts from working. An example is the touch sensor on iPhones and iPads where Apple will not provide the replacement touch sensor to any independent shop or to consumers and if any non-Apple sensor is used the device will not function. Notably, Apple is profiting handsomely from this anti-competitive behavior because they can charge 10 - 100 times what an independent shop would charge for a similar repair. Tesla uses similar behavior to prevent anyone but them from repairing any Tesla automobile. If the FTC does not take firm action to prohibit the following anti-consumer, anti-competitive behavior the consumer will be negatively impacted: Abuse of the DMCA to take down repair instructions and reverse engineered diagrams Use of software encryption combined with DMCA to prevent non-OEM components from working without a strong reason and if the component and or encryption is absolutely mandatory the OEM must sell the component to any consumer or independent shop with appropriate instructions on its use Use of proprietary fasteners unless consumers or independent shops are able to purchase the tooling at reasonable costs We need to strongly affirm that the consumer owns the products they purchase and OEMs do not get a second bite at the apple by using anti-competitive methods to prevent information required to repair their products from being disseminated and the use of patents, copyrights, and/or trademarks to prevent consumers from repairing their own products.

I feel that I have personal/professional experiences that I would like to share with the surevy/study and take a professional lead to combat this detrimental crime. Thank you and I really am looking forward to hearing from you. Greg

comment: Loot boxes were a interesting way of acquiring in-game items when first introduced, but it has become apparent that video game producers now implement them in an almost predatory way to earn more money from weak-willed players. I like to use a personal experience as an example: In the Overwatch 2017 Summer event, the character Soldier 76 got a cosmetic item, named "Grillmaster", which dressed up the character in humorous barbecue attire. I had set my sights on this cosmetic item because I really enjoyed the way it looked and wanted to use it myself. The items was only available for a limited time, because of this I purchased numerous loot boxes in pursuit of acquiring this item. I had purchased 35 Euros worth of loot boxes. But because of the rarity that was artificially assigned to this skin, none of these boxes contained the item. In the end, I was able to acquire the item with Overwatch's coin currency that was also distributed (in random amounts) within the loot boxes. Only after I acquired the item, I realized that the amount of money I've spend on loot boxes was almost equal to the price I paid for the game itself. I also felt mistreated, considering other, more lucky players might have gotten the item while spending a lot less money on the boxes. It feels very unfair, that each individual can only acquire said items through complete random chance, without having a more direct, sure fire way to acquire them through, per example, trading with other players or purchasing the item directly from the producer. After this experience, I've sworn off to ever buy loot boxes in the future. But I can see how other, less fortunate players are still coaxed into buying these loot boxes. Especially due to the limited, timed availability of the items involved, there was a certain desperation to acquire the item before it was no longer available. This desperation blinded me to financial implications that buying all the loot boxes would bring. I can imagine that players with a lesser control over their buying impulses might be very sensitive to be influenced by this, causing financial damage to these players. Because of this, I strongly believe that the concept op loot boxes should be regulated, if not outright banned.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. It is unnecessary burden. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. My understanding is that the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. John Scibal, O.D.

comment: In my opinion, as a former ETSU Assistant Clinical Professor of Pediatrics staffing a MSHA-now-Ballad facility in Virginia, the Ballad Health COPA has been nearly criminally mismanaged and very poorly overseen by the states of Tennessee and Virginia - to the wholesale detriment of Ballad and ETSU clinical/other employees and patients alike. The lack of foresight is simply staggering. Based on my experience on his front lines, Alan Levine is a corporate menace who has repeatedly lied to the public about his intentions/methods, and whose leadership fosters an openly hostile and abusive-of-clinical employees work environment in his pursuit of complete domination/monopolization of an entire regions medical resources - FOR MONEY. Communication is utterly horrible and internal accountability of management is virtually non-existent. Retaliation is ingrained in the culture. I lived it. And I spoke out against it before almost anyone else. The attached letter is a modified/updated version of the letter I submitted to the Ballad Health COPA Committee at a hearing in Blountville, Tennessee on 2/7/2019. I spent eight hours on-the-road (traveling to and from my home in NC) to make my statement and submit the letter. I have yet to receive any kind of follow-up or response from either the Tennessee/Virginia Departments of Health or Attorneys General. I believe that this is because the state of Tennessee is downplaying its own liability both within and without the framework of the COPA. The state of Tennessee is obliged to defend the actions of ETSU no matter how heinous or how they might fly in the stated intent of the COPA. The Commonwealth of Virginia unfortunately appears to be just along for the ride. Erik Bodin (at the Virginia Department of Health) has much to answer for in terms of institutional enforcement of Virginia statute to protect a medical whistle-blower who has begged for his help for over 18 months. I have also presented a significant conflict-of-interest in terms of the CMS assessment of the second potential EMTALA violation I reported as CMS investigators based in Virginia worked for the former MSHA Regional Medical Director who helped recruit me to JMH and who, in conjunction with former ETSU Pediatric Chairman, David Wood, botched the negotiated terms of my ETSU/MEAC contracts. Given the nature of the problems I reported . . . most specifically blatant sex/age discrimination on the part of East Tennessee State University (in deference to MSHA-now-Ballads openly hostile/abusive and retaliatory work environment), and #2 potential EMTALA violations (which threatened the lives of two infants) the second incident featuring a violation of Virginia Code 8.01-581.17,H on the part of Johnston Memorial/MSHA-now-Ballad executives (i.e. no employer shall take retaliatory action against an employee who in good faith makes a report of a patient safety date to a patient safety organization) . . . I find the good-faith oversight of the Ballad Health COPA to be significantly lacking. The states have created an inter-jurisdictional nightmare in which established state and Federal mechanisms of employee redress have little or no chance of working. I believe that Wellmont-MSHA assets should not be merged in any kind of permanent fashion until clinical employees of both Ballad and ETSU are afforded adequate protections of time, livelihood and health under the COPA. It is my hope that the Federal government will now take a much more active role in STOPPING the finalization of this merger - and bringing more scrutiny to bear to the entire process/operation. An outside/Federal review of any/all downgrades (particularly of Neonatal, Pediatric and Trauma services) free of the incestuous/conflicted interests that have plagued this endeavor since its conception (by the self-described Hole-in-the-Wall-Gang") is imperative. I thank the FTC for its attention and the opportunity to share my story. Ballad Health did not listen. I hope you do. Mary H. Johnson, M.D., FAAP

comment: I am a manager in a high-tech, US-based, secure computer design and manufacturing firm. We have run into significant problems from certain component vendors that overlap with right to repair legislation. Specifically, certain vendors require all firmware components to be signed with their vendor key in order for the firmware to execute. This severely impairs the repair capability of their devices, increases e-waste when the vendor is unwilling to fix known bugs in their firmware (recommending for instance to buy a newer or more expensive device and discard the old one) and also severely limits innovation in fields that the vendor has not considered. When the vendor is the only manufacturer creating a specific class of computing peripheral, this has the effect of not only stifling repair of entire classes of devices, but also encouraging foreign (usually Asian) companies to innovate where US citizens and corporations are locked out by vendor decisions. Any right to repair guidelines in today's high tech, firmware-driven world must address the issue of vendor cryptographic signatures being required to replace existing malfunctioning firmware on hardware devices. Ideally this would take the form of an alternate operating mode being required that does not check the firmware signature, but also indicates the device is operating outside of the vendor controlled mode. This would allow e.g. DRM systems to function on the vendor firmware, but still allow owner repair / replacement of firmware with deactivation of the DRM systems (i.e. inability to decrypt protected content using unsigned firmware, but the ability to repair the rest of the device functionality). We have already seen significant damage in the overall economy, ranging from impacts caused by the signed Intel ME/ AMD PSP along with, for example, NVIDIA's cryptographic signing forcing continual replacement of otherwise functional cards. This requirement to replace and discard is usually due to firmware or firmware-enforced driver bugs that NVIDIA is unwilling to fix for commercial reasons. Please take action and put a stop to this, allow American companies to innovate again, reduce our e-waste, and restore the right to repair complex firmware-driven systems.

The surveillance commercial businesses are able to do are mind blowing and most consumers are clueless about it.

comment: Hello, I am currently a third-year Optometry student at the Ohio State College of Optometry. As we learn about contact lenses in our coursework, we learn about the numerous complications that can occur from an improper fitting, improper materials, and improper wear. It is our duty as future doctors to select the correct lens for our patient, evaluate the fit, and ensure these patients are using the lenses safely for the health of their eyes! Without proper materials and wear, contact lenses can greatly reduce oxygen to your eye and can lead to nasty infections, ulcers, and potentially permanent vision loss. The business models of several contact lens companies like Hubble and 1800Contacts are driven by revenue, not by patient care. Medicine and medical devices should not be accessible through a "dollar shave club" format. These companies use extremely outdated materials for their contacts and mislead patients with their "online vision tests." This is a public health concern, and I would like to see a more robust plan to protect the public from these companies. The profession of Optometry is not against telehealth, but we are against the disruption of the doctor-patient relationship (true patient care). More reasonable guidelines need to be set for prescription requests from these companies to doctor's offices. As experts in eyecare, there should be more communication and involvement of the doctor in the final product that the patient is receiving. Thank you for considering my thoughts on this pertinent issue. Best, Veronica Schuver American Optometric Student Association Trustee Ohio State University College Of Optometry, OD Candidate

comment: As a practicing Optometrist for the past 22 years, I am deeply concerned about this legislation. I have personally handed contact lens prescriptions to my patients at the end of my exam for 2 decades. I point out the contact lens prescription and the expiration date to the patient so they know they have it. It is the law that I present them with the prescription and it is ethical and right. They are free to purchase their contact lenses anywhere they chose to, and have always been. I also write the expiration date on my prescriptions for 2 years, because that is the law in the state I practice in (Utah). I personally don't agree with 2 year expiration dates, but that is the law, and I obey the law. There is no restriction of patient choice in my practice, and quite honestly I don't know of any colleague of mine who does not comply with the existing law. My experience has been that many online retailers don't obey the law. The online retailer referenced in this legislation is the worst. Many prescriptions are filled after expiration dates. At times contacts are dispensed that don't match a valid prescription. I find it flabbergasting that so much credence is given to the voice of a company that is clearly only motivated by profit. The health care provider has a relationship that would be jeopardized if he or she were to deny the patient access to their legal rights to a prescription. Why would a patient ever return to such a practitioner, and yet our voice is presented as one driven by profits and self interest. It is ironic to the ultimate degree that the voice of online retailers whose sole motivation is profit, who have no interest in the individual patient, is seen as the voice representing the patients best interest. This legislation adds so much work and cost to an overburdened health care system, without benefiting patients. There are already laws that direct the patient-provider relationship. I already have more patients wanting to be examined in my practice than I have time to see. This burdensome legislation would slow down the delivery of health care in my office, and waste valuable time that now utilized to provide vision improving and saving care. I ask you to consider the source. The claims by retailers that this is a patient protection issue, and their assertions that problems and violations of current laws exist are spurious at worst and exaggerated and self motivated at best. Please view this issue with some reason. Who is more motivated to care for the patients. A practitioner who has a 20 year relationship with the individual, or a company interested in a quick sale. I invite you to call me or any of my patients and ask them if they have access to all the information necessary to allow them to purchase eyewear and contact lenses in any establishment they chose. Respectfully Dr, Robert M. Wilkes O.D.

comment: FTC HEARING #12: THE FTCS APPROACH TO CONSUMER PRIVACY We are university students from all over the United States who came to Italy to study abroad and took a law class. During the course we recognized the importance of law for the development of both our economy and day-by-day life. Today data represents the new oilthus the most valuable resourceand how data will be regulated is crucial. We want to contribute as U.S. citizens to the debate over privacy regulation benefiting from our study abroad experience. We are in our twenties, thus among the people that are going to be more affected by this regulation. We would like to thank the Federal Trade Commission for giving us the opportunity to speak out and express our opinion on such a fundamental matter. Law Class, Spring 2019 (Cimba Italy)

comment: After reading the COPPA rule, the amendments, the statements from each of the Commissioners who ruled on the YouTube settlement, and talking on the phone with your Assistant Director, Division of Privacy and Identity Protection, I am incredibly frustrated by the lack of a clear, precise definition of "child directed content". Without a solid, legal definition, what I think is a general audience, science education video might or might not be considered to be child directed, depending on the mood and personality of whoever sees it. I produce science education videos (https://thehappyscientist.com/) and until recently my videos were only available to people who paid a subscription fee. As schools cut budgets, and teachers were forced to pay that fee out of their own pocket, I decided to move my videos to YouTube, taking the financial burden off the teachers. Now I am being told that I have to decide if a video on how to identify minerals is child directed or not. Most of the people who "click the button" on my videos are teachers, but they are usually showing the video to their students. If the teacher clicks the button, but a class of 13 year old students watch the video, is that child directed? Who's information is being collected, the students or the teacher? The teacher is using their account to log in, but the students are viewing the content, and would see any advertisements. The same applies to homeschool families. Is the adult who decides the children should learn about minerals today the one who has their information collected, or the children who are told to watch? I think you are going to find that most educational content is going to meet the same challenges with the lack of clear guidelines. I can't afford to risk huge fines based on the whim of someone at the FTC.

comment: I believe the FTC may have the authority to prohibit personalized pricing where the pricing can be found to have been on the basis of any protected status of the consumer (race, color, sex, gender, religion, national origin, disability, or age). There may be other avenues to prohibit so called "surveillance pricing" within the scope of federal law, when the data used to inform the pricing decision violates either the privacy act or HIPAA. Additionally, there may be prohibitions built into banking regulations to prevent the use of purchase data (either credit or debit card transaction data) in pricing decisions. Together, a strategy of federal regulation may be achieved by which companies will decide the compliance and liability risks are too great to continue this obviously discriminatory behavior.

comment: To whom it may concern, I have multiple stores that advertise with Google. Google has recently started pulling almost all of our ads down - even when not including "phone repair" or related search terms in the keyword scope. While customers find us organically very often, Google Ads allow us to stay competitive with larger retailers like Best Buy, Walmart, and Apple. Limiting our ability to post ads with Google (which is, by and large, the biggest search company) is a hindrance to our growth. This seems more of a handshake between Google and electronics manufacture(s) than protecting the general population from scams, etc. My stores are trusted, local, retail locations that specializes repairing computers, phone, and tablets. We are very transparent with our customers when it comes to them having confidence in us with their devices, and we even back our services with a great warranty. Whether through my stores, a competitor, or by their own means, people should have the right to repair their products without needing approval from or being restricted by the manufacturer. I am not required to go to a branded car dealership to get an oil change, so why must anyone be required to go to the original manufacturer to get a battery or screen replaced in their electronics? Sincerely, Joshua Muir Experimax, Brand Development Manager

comment: Effects of COPA in terms of price, cost, and quality of healthcare services; access to healthcare services...or other dimensions of healthcare competition.: Since the approval of Ballad Health's COPA my family has been fortunate to not need treatment at a hospital. In the past, Holston Valley Medical Center (HVMC) was the facility we used for emergencies, hospitalizations due to trauma, scheduled surgeries, and for end-of-life Hospice care. I have extended family and friends who have needed services at this facility since the merger began. My comments are based on my prior knowledge and their recent experiences. Their experiences include: hrs. of waiting, once in an ER cubicle not having anyone return for an hr. or more, an IV that never dripped during an ER stay, being admitted & then waiting 20 hrs for an available bed, not being allowed to be with a 90 year old parent who was on a gurney in the ER hallway for two hours, being sent home from the ER only to be sent back the following day and that time admitted, and unclean rooms. To some this is "hearsay" but there is no doubt in my mind that I was given factual information. Do we still have access to care? Yes. Timely care? No, not the majority of time. There has been, and continues to be, a decline in the quality of services being received in the ER. The physicians and nurses are highly qualified and working tirelessly to do all they can do to ensure patients are given the care to which they are entitled! The facility(s) are understaffed in areas of: housekeeping, nurses to meet patient ratios, & availability of physicians. There are beds, there aren't enough nurses & other staff! These inadequacies fall directly on the shoulders of Ballad's leadership and management. Costs for some services have increased. Ballad spent millions renovating an empty facility in order to relocate an existing infusion facility to a hospital campus. Once open they were able to bill patients a facility fee that was not charged prior to the relocation. Downgrading HVMC's Level 1 Trauma Center (the first Level 1 in this area) to a Level III and downgrading the Level III NICU to a Level 1 has increased costs for patients. Ballad chose to keep Johnson City Medical Center's (JCMC) as the only Level 1 Trauma. HVMC is located in the center of Ballad Health's Geographic Service Area, an area the size of New Jersey, that serves 1.3 M people. . Downgrading HVMC's Level 1 Trauma while maintaining JCMC's Level 1 actually placed 84,000 people outside of their "Golden Hour" of receiving care in a major trauma situation, a time critical to survival and recovery. Of the 23 counties in Ballad's GSA, 8 of them are within the hour's drive to JCMC, while 11 of the 23 are within the hour's drive to HVMC. HVMC is located in a town that is home to a major chemical company, an ammunition production facility, and a large paper manufacturing company. Physicians have spoken out against the downgrade of this facility & the fact that it leaves a gaping hole in the area's trauma care. Allowing this many people to be outside their "golden hour" would appear to be a decision based solely on money as opposed to one based on saving lives through access to care! According to Ballad, operating only one Level 1 Trauma center will save hundreds of thousands of dollars annually. HVMC, right now, today, is the facility that is best equipped to be a Level 1 Trauma Center. It is larger, better equipped, has more beds, can break down trauma cubicles into a surgical suites and can land multiple helicopters. Millions of dollars are going to have to be spent to upgrade the JCMC Level 1 Trauma to bring it to the level of HVMC's Level 1 Trauma. So, we're saving money in order to spend millions more to improve a facility instead of using one that already exists, that needs no improvement....one that is in the center of the GSA and the one we chose to downgrade?! These changes have resulted in more transports by air to the only Level 1 Trauma and Level 3 NICU, as they are not located in the center of Ballads GSA. Patients & their insurance companies are going to experience the burden of these additional expenses. A COPA created MONOLOPY - 78% of Inpatient care! It was designed to improve Population Health (read it and see). It also became apparent that Ballad and ETSU were/are relying heavily on each other in order to provide the money for the research needed for improving population health & for becoming a national model for improving rural health. Since the COPA is first and foremost designed to improve population health, wouldn't one expect that when those improvements begin to be noticed, and supported by data, the need for services would decline and health services could be pared down? It will take years to see these health improvements! It seems that this merger has the "cart before the horse"...reduce services before improving health! Public Advantage? No, not enough evidence yet!

comment: BAN SO-CALLED “PERSONALIZED PRICING”. You can use any euphemism you want to soften it, but I’m tired of my personal data being used against me. As a consumer, it’s bad enough that I’m already a captive audience to some of the most unfair pricing by companies and corporations that provide less and less while we pay more and more. Surveillance pricing discriminates against me because of who I am and where I am, and if the FTC allows this practice to continue, as a voter, I will hold the Republican party and President Trump responsible. It’s the opposite of fair market practices. It’s nothing more than a high-tech form of price gouging. Simply requiring disclosures is stupid and insufficient; forcing individuals to navigate hidden algorithmic pricing models places an unfair burden on the public. The FTC has a responsibility under Section 5 of the FTC Act to protect consumers against unfair methods of competition and deceptive practices, and must ban the use of individual data to establish discriminatory, targeted pricing.

She's 86 years old. She was taken to Indian Path hospital first because it was the closest hospital with an ER. They didn't have the staff to treat her, while her skin is melting away she was told to go to Holston Valley Medical Center. You read that right she was sent to another hospital instead of being treated. They put an 86 yr old woman with 2nd and 3rd degree burns on her upper body her stomach, her chest, her face, her head and her right hand where she was trying to put out the fire in her hair, they put her in an ambulance for a 5 1/2 hr ride through the mountains to Winston Salem NC. But, those burns had they been treated before she was shipped would probably have stopped cooking. Had she been life flown to Winston Salem NC they could have put out the internal fire. They deserve the best medical care available with the technology we have today. I realize not every hospital can have everything, but you need to examine closely what Ballad has proposed. If you as a whole are looking to make this region a ghost town a thing of the past, your'e well on your way. I'll stay in sunny hot as hell Florida and suffer the torrential downpours and 100% humidity and sweat profusely in my old age, but hey at least with out health care system down here. I will get older.

comment: Our current Lens.com customers are being put through the wringer by bad actors who simply wont release their prescriptions or provide copies of their prescription to their designated agents. Our ability at Lens.com to grow our business and attract new customers by providing more choice and competition in the marketplace is being severely hampered by the fact that patients cant get a copy of their own prescription after an eye exam. As you correctly point out in your NRPM and in the new amendments proposed in the SNPRM, the status quo is unacceptable. The FTC needs the ability to enforce the FCLCA and crack down on bad actors who are deliberately violating the law. The FTC clearly needs more tools to help protect consumers and increase competition. We believe you have struck the correct balance with the requirement that patients proactively acknowledge they have been given a copy of their prescription and prescribers keep the record of this acknowledgment on file for three years. Lens.com has consistently supported the idea that optometrists must demonstrate that they have provided patients with their prescriptions once they have completed their exam. This is because many optometrists do not provide patients with prescriptions despite being required to by law. We know the reason for this is because optometry offices actually make the majority of their revenue from selling contact lenses and glasses, not providing eye care services. In the SPRM, you raise the idea of providers giving patients digital copies of their prescription as a way to acknowledge and demonstrate that they have complied with the FCLCA. As an online provider of contact lenses and an early adopter of consumer-friendly contact lens technology, we very much appreciate your desire to make it easier for customers to receive their prescriptions in a manner that allows them to easily share it with the seller of their choice. We also appreciate your desire to ensure prescribers dont skirt the law and instead give other sellers what is needed to ensure customers get the product that they want through the seller of their choice. Therefore, we support the general idea of digital copies of prescriptions. And while we support the general idea of digital copies, the operative word is copy. This is not and either/or proposition but rather, both: a digital copy may be retailed by the office and provided for the convenient retrieval by the patient after a written prescription has been provided, per the original draft of the FCLCA. However, we believe that the devil will be in the details and that the FTC must provide more clarity and stronger protections around what constitutes a digital copy and a portal and what constitutes electronic delivery. Prescriptions are the property of patients, and shouldnt be trapped in some confusing portal of the prescribers making. The FTC needs to outline guidelines to ensure that customers can access their prescriptions via these portals with minimal hassle immediately after leaving the doctors office. As we have pointed out in each of our earlier comment letters to the FTC around the Contact Lens Rule, the current system is rigged against consumers and companies who compete with prescribers, because unlike anyone else in the medical profession, contact lens prescribers still have the right to both prescribe and sell contact lenses at the same time and to determine what brand customers must wear. They simply have no motivation to build systems that allow their patients to take their prescriptions and shop elsewhere and have worked to erect barriers to delay, slow and do end runs around educating consumers about their rights and following the FCLCA which requires automatic prescription release. The FTC must be vigilant about ensuring that any process or system for the digital release of a prescription is easy, accessible and follows the letter and spirit of the FCLCA. We hope your final rule takes these concerns into account. In addition to your commitment to patient acknowledgment in the SPRM, Lens.com also supports the provisions in the SPRM which call for patients to be guaranteed the right to additional copies of their prescription. We believe that for too long the burden has been unfairly placed on consumers to have to fight for what is theirs - their prescription - and to have to go out of their way to get something which is their property and they have paid for. In some ways, it is very sad and disappointing that the FTC has had to actually make this part of the law and spell it out because providers havent been keeping up their side of the bargain that was the FCLCA. The most important thing that the FTC can do is to wrap up the SPRM and swiftly finalize You have weighed the evidence, gone out of your way to address concerns, and written a strong rule. Lens.com is grateful, and our millions of customers will benefit as a result. Please move with all haste to enact the rule as drafted.

comment: Loot boxes should not be regulated as they are not gambling. To be gambling, there must be an intrinsic monetary value to the award that is received through luck, however with loot boxes, these items cannot be exchanged for money and are tied to the account being used, therefore there is no monetary value. Furthermore, in the vast majority of games that use loot boxes, the items in the loot boxes can be earned by playing the game normally; the loot boxes serve simply as a way to unlock these items faster should the player choose. Loot boxes do not restrict the player's ability to play the game and simply serve a cosmetic function, changing either an in game weapon's skin or a character's skin, or adding some sort of visual effect. As there is no game mechanic altering function in loot boxes, nor is there an intrinsic monetary value to the items in loot boxes therefore making it not a form of gambling, there should be no government regulation on the topic.

comment: I support the FTC’s proposed policy statement and urge the Commission to enforce meaningful disclosure requirements for personalized pricing. Consumers should not have to guess whether the price they see is the same price offered to everyone else—or whether it has been increased because an algorithm has inferred they are less likely to comparison-shop, more urgent, or more willing to pay. If a company uses a consumer’s profile, browsing behavior, purchase history, location, device, household characteristics, or data obtained from third parties to set a price, it should disclose that plainly before purchase. Disclosure should include: - That the price is personalized rather than broadly available. - The principal data categories and factors used to set it. - Whether the consumer is receiving a discount or paying more than a generally available reference price. - The dollar amount—or, at minimum, the percentage—by which the personalized price differs from the standard price. A vague statement such as “a specially selected price for you” is not transparency. It can conceal a penalty imposed because a business believes a consumer lacks alternatives or faces an urgent need. Consumers deserve enough information to decide whether to buy, comparison-shop, change their privacy settings, or take their business elsewhere. Market forces cannot operate effectively when sellers have asymmetric access to personal data and can quietly charge different customers different prices for the same item at the same time. Transparent pricing supports real competition: consumers can compare offers, reward brands that price fairly, and avoid those that exploit personal data to extract more from them. The FTC’s proposed approach appropriately recognizes that undisclosed personalized pricing can be deceptive or unfair under Section 5. I encourage the Commission to make clear that adequate disclosure must identify both the existence and meaningful basis of personalization, and should require a usable price comparison so consumers can understand the financial impact. Thank you!

comment: To whom it may concern: Any requirement to have patients that wear contact lenses sign a notice that they can purchase their materials elsewhere is the definition of a mandated anticompetitive action (leveraged against practitioners by the lobbying of large online retailers). It's akin to having Target have a big sign next to their own that states "You can get everything here at Wal-Mart as well!" How this is even an idea that is being considered is beyond me. Do orthodontists have to have these waivers signed for patients in retainers given there's an online "smile club" now? The administrative time, burden of materials (paper, toner, pens) and securely storing electronically and/or paying for a storage room elsewhere to retain these releases is unreasonable. Passive verification is a joke. Patients constantly request expired contact lens prescription through online websites that we have to deny(typically more than once). People that are not even our patients do this to our clinic. We should not be the gate keeper. Pharmacies have to have a valid copy of the Rx for drugs to be able to fill it. This should work the same way. The patient needs to have to fax or scan/email the Rx to these companies (not us) and if they cannot provide a valid Rx then they cannot order the lenses. That would solve the issue of passive verification. BUT then the online sellers would be limited in their ability to illegally fill prescriptions and "make the sale"... I am hopeful that the FTC will use common sense and reasonable judgment not to place further burden on the doctors taking care of patients. I am not hopeful that the relentlessness of the online industry will be held in check by the FTC. Still, you have an opportunity in making the appropriate decision here. If there is one thing you can rest assured of it is that the decisions of an MBA never have the patients well being in mind - it is entirely about the dollar. I highly doubt the same can be said about your local eye doctor. ps - i have had robocalls for verification on my cell phone from Hubble. i have had patients with nonFDA approved contact lenses from malaysia come into my office with terrible corneal ulcers. i have had patients show up 3 years later and tell me they have been ordering their contact lenses online from 1800 the whole time(we didn't get a single notice). i have had patients say that Hubble just sent them contacts without verifying any prescription. i have had patients lose vision from their contacts. i have patients on a weekly (if not daily) basis that incurr medical costs from inflammation and infection from contact lens wear. i pay my staff but they have to monitor the passive verification notices...it happened today...again, because this is a daily chore.

comment: To whomever it may concern, The COPA and merger of these two health care systems has caused a significant drop in quality of current care and the outlook for future care is quite grim! Let me give you an example. My husband had an allergic reaction to something unknown. His face, lips, hands, and arms began to swell. We rushed to the Emergency Room at Holston Valley Medical Center. We "checked in" and explained his symptoms and he was visibly swollen. They had us to sit in the waiting room. We sat in that waiting for 3 hours. During this time, he developed a "tickle" in his throat. This was a potential sign of airway swelling and obstruction. We informed the desk but nothing was done. After three hours of waiting, we were brought to the triage room where his vitals were taken. We were then shuffled to the side in a "room" which cinsisted of curtiains for walls. We could clearly see into the waiting room and also see the patient in the next bed. They could hear my husband's medical information and like wise, we heard theirs. This was a clear HIPPA violation. We waited for a nurse practioner to come speak with us. She looked my husband over, said he was having an allergic reaction (we knew this.) She prescribed a steroid shot and 10 days of oral steroids. In this "curtain room" where we could see other people, so they could probably see us, my husband pulled his pants down and a steroid shot was given. They quickly discharged him and sent him on his way. They did NOT wait to see if the swelling was going down. His lips were still visably swollen and he still had a mild "tickle" in his throat. This is UNACCEPTABLE. We had a positive outcome from this, but no thanks to Holston Valley and their "care". People WILL and HAVE lost their lives due to this merger and the company Ballad Health. I would be deceased if it were not for Holston Valley Medical Center's Level 1 trauma status. 11 years ago, I presented with nausea, vomiting, and extreme fatigue. Within an hour, I was in full cardiac arrest. CPR was preformed and 35 minutes later, a pulse was found. Its took several world class Dr's and Surgeons to figure out I had a tumor growing in the left atrium of my heart. They consulted with other Dr's from all over the United States trying to figure how to remove this tumor. Dr. Greenfield was the Dr to preform the surgery. He was on the President's list for Cardiology. I say all that to say, I would NOT have survives transport to Johnson City for open heart surgery. I could not be moved for 2 weeks because the fear of the tumor lodging in the artery again was too great. The trip, literally, would have killed me. Holston Valley and the region was full of wonderful physicians who were able to take on an emunexpected situation such as mine. Now, our doctors leaving because of the patient load that Ballad is forcing upon them! As for the NICU and Holston Valley Medical Center, my son was an unexpected patient of that wonderful facility. The care he received was exemplary! The care and kindness from the nurses and staf that I received was amazing. Im not sure my son would have survived a transport to JCMC. They were unprepared for how sick he was. He was a "cord accident in progress". He had "hog tied" himself with his cord. It was wrapped around his arms, legs, chest, and neck. Without the immediate response from NICU, I feel we would have had a different outcome. When your child comes out GREY, not blue like you hear, but GREY, those NICU nurses are angels. I know I am not the most eloquent person with words. But PLEASE hear us. PLEASE look at the data. PLEASE know that we are SCARED! Financially, medically scared. This COPA and these people (BALLAD HEALTH) are about greed. "It's your story", "We're listening" is their slogan. Our story is fear and anger. They are NOT listening. Please, listen to us. Thank you for you time

comment: As a practicing ophthalmologist, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. While I would welcome changes to the Contact Lens Rule that prioritize patient safety, the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. I am a member of a 3 provider practice in a rural town. I would need another employee to comply with these additional requirements. We have EMR and already give a written prescription to every patient regardless if they buy contacts from us or not. To require retaining a signed receipt for 3 years only if you give a patient of having their prescription filled locally is unfair. Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses that are already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that we believe puts our patients at risk. While we appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

comment: 1) Is there a continuing need for the Leather Guides as currently promulgated? Yes, there is a continuing need for Leather Guides because the guide as it currently stands serves as an explicit rule that serves to note the limitations placed on identification of genuine or imitation leather and is still considered an important separation in the eyes of the consumer. (2) Are any specific provisions of the Leather Guides no longer necessary? No. All provisions are necessary as to their language and what they address. The following as is provide a relevant and applicable approach to understanding the Leather Guide's purpose: 24.0 Scope and purpose of guides. 24.1 Deception (general). 24.2 Deception as to composition. 24.3 Misuse of the terms waterproof, dustproof, warpproof, scuffproof, scratchproof, scuff resistant, and scratch resistant. (3) Are the deceptive or unfair practices addressed by the Leather Guides prevalent in the marketplace? Are the Guides effective in addressing those practices? Yes, unfortunately there is a lot of unfair practices, especially by smaller leather vendors that seek to take advantage of the vulnerable consumer. These Guides can serve as a warning to help alleviate the prevalence. (6) What benefits, if any, have the Leather Guides provided to consumers of the products affected by the Guides? Do the Guides impose any significant costs on consumers? The benefits that the guides provide to consumers is to is that it ensures that consumers will not be deceived as to whether their product is real leather or imitation leather, as stated in the Leather Guides: 24.2 Deception as to composition. Especially necessary includes this portion of the Guide: "(a) Imitation or simulated leather. If all or part of an industry product is made of non-leather material that appears to be leather, the fact that the material is not leather, or the general nature of the material as something other than leather, should be disclosed. For example: Not leather; Imitation leather; Simulated leather; Vinyl; Vinyl coated fabric; or Plastic." This helps ease the minds of customers that there is a requirement on the part of the seller to disclose this type of information. This is also especially important because most consumer cannot truly tell the different between either leathers and that may encourage sellers to take advantage of the consumer and charge higher amounts for imitation leather at the consumer's deception. (7) What impact, if any, have the Leather Guides had on the flow of truthful or deceptive information to consumers? The large impact that the Leather Guide may have on the flow of truthfulness should not be underestimated. These provisions not only serve as awareness of the industry standard but they also serve as a good scare tactic on larger industries including the leather producing industries. 10) What changes, if any, should be made to the Leather Guides to reduce the burdens or costs imposed on businesses? How would these changes affect consumer benefits or business costs? No changes should be made to the guide as it stands. This is because it already provides for a cost efficient way to communicate to the customer using labels to properly characterize their products. 11) Do the Leather Guides overlap or conflict with federal, state, or local laws or regulations? Do the Guides overlap or conflict with any international laws or regulations? The Leather Guides do overlap, but however, to my knowledge do not conflict with Federal laws. The overlap is seen in Federal UCC provisions that prohibit the misrepresentation, fraud or mischaracterizations of consumer products from the seller to the buyer. However, it is good to include provisions specifically on leather in the Leather Guide to ensure its application and provide another specific response to this foreseeable issue consumers may have regarding the characterization or mischaracterization on leather products. (12) Have consumer perceptions changed since the Leather Guides were issued and, if so, do these changes warrant revising the Guides? No, consumers are continuously cautious of their purchases and wish to have the sales of their products, including for leather in the Leather Guide, to be regulated and controlled in order to ensure consumer protection.

comment: Re: Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing, Docket No. FTC-2026-1057 I submit this as an individual consumer. I am not affiliated with any company that does personalized pricing, and no one is paying me to file this. I am not defending the conduct in the Commission's examples. Charging more for a hotel room because data suggests someone is traveling to a funeral, or more for milk because a household has children, or more for a security camera because someone was recently robbed, is predatory. I would support the Commission going after all of it, hard. My concern is that this Proposed Statement will not accomplish that, and may make things worse for consumers like me. I have six objections. 1. Disclosure legitimizes the practice instead of stopping it. The remedy proposed is that companies disclose personalized pricing rather than stop it. Applied to the Commission's own examples, that produces an absurd result: a hotel posting "this price is higher because our data indicates you are traveling for a funeral" would apparently comply. Footnote 20 admits the Commission has not decided whether that conduct is unfair even when disclosed. The document describes conduct that outrages people, then offers a remedy that permits it with a notice attached. I do not want a disclosure. I want the practice prohibited where it is clearly exploitative. 2. The disclosure will not inform me, because none of them do. I have never read a cookie banner or a privacy policy, and neither has anyone I know. The Commission proposes that companies disclose "the basis for that personalization and the types of data on which the personalization is based" at the moment a price is shown. In practice that is a dense paragraph I will click past like every other notice, and the company will have met its obligation. That is a compliance checkbox, not consumer protection. 3. What I actually want is an opt-out, and it is not in here. The Commission says the purpose of disclosure is to let consumers "take steps to avoid the higher prices." But the Proposed Statement never requires companies to offer any way to do that. Telling me my price is personalized while giving me no way to turn it off leaves me exactly where I started. I would ask the Commission to require a simple, working opt-out to a standard non-personalized price. That one requirement would do more for consumers than every disclosure in this document combined. 4. The undefined scope threatens discounts I actually use. Nowhere does the Commission define "personalized pricing." The operative phrase is prices that "vary based on their personal data." That covers my grocery loyalty card, emailed coupons, and app-only prices. Those save me money. If businesses cannot tell which practices are covered, the safe response is to stop personalizing altogether, and the first thing to disappear will be the discounts, not the surcharges. Please state explicitly that loyalty and membership pricing, coupons, promotional codes, and randomized price testing are outside the scope. 5. The Commission has not established what consumers actually expect. The deception theory rests on the claim that consumers reasonably expect prices not to vary by person. I do not hold that expectation, having shopped at stores where the shelf tag openly displays a member price and a non-member price. The research cited measures whether people think personalized pricing is fair, which is a different question from whether they expected it. The Commission should test the premise by asking consumers before building enforcement on it. 6. The Commission admits it does not know the effects. The Proposed Statement says the extent of personalized pricing "is not well understood" and its effects "are unclear," and cites research calling the welfare effects "ambiguous and thus a matter of empirical measurement." I take the Commission at its word, and that is my point. That describes something needing study, not a basis for announcing that conduct is likely unlawful. What I am asking for: - Prohibit outright the use of data indicating vulnerability, illness, bereavement, disability, or emergency to raise prices. Do not make it disclosable. Make it illegal. - Require a functioning opt-out to a standard price, not just a notice. - Define personalized pricing, and exclude loyalty pricing, coupons, and promotional discounts so consumers do not lose them. - Conduct a 6(b) study and real consumer-perception research before enforcing. - Resolve the question left open in footnote 20 before this takes effect. I appreciate the Commission taking this issue up. I am asking it to write the narrow, strong rule instead of the broad, weak one. Respectfully submitted, Jesse Shettleroe

comment: Contact Lens Rule Review, 16 CFR Part 315 The Contact Lens Rule is in favor of not only the Optometrist but also the contact wearer. The Contact lens rule is there to show proof of supply and distribution of the correct product, which is considered a medical device. If there was something wrong with the contact, the supplier would be able to track how many people received the product. The Optometrist would be able to then contact his patients if needed. It could also be helpful in guarding the Optometrist against a civil action lawsuit if a patient said they received a wrong or damaged contact lense which may have injured them in anyway. Without this rule in place it might be easy for someone to say they did not receive the right contact lens perscription from their optometrist.

comment: The Federal Trade Commission is doing a great job in the area of information security and privacy. I strongly support your work, and the approach you have taken. I agree with the FTC's focus on "reasonable and appropriate" security and privacy, as that relates to a specific organization. Information security and privacy must be tailored to the organization in question and thus it is often at odds with the rigidity, definitive character, and slow pace of change found in the realm of laws and regulations. If the FTC should further elaborate on what exactly it means by "reasonable and appropriate" and how it goes about determining this conceptual line. That specificity would help organizations justify, and later install and operate the proper information security and privacy controls. There is one conceptual shift which I urge the FTC to adopt and that has to do with the parties that can actually make changes so that "reasonable and appropriate" information security and privacy can be manifested. Many of the consent decrees which the FTC has reached appear to assume that a user organization is fully responsible for, and the party in a position to manifest, a "reasonable and appropriate" level of information security and privacy. In many cases this assumption does not match up with reality. With the exception of the largest and most successful firms, user organizations must use the technological tools that they can buy, rent, lease, or subscribe to. Their "bag of tricks" is thus defined by the marketplace. The vast majority of user organizations are not in a position to invent new tools, technologies, and/or approaches. They can only use what is on the marketplace, and attempt to cobble together some combination of those market offerings, and then hold all that together with some internal infrastructure, like training, policies, and procedures. The offerings in this "bag of tricks" are very limited, and often the firms that make these offerings available do not place a high value on security or privacy. The vendors providing the tools for information security and privacy need to be held liable and culpable for problems related to the information security and privacy impacts of their tools much more often than they are now. To expect things to change because the FTC pursues user organizations rather than the vendors, is assigning blame, liability, and culpability to the organizations that do not have the power, knowledge, or expertise necessary to make changes to the tools used to establish and maintain "reasonable and appropriate" information security and privacy. A much greater focus of the FTC's enforcement activity should thus be on the information systems and network vendors, and whether they have provided the tools which can in fact establish a "reasonable and appropriate" level of information security and privacy. Furthermore, assigning civil liability and criminal culpability to the vendors of tools will help to motivate them to upgrade their tools, so that the user organizations can then, as a result, operate with "reasonable and appropriate" information security and privacy. The burden placed on user organizations these days, for instance to stay on top of all the patches issued by vendors of software, is excessive and inappropriate, and it entails a transfer of legal responsibility for information security and privacy from the vendors to the user organizations. The responsibility should, in large measure, be shifted back to the vendors, because the vendors are often the only parties which are in a position to do anything about the types of tools available, and the embedded security and privacy found in those same tools. - Charles Cresson Wood, Esq., MBA, MSE, CISA, CISSP, CISM, CGEIT Independent Information Security and Privacy Consultant with 40 years of experience in the field

comment: I support the FTC’s proposed enforcement policy statement, but I do not think disclosure alone is enough to address surveillance pricing. When I shop for a product, I expect to see the same price offered to another person shopping for that product at the same time. I find it deeply troubling that a business could use my browsing history, location, purchasing habits, financial circumstances, or other personal information to decide that I am willing, or desperate enough, to pay more. The FTC’s own examples show the potential harm. A person should not be charged more for transportation to a medical facility, food delivery when they cannot leave home, or a hotel room when traveling for a funeral merely because a business has data revealing their urgent circumstances. Simply telling consumers that a price has been personalized does not make the practice fair. Most people have no realistic way to know what information a business has collected, whether that information is accurate, or how to prevent it from being used. Consumers should not have to use a private browser, hide their location, or conceal their identity to receive a fair price. I recognize that ordinary dynamic pricing based on objective market conditions may be legitimate and that individualized discounts may benefit some consumers. But those potential benefits do not justify charging someone more based on a hidden profile of that person’s finances, behavior, vulnerability, or willingness to pay. The FTC states that it is not presently taking a position on whether some personalized-pricing practices may be unfair even when fully disclosed. I urge the FTC to examine that issue through rulemaking. Any rule should distinguish ordinary price changes based on supply and demand from prices tailored to an individual consumer. It should prohibit businesses from charging a person more based on sensitive personal information, an urgent need, a perceived vulnerability, or information purchased from data brokers. Congress should also enact legislation that clearly prohibits abusive surveillance pricing and gives the FTC the authority and enforcement tools needed to protect consumers. The proposed policy statement is a good first step, but it should not be the last. If surveillance pricing is allowed to become standard business practice, it will be much harder to control later. The FTC and Congress should act before that happens.

comment: The Commission's intent is misguided. Price discrimination, although perhaps unpleasant to the ear of some, is a long-recognized economic tool observed in in any robust retail market. Price discrimination is a basic form of personalized pricing that allows sellers to offer discounts to customers who are otherwise less likely to purchase while still maintaining a price above the marginal cost of production. A coupon (whether targeted or made available all), a rebate, even a weekly sale are all forms of price discrimination, often discriminating in favor of the buyer willing to make the extra effort to utilize the discount. The Commission errs when it seeks to restrict the actions of free actors in the market based on what the Commission decides consumers reasonably expect. The long-established norm the Commission must recognize is that sellers may use any legally obtained information to set prices in their best interest, and buyers may and should be encouraged to do the same. The Commission may encourage consumers to take economic classes, but they must not require sellers to teach them at every checkout opportunity. The example provided in section III, in which the Commission indicates a straightforward indication of personalized pricing would be insufficient because does not contain an unspecified amount of information, suggests the Commission intends to apply a standard to online purchases not currently applied to the price discrimination examples given above. The Commission should not shape the future of commerce. Governments do consumers no favors by seeking to restrict prices or commerce in general. The Commission must not seek to prohibit personalized pricing of any sort without highly specific evidence of significant harm that outweighs a benefit to the overall market. The theoretical examples provided do not meet this standard and are generally not examples of consumers being vulnerable to personalized pricing but rather of consumers being vulnerable to a lack of competition. The Commission should encourage removal of barriers to entry in these markets rather than making it more costly and more risky for companies to operate in them.

comment: I am deeply concerned about the inclusion of lootboxes in video gaming. Video games are being designed around "encouraging" players to spend money in order to play the game. Gates are put into place for the express purpose of forcing players to give money to continue to play, or to play on an even playing field. Games are designed to slow a player's progression in the game, or in some cases halt it, until they pay more money. In console and PC games, this is an effort to tie game progression to lootbox purchases ala Electronic Arts "Star Wars Battlefront 2". This type of game design is predatory. For the average gamer, it looks like the purchase price is X, but they cannot tell that the purchase price is some large multiple of X until they get home and the carefully designed dependency on lootboxes to continue to play is instituted. Worse, these products are often played and even marketed to children, who don't understand financial responsibility yet. They are exposed to these hooks and see their friends playing and become subject to ongoing pressure to spend money. Their birthday money, their allowance, instead of going towards something constructive like books, or experiencing games for a single obvious price, gets siphoned off by these companies. Teens and young adults who haven't yet learned financial responsibility are targeted, and exposed to hooks designed to prey upon those who don't yet know they're prone to gambling addiction. So money that could be going towards paying off student loans, or buying their first home, goes into these predatory games. It's key to understand, these games are not fundamentally different from those made 5, 10, or 20 years ago. Video game companies are simply taking the same game designs, and implementing gambling as a gate to progressing through the game, whereas in past games you simply played the game to progress. It's telling that these companies study how to make their products more predatory, using gambling industry terms like "Whales", and hire resources dedicated towards making their products as "Profitable" as possible by maximizing gambling. Or worse, patents like Activision's recent patent which patented a system to encourage players to spend money by first exposing them to a player with some premium item, then offering to sell them the same item, then pairing them against "Easy wins" to make them feel like the expense was validated. Keep in mind, video games are played at home, this is a constant temptation dangled in front of consumers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It's a constant promise of a dopamine hit, a constant promise of "Maybe I'll get something to make me feel better", ready at the push of a virtual button. Bad day at work? Push the button at lunch. Bad day at School? Push the button. Girlfriend broke up with you? Push the button. Etc. It's always accessible, unlike a regulated casino which requires significant effort to go to. In many cases driving for hours to go to another state. But video game "Lootboxes" offer all the benefits of a slot machine, at home, at any time. For decades, video gaming was an interactive entertainment experience, but it's become a interactive slot machine as companies do everything to maximize their profits through exploiting gamers, particularly vulnerable targets many of whom may not even know they are at risk for gambling addiction. This can't be allowed to continue, it is turning a lucrative industry into a exploitive money pit, it is normalizing gambling amongst children, and it is harmful to the long term health of young adults who are dumping money into these products that could be going towards paying debt. Companies are literally designing products with the purpose of draining as much money as possible from customers with no upfront and honest statement for customers to base a sound judgement upon. Because honestly, if Electronic Arts put "It will cost $5,000 dollars to obtain all the players" on FIFA's box, or "It will cost $1,000" dollars to maximize your game in Star Wars Battlefront 2, no one, no parent, would purchase that game. L Let's give them the chance to make that purchase design. Either ban lootboxes or force companies to put the total cost clearly on the description.

comment: Loot boxes function as mini slot machines that allow individuals to use real money to gamble for digital rewards. Much like a slot machine, you hit a button and wait for the brightly colored objects to apear that tell you your reward. Each reward has odds to be won with power or complexity hidden behind lower chances of winning. While some items are purely cosmetic (which could be sold for a flat price anyways), some items make a character more powerful, the game easier, or open up new options in the game with creates a, "Pay to win," experience. It raises the question of how profitable is it to make a game more obtuse to create an environment that drives an individual to buy extra things just to play; i.e. you add extra barriers to a players experience only for the purpose to offer then a reward that removes those barriers (time limits or requirements are easy barriers to add to games). It could be thought of as having to pay a casino extra money to get your second pocket card in hold'em poker to feel like you have gotten the full game. Rewards, extra power, and arbitrary barriers in a game easily drives a, "One more pull," mentality in pursuit of the big ticket reward. Since many games function as live services, payment options are registered when buying the product which can further lower the barrier to buy loot boxes as your credit card/debit card information can be stored and readily available to just click and gamble on demand. While some individuals don't fall prey to these items, much like some people don't play slot machines, there is a demographic of adults and minors that can fall prey to these business practices. With slot machines an individual must be of legal gambling age to play, but loot boxes are in games available to minors. On cell phone games, free to play games online, and packaged in fully priced games, loot boxes are at every person's finger tips regardless of age. All it requires is access to technology. Payment options are needed, but with an increasing digital market place this isn't as difficult as it once was. I personally have had financial information stolen to buy these digital goods. While my financial institutions were helpful and the problem was quickly resolved, it shows the extent that individuals will go to in their goal of pursuing this digital gambling.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, This not a form letter. I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in Springfield, MO. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. You are discussing an FTC rule for a problem that doesn't exist forcing us as doctors to comply with yet more paperwork... WHILE THE FTC DOES NOTHING TO STOP ILLEGAL SALES OF CONTACTS. Putting patients at risk of eye injuries. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: -Merit Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Special Considerations for Small Practices: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) developed the framework for MIPS acknowledging the regulatory burden that health care providers already are facing. Considering that reality, CMS reduced the number of clinicians that are required to participate. CMS supported this effort out of the agencys desire to give physicians more time with their patients, not computers. Additionally, CMS is mindful of the unique challenges that face smaller physician practices and added new bonus points for clinicians caring for patients in those settings. -Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients. -Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA): Currently, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is considering eliminating or modifying the requirement for covered health care providers to make a good faith effort to obtain individuals written acknowledgment of receipt of providers Notice of Privacy Practices. The stated aim of this potential change is to reduce burden and free up resources for covered entities to devote to coordinated care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. Quite frankly this is government being government by instituting regulations that make zero sense for a problem that doesn't exist. Does the FTC really think patients aren't smart enough to know there is a choice out there? I have to have them sign it like I am their teacher? Out of touch policy is what you are discussing. Matthew Scullawl, O.D. Springfield, MO
